Kruse argues genome size reflects how efficient a species' "water battery" is: a slow, low-voltage animal piles up non-coding DNA as ballast against electromagnetic noise, while humans get by with a lean genome because charged water keeps the battery full. Indoor life under screens, he says, makes humans run like the lungfish without its buffer.

sections.heading: Time-stamping
sections.body:
The cell's daily clock is a loop in which the CLOCK and BMAL1 genes switch on the Per and Cry genes, whose proteins return about every 24 hours to switch themselves off. Kruse stresses that this loop also decides *when* proteins get their chemical tags (phosphate, methyl, acetyl and ubiquitin groups). He calls this "time-stamping." The PER2 network in the retina, he adds, is the distal readout: circadian mismatch begins earlier, when magnetism fails at the inner mitochondrial membrane and lipids lose their dielectric order.

He describes the clock's own proteins, Period and Cryptochrome, as semiconductors and "magnetic buffer tanks" built to hold a charge from Earth's field. The whole loop, in his view, is a governor that keeps the spin of ATP synthase in step with the planet's field. Its built-in delays are speed limits set by how thick the cell's water is: in deuterium-heavy "78" water the clock proteins travel more slowly to the nucleus, the cycle stretches toward 25 or 26 hours, and sleep breaks up in the small hours.

Light, in his account, also lets cells keep time with one another. He cites Soviet-era experiments in which fish embryos of unequal ages, set side by side, synchronized through bursts of ultra-weak photons. Indoor living and nnEMF, he says, erase the day–night swings in temperature and field that the clock relies on. Proteins are then tagged at the wrong time, flagged as damaged and scrapped at a heavy cost in ATP and NAD⁺. He calls this costly loss of stored order "Landauer liquidation."

sections.heading: Mass on the base chain
sections.body:
Kruse borrows a Bitcoin analogy. DNA is the "base chain," and daily circadian tagging is a "layer two" that adjusts genes without rewriting the code. Methyl and acetyl tags, and deuterium, add literal mass to that base chain. When deuterium enters the methyl pool used to tag DNA, he says, vibrations slow, enzymes drag and the epigenetic clock stalls. He faults chronobiology for treating the clock as chemical software and missing the planetary "hardware" that powers it.

In his account, guarding the base chain is the clock's original job. Daily timing arose in cyanobacteria about three billion years ago, around the time oxygen first built up, and its deeper task was managing heavy water so deuterium could not contaminate methyl groups. DNA methylation still runs on a daily rhythm so that at night, when the body's deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio is lowest, the cell can swap out methyl groups that have picked up deuterium; the fully heavy form, CD₃, is the worst. The problem can begin before birth: a fetus flooded with deuterium, he says, receives altered methylation that silences genes for fat metabolism and mitochondrial repair.

He also describes a protective brake. FOXO3, a gene common in very long-lived people, can pause cell division. Kruse calls this a "clock dampener" that opens a window for light-driven repair. Under LED light, nnEMF and a weakening field the opposite happens: rushed copying fractures the repeats and a p53 surge pushes cells into permanent retirement.

In practice, Kruse tells people not to rely on epigenetic "Horvath" clocks, saliva telomere tests or supplements that, in his model, read or poke at outputs rather than causes. His rule is to avoid anything that adds "atomic mass" to the base chain. Instead he says to reset the physical environment: barefoot grounding under full sun, in a place with a horizontal magnetic field, and dark nights that let the clock do its overnight clean-up.

articles.title: Information, erasure and the chromosome 2 "safe mode"
articles.summary: Kruse frames ill health as lost information rather than low energy: corrupted proteins and falling voltage are "erased" at a cost in heat, and under enough stress a fuse on chromosome 2 drops the body into a primitive safe mode.
keyPoints: Kruse says the precision of the cell's spin signals matters more than the amount of energy it has.
In his model every misfolded protein or lost millivolt is "erased" at a heat cost, and that heat corrupts more proteins.
He says deuterium is "mass where it does not belong," raising the heat price of every bit the cell or brain processes.
Under extreme stress, he argues, a fuse on chromosome 2 trips and drops tissues back to older, simpler designs.
He reads safe-mode signs as a message to change the environment: whole-spectrum sunlight, grounding, stable fields, less wireless exposure.

sections.body: Kruse argues that ill health is, at root, a loss of information rather than a shortage of energy. Damaged proteins and a falling cell voltage are "erased," and every erasure costs heat. Under extreme stress, he says, a built-in fuse on chromosome 2 trips and drops the body into a primitive "safe mode." In his model this explains why the modern body so often looks as if it is deliberately downgrading itself.

sections.heading: Information matters more than energy
sections.body:
In Kruse's view, the precision of the cell's spin signals matters more than the amount of energy it has, because energy without direction is only heat. Blue light, nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields) and a weakening magnetic field harm cells mainly by turning their data into noise, not by cutting ATP output. Wrong atomic mass in the membrane — his "dopants" — is the same class of error: it forces Landauer erasure and shows up as heteroplasmy, the cell's mixed, incoherent energy state.

He adds that life buys its precision with time rather than energy. Circadian gating, letting each chemical step run only at its set hour of the day, keeps every proton in its place much as a particle accelerator keeps its beam focused. Small, timed breaks in symmetry like this, he says, are what keep DNA far from equilibrium and define life itself.

sections.heading: Erasure and its heat
sections.body:
He builds on physicist Rolf Landauer, who showed in 1961 that erasing one bit of information must release a minimum amount of heat. Kruse treats a well-folded protein as a clean channel through which electrons pass with almost no waste. When the cell's structured water degrades and magnetic pinning is lost, the protein's bandgap (the energy step that lets it act as a semiconductor) narrows, electrons stall and the protein misfolds. It has become, in his words, a "corrupt bit."

The cell's answer is ubiquitin tagging. Enzymes spot the protein's lost native field, mark it with ubiquitin (a small "delete" label), and the proteasome, the cell's shredder, unwinds and cuts it. Kruse calls this Landauer erasure in molecular form.

He applies the same logic to voltage. A cell's resting charge is, for him, its information capacity, so the slide from a healthy −70 millivolts toward a fermenting −15 millivolts counts as information being erased. Each erasure dumps heat, the heat dries out structured water, and drier water corrupts more proteins. The cell is trapped in a failure-and-clean-up loop that bankrupts its ATP and NAD⁺ (its main electron carrier). Summed across a tissue, he says, this heat is what people feel as a flush of warmth.

Man-made fields add to the bill because they are pure information noise. Mitochondria are pushed into the role of Maxwell's demon, the imaginary gatekeeper of physics, forced to sort billions of chaotic signals every second, and each act of sorting costs heat.

He finds support in a 2025 Nature Physics experiment that probed Landauer's principle in ultracold atoms, which he reads as showing that extra inertial mass makes every irreversible step of information processing cost more heat. Extra deuterium (heavy hydrogen) is, in his phrase, "mass where it does not belong," raising the heat cost of every bit erased and every metabolic decision. When glucose is forced into a cell that is already heavy and at its limit, the waste heat, he says, "melts" delicate tissues such as the retina, the kidney's filters and myelin, the insulating sheath around nerves.

sections.heading: Repair before erasure
sections.body:
Kruse says the cell first tries a local repair, which he calls the "ubiquitin–G3P pivot." Ubiquitin brings glucose to the misfolded protein, and the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle there supplies deuterium-poor electrons that let it refold.

In his account ubiquitin flags a deuterium-loaded protein, a "stalled semiconductor," for replacement, and the sugar stored nearby supplies a fast burst of light protons that washes the deuterium off while the new protein folds into place. He calls ubiquitin the "lattice janitor." Fat is his long-game fuel; sugar is the emergency "flash-wash."

The unfolded-protein response, the alarm raised when proteins fold badly, is his "error log." If the deuterium load or field loss is too great, repair gives way to cell death, which he marks as a final red-shifted burst of faint light.

sections.heading: The brain's brake
sections.body:
Kruse applies the same accounting to thought. Every bit the brain processes carries a heat price, and the price climbs as deuterium builds up in spinal fluid and microtubules. He likens it to hanging stray weights on a chain of linked oscillators: instead of ringing cleanly, the chain rings chaotically.

He describes the brain's fluid spaces as the place where that load is measured. Spinal fluid passes from the third ventricle through the narrow cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle in the brainstem. In his model the narrowing speeds the fluid up like a nozzle, so heavier deuterium separates out as it enters the fourth ventricle, much as in a mass spectrometer. Sensors in the floor of that ventricle then read the isotope density. When it runs too high, he says, they signal the hypothalamus to throttle hypocretin, the brain's wakefulness signal, so firing rates drop, the heat price falls and the brain avoids overheating.

sections.heading: The chromosome 2 fuse
sections.body:
Human chromosome 2 formed when two ancestral ape chromosomes fused. A leftover stretch of telomere sequence (chromosome-end cap) remains inside it at the fusion point, and Kruse treats it as a field-sensitive fuse. Under the TRCS model he follows, when a voltage crash threatens to erase the genome, this loop "blows." Triggers he names include cosmic rays and stray light during field loss, poor sleep, very low cholesterol and deuterium-heavy food out of season.

A surge of p53, the genome's guardian protein, then forces what he calls an "atavistic retreat": tissues revert to older, simpler designs, like a satellite powering down to safe mode as it crosses the South Atlantic Anomaly. Nerve, myelin and pigment tissue shrink so the body becomes a "worse antenna" for electromagnetic noise. The cell also stops spending energy on rigid collagen, loosening connective tissue on purpose to buy time, and the diaphragm and the valve at the top of the stomach slip back to a looser template.

The fusion site, he says, sits among four genes that shaped modern humans, which he calls a "quantum blockchain": POMC for melanin, EDAR for sweat glands, GCG for glucagon and gut hormones, and BCL11A, which switches blood from fetal to adult hemoglobin. In the safe-mode surge, he says, blood shifts back toward the fetal form to fuel repair.

sections.heading: Sunlight and the p53 balance
sections.body:
Kruse adds that whole-spectrum sunlight activates p53, which promotes DNA repair. That stops stray chromatin fragments from piling up outside the nucleus, where, he says, they trip the cGAS-STING alarm and the inflammatory signaling of aged cells.

In practice, Kruse reads safe-mode signs as a message to change the environment that caused them, not to suppress them. To keep DNA damage low and p53 working, he points to whole-spectrum sunlight, avoiding toxins, and strong magnetic pinning (living under a stable local field while grounded and sunlit). He counts wireless exposure and stimulant chemistry as added noise that raises the heat price of every bit, so cutting them lowers the erasure bill.

articles.title: Water: the "160 vs 78" battery
articles.summary: Kruse says healthy mitochondrial water is structured, with a dielectric he numbers at 160, and modern stress collapses it to ordinary bulk water at 78; the healthy state is set at conception and held up by potassium, light and a strong field.
keyPoints: Kruse says the water lining the inner mitochondrial membrane is a structured battery with a dielectric of 160, versus 78 for ordinary water.
In his model sunlight builds this layer, a horizontal magnetic field anchors it, and potassium with melanin holds it in place.
He says the main product of respiration is light, ordered water, with ATP more a helper than the fuel.
When water collapses to 78, he argues, electron flow stalls, deuterium gets in, and the brain drops into a cruder mode.
His route back to 160 is environmental: morning sun, grounding, a stable field, potassium, and protecting the parents' environment before conception.

sections.body: This is the hinge of most of Kruse's teaching. He says the water lining the inner mitochondrial membrane is not ordinary water but a structured layer that stores a great deal of electric charge. He describes its state with a single number, a dielectric constant of 160, and says modern stress collapses it to ordinary "bulk" water at 78. Nearly everything that goes wrong in his model passes through this collapse.

sections.heading: What the numbers mean
sections.body:
A dielectric constant measures how much electric charge a substance can hold and how strongly it buffers electric fields. Kruse treats the structured water at the membrane as a battery, or capacitor, with a high value of 160, and ordinary water as a much weaker one at 78.

He ties the number to the fine-structure constant, the figure of about 1/137 that sets how likely an electron is to catch a photon. Structured water, he says, tightens that grip and deuterium (heavy hydrogen) loosens it. That is why he calls the dielectric constant, rather than genes or proteins, the "transformer of life," and counts this link, which joined his work to Gilbert Ling's, as the most important part of what he teaches.

He identifies the structured state with Gerald Pollack's exclusion-zone (EZ) water, an ordered layer that forms against surfaces and pushes dissolved particles out. In his model dawn UV-A and near-infrared light build this layer, and a horizontal magnetic field anchors it so it does not discharge. In his division of labor ultraviolet supplies the "voltage," lifting electrons into long-lived coherent states, while infrared supplies the "volume," spacing the water's tiny electric poles so they vibrate together.

sections.heading: Potassium and melanin
sections.body:
Following Ling, Kruse says potassium anchors this "water table," with melanin as its partner; he calls the two "brothers." Potassium holds its own shell of water more loosely than sodium does, so it can sit right against proteins and lock nearby water into stacked, polarized layers, lifting the value from about 78 toward 160. Melanin amplifies the effect. Disturbed potassium handling is therefore, in his view, the first sign of breakdown. In his account the exclusion zone also does the sorting. A healthy, potassium-held EZ physically pushes deuterium out into the bulk "waste stream." Strip the potassium and the EZ collapses, deuterium floods the cell's "inner sea" and the fluid thickens. The same ionic stress, he says, switches off MITF, the master switch of melanin-making, so the person loses melanin as well as water.

In his summary, melanin is the hardware, potassium the stabilizer and structured water the medium. A UV-A photon striking melanin, he says, launches a ripple through potassium-held water that lets millions of reactions coordinate at wave speed; without potassium, signaling falls back to slow chemical diffusion. Sodium has a separate job: it raises the dielectric of blood and spinal fluid, and without enough, these fluids thicken like ketchup.

sections.heading: Water as the main product
sections.body:
Kruse turns the textbook account of respiration around. Its main product, he says, is not ATP but water: the electron chain exists to "distill" the mitochondrion's interior, and cytochrome c oxidase is a forge for ordered, deuterium-poor metabolic water, which he equates with Pollack's "fourth phase." ATP, in this picture, is a by-product that acts more like a helper keeping the water ordered than like the fuel itself. The same water gives the membrane enough dielectric strength to hold its field of about 30 million volts per meter.

Burning fat, he adds, yields light, high-dielectric water that protects DNA's faint photon signals, while stalled mitochondria make heavier water.

sections.heading: Water's two spin forms
sections.body: Kruse also explains the two states through spin. Ordinary water is a fixed 3-to-1 mix of ortho-water, whose hydrogen nuclei spin in step, and para-water, whose spins cancel. He calls ortho-water the "grease": magnetic, sticky and viscous, the 78 state where deuterium builds up. Para-water packs into the ordered 160 layer that lets protons pass without friction; he calls it the "superconductor." When the body holds on to carbon dioxide and tissue pH sits around 6.8–7.1, he says, water shifts toward the para form and hemoglobin releases oxygen gently.

sections.heading: What the collapse does
sections.body:
When water falls from 160 to 78, Kruse says electron and proton transfer slow about 1.43-fold. That pushes the respiratory chain into "Marcus inversion," his name for the stalled state in which pushing harder moves fewer electrons. Stalled electrons release heat, which melts more structure; in a full meltdown the membrane's charge swings positive and the cell leaks faint light. At 160, he adds, the water acts as a mass filter that keeps deuterium away from DNA; at 78 heavy isotopes get in.

The brain feels the collapse directly. Kruse describes microtubules, the fine tubes of the cell's skeleton, as waveguides for signals. In ordinary 78 water, he says, their quantum states would scramble within trillionths of a second, while potassium- and melanin-structured 160 water creates a "quiet zone." As the dielectric slides toward 78, the brain drops into a cruder operating mode and thinking narrows into survival-driven reaction.

He lists everyday causes of the collapse. Isolated blue light from screens and LEDs lacks the red and infrared needed to rebuild structure. nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields) and loss of magnetic pinning do similar harm. So, he says, do petroleum and silicone lotions on skin after a warm shower, and chlorinated pools, which support far less exclusion-zone water than saltwater pools. Sound can push the other way: kind speech and steady chanting, in his account, arrange the body's water into ordered domains.

sections.heading: Set at conception
sections.body: Kruse says the egg cell is held at 160 as a protected core. Before fertilization it keeps Complex I, the entry point of the electron chain, switched off and uses melanin to keep deuterium out. Fertilization switches Complex I on, and from then on the environment begins writing the body's traits. If the mother lives under a weakening field or amid heavy nnEMF, her deuterium-sorting fails, deuterium settles in the embryo's brain ventricles and cristae, and its water slides toward 78.

sections.heading: Spirals and the heart
sections.body: Kruse says spirals order water; his rule of thumb is "three turns sense, seven turns resonate." In his model the heart's helical chambers work as a centrifuge, flinging deuterium outward so blood serves as a reservoir while the inside of cells stays light. That gradient creates a standing suction that lets the vagus nerve draw deuterium from the brain and spinal cord toward the gut; man-made light, he says, reverses it. In practice, Kruse's route back to 160 is environmental. He points to morning sun (UV-A plus infrared), grounding and magnetic pinning (living under a stable local field while grounded and sunlit), together with restoring potassium. He also suggests drinking water from deep volcanic fissures ("primary water"), skipping petroleum or silicone lotions after showering, choosing saltwater over chlorinated pools, and using voice and chanting to help order the body's water. For anyone planning a family, he says the parents' light and field environment before conception matters as much as their own condition.

terms: Three turns sense, seven turns resonate

articles.title: Oxygen's spin and the paramagnetic gate
articles.summary: In his model Earth's field keeps oxygen in its safe triplet state at the end of the electron chain, and a weakening field flips it to reactive singlet oxygen, leaving cells starved even when blood oxygen looks normal.
keyPoints: Kruse says Earth's magnetic field keeps oxygen in its calm triplet form, where cells can use it safely.
In his model a weakening field, man-made fields, blue light and deuterium flip oxygen into reactive singlet oxygen that burns tissue.
He reads a 540-million-year match between oxygen levels and field strength as proof the planet's core is the master and oxygen the servant.
He argues blood can be full of oxygen while mitochondria get none, so a normal oximeter reading proves little.
His answer is "pin first": fix the magnetic and wireless environment, then add morning light, then change exercise or diet.

sections.body: Oxygen can exist in two spin states, and Kruse makes the difference between them a master switch for health. In his model Earth's magnetic field keeps oxygen in its calm "triplet" form where cells use it. A weakening field, or man-made fields and light, flips it into reactive "singlet" oxygen that burns tissue.

sections.heading: Why ordinary oxygen is safe
sections.body:
The oxygen we breathe is triplet oxygen: its two outer electrons spin in the same direction. That makes it paramagnetic (weakly drawn to a magnet). Kruse stresses that the molecules of our tissues have paired, opposite spins, so oxygen cannot react with them directly without breaking the rule that spin is conserved. This "spin barrier," he says, is what makes air-breathing life possible. Oxygen only reacts when a precise catalyst realigns the spins, which is exactly what the cell's electron chain does.

Singlet oxygen is the same molecule with its spins paired. In his account it is diamagnetic (weakly pushed away by a magnet), does no useful work and reacts violently.

sections.heading: The paramagnetic gate
sections.body: At the end of the electron chain sits cytochrome c oxidase, or Complex IV. Kruse calls its copper–iron center a "paramagnetic gate," a checkpoint that matches incoming electrons to oxygen's spin with the help of Earth's field. When the gate works, spin-aligned electrons tunnel in smoothly, oxygen becomes deuterium-depleted water (water low in heavy hydrogen), and the membrane holds about −70 millivolts. He cites a 2025 study by Beutner and colleagues as support for the field's role. Isolated mitochondria placed in a weak static magnetic field, far weaker than a fridge magnet, raised their oxygen use by about 40% while making fewer damaging oxygen by-products, but only within a narrow sweet spot. He reads this as the field keeping electron spins parallel. Melanin, DHA and cholesterol, he says, help a strong field hold oxygen's spins in place, and grounding supplies free electrons that do the same.

sections.heading: The planet's oxygen and its field
sections.body:
Kruse reads a 2025 Science Advances paper by Kuang and colleagues, which tied Earth's oxygen levels to the strength of its magnetic dipole over 540 million years, as proof that the planet's core is the master and oxygen the servant. The two rose together, strongest with no time lag at all. In his telling, the field locked oxygen in its triplet state and made the Cambrian explosion of complex animals possible.

He takes the story further than the paper. As Earth's inner core hardened, he says, it gave the dynamo enough torque to re-anchor its field lines, and the field then sorted deuterium out of the oceans and air, so oxygen rose because of the field and not simply because plants multiplied. Mammals, in his account, need this lock most. With a constant body temperature and a very high-voltage inner membrane, they required the tightest coupling to the field. He calls them "high-flux" creatures, and notes that the earliest ones lived in burrows, in constant contact with the ground and so, in his phrase, wired straight to the dynamo.

sections.heading: When the gate fails
sections.body:
Because magnetism controls spin, Kruse argues, a weakening core field is now pushing oxygen toward singlet in many zip codes and "liquidating" tissue. nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields), isolated blue light and deuterium do the same locally; the heavier bond deuterium forms with oxygen, he says, resists normal triplet chemistry. Once oxygen flips, it attacks cardiolipin (the membrane's insulating fat), mitochondrial DNA and iron–sulfur clusters. Voltage falls toward −15 millivolts and production of clean water stops.

He dates the present slide to 1859, the year of the great Carrington solar storm. A falling field, in his account, lowers the pull that draws electrons toward oxygen, so melanin breaks back down into dopamine and heavy water loads the tissues. He spells out how man-made fields do their local damage. In a healthy field, radical pairs formed during oxygen metabolism swing between singlet and triplet states, and that swing times the reactions. At Complexes I–III the pair he names is flavin semiquinone with superoxide — the human checkpoint that birds run in the eye. Radio-frequency fields, he says, break the hyperfine coupling (the link between an electron's spin and nearby nuclei) and freeze the pairs in the wrong state. The reactive oxygen that results slips past the cell's own clean-up enzymes and gives off incoherent faint light.

sections.heading: Oxygen everywhere, none in the engine
sections.body:
Kruse says the more nnEMF and blue light surround a person, the more the Bohr effect takes over; this is hemoglobin's habit of releasing oxygen as tissue turns acidic. Without the sun's UV-A and infrared, the structured water at the membrane collapses, protons flood the cell and the tissue turns acidic. Hemoglobin dumps its oxygen, but with the water's charge-holding capacity lowered the oxygen cannot tunnel into the mitochondria. He sums it up as oxygen everywhere and none in the engine.

For the same reason he calls a normal 99% pulse-oximeter reading a trap. Without nitric oxide and carbon dioxide to loosen it, he says, oxygen stays bound to hemoglobin and cannot fall into cells through thickened, deuterium-heavy water. A person can be suffocating amid plenty, with the brain slipping into local fermentation.

Red light helps cytochrome c oxidase make water and UV builds melanin, he says, but only in someone who is grounded. Without sunlight and grounding, oxygen at the end of the chain becomes toxic and the brain turns breathing down. Oxygen, in his account, has a U-shaped dose curve, harmful at both too little and too much, a sensitivity he traces to the Great Oxidation Event, when oxygen first flooded Earth's air some 2.4 billion years ago.

sections.heading: What singlet oxygen destroys
sections.body:
Kruse lists the damage. Collagen needs triplet oxygen for the enzyme that builds hydroxyproline, one of its key amino acids. When oxygen goes singlet, he says, collagen production stalls and tissues loosen. Melanin, tooth enamel and fats burn, and heme proteins, including the liver's CYP enzymes and hormone machinery, are lost. He calls singlet oxygen a "thermal hot potato" that cooks retina, skin, hair and mitochondria.

It also corrupts the cell's light. In Kruse's model triplet oxygen releases energy quietly, with very little stray light. Singlet oxygen sets off chain reactions in fats whose decay throws out disordered bursts of faint light, and that noise drowns the coherent UV signals he says guide cell division. Ultra-weak photon emissions, he adds, are coherent when the spins that made them are parallel and incoherent when they are not — so the mitochondrion must keep spins parallel for tissue coherence. Not every oxygen by-product is bad, though: brief superoxide pulses act as healthy signals, like Morse code between the nucleus and mitochondria.

In practice, Kruse's answer is the "pin first" order: fix your magnetic and wireless environment first, add morning light second, and change exercise or diet only after that. He also warns that moving to a different magnetic field flips oxygen at once and costs the vagus nerve its ability to clear deuterium, so a move should be deliberate. To stand in for a weakening field, he suggests a north-seeking static magnetic pad, pure DHA and raw morning UV-A. Extra oxygen under pressure, he warns, does nothing for spin if the person is already living singlet — magnetic flux does. He does not treat a normal oxygen reading as proof that cells are getting what they need.

articles.title: Marcus inversion and the Warburg shift
articles.summary: Kruse's core failure state: electron transfer stalls in Marcus's "inverted region," and cells retreat to fermentation as a protective emergency mode.
keyPoints: Kruse says electron transfer can stall in Marcus's "inverted region," where pushing harder moves fewer electrons, so a stuck chain cannot be forced.
In his model that physics event is what biochemists rename as heteroplasmy, electrical resistance or reverse electron transport.
He says lost magnetic ground plus linoleic-heavy cardiolipin stretches the complexes apart and tips the chain into that region.
He reads the Warburg shift to sugar fermentation as an adiabatic retreat that shields DNA when the chain has already inverted.
The way out, he says, is removing what pushed the cell in — not forcing more oxygen or red light through the jam.

sections.body: Kruse's central picture of how cells fail comes from chemistry. Electron transfer, he argues, can stall in a state where pushing harder makes things worse, the "inverted region" described by Rudolph Marcus. Cells caught there retreat to fermentation as an emergency mode. In his model this one sequence underlies much of what goes wrong in modern bodies, including faster aging.

sections.heading: The inverted region
sections.body:
Marcus's theory, which won him the 1992 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, describes how fast an electron jumps from one molecule to another. Up to a point, a bigger driving force (the energy pushing the electron) makes the jump faster. Past a peak, set by the energy the surroundings must spend rearranging themselves, the rate falls again. That falling side is the inverted region. Kruse likens it to an electronic tunnel diode, where raising the voltage lowers the current. That is why, he says, a stuck chain cannot be fixed by pushing harder.

He places health at the top of this curve, matched with Martin Picard's "just-right" zone of energy resistance. Distance matters too: in his model, pushing the respiratory complexes just one ångström (a ten-billionth of a meter) farther apart cuts tunneling about tenfold. When electrons back up on Complexes I–III, biochemistry papers call the jam heteroplasmy, electrical resistance or reverse electron transport; Kruse insists those are synonyms for one physics event, a Marcus inversion.

sections.heading: What pushes cells there
sections.body:
Kruse names field loss, nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields), blue light and calcium overload as the main pushes. When the mitochondrial matrix loses its magnetic ground, he adds, tissue linoleic acid rises and cardiolipin — the membrane's magnetic fat that holds Complex I–IV at the right spacing — loads with polyunsaturated chains; the geometry stretches, and inversion becomes more likely. Deuterium (heavy hydrogen) adds its own: with twice hydrogen's mass, he says, its spin precesses (wobbles) out of step with the chain's spin filter, causing backscatter and friction.

A weaker magnetic field also widens the circle an electron traces as it moves (its Larmor radius). Once that path exceeds the 14-ångström limit he credits to Dutton, tunneling collapses and the whole chain stops. He calls this a "cyanide-like" lock that is physical rather than chemical. Living or sleeping near smart meters, Wi-Fi routers or 5G arrays with an already damaged system, he says, can act like a small field collapse inside the tissue.

Borrowing from cryptocurrency, he calls modern technology a "51% attack" on the inner membrane, the way a network falls to whoever controls most of its computing power. Once nnEMF, processed food and blue light outweigh the cell's ability to dump deuterium, they take control and force it into a defensive danger mode and fermentation. Life then runs, in his words, backward in time: an ancestral survival program operating inside the newest mammalian anatomy.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.body: Stalled electrons spill their energy as singlet oxygen (the reactive form of oxygen) and heat. In Kruse's account the heat melts the structured water at the membrane from its healthy "160" state to ordinary "78" water, which slows electrons further. The membrane's charge then swings toward positive, faint light leaks out, and the 71-terahertz timing signal to the nucleus goes quiet. He applies the same picture to the brain: in sleep-deprived, ungrounded, screen-lit people, he says, navigation cells "smear" positional signals like a telegraph on an overloaded wire.

sections.heading: A circuit breaker, not just a fault
sections.body:
Kruse increasingly frames the inverted region as protection. On a planet whose field varies, he says, nature uses it as a built-in circuit breaker, his "topological insurance." When the field sags or technology warps the cristae, entering the inverted region clamps electron flow before a runaway thermal meltdown.

He describes a milder breaker that adults use under deuterium stress, modeled on the egg cell, which keeps Complex I, the chain's main entry point, switched off entirely. A stressed adult copies it partway through the glycerol-3-phosphate shunt, which feeds electrons in further down the chain and bypasses a Complex I jammed by deuterium. This keeps the cell's water from collapsing toward 78 but costs membrane voltage, which he says shows up as mental haze. Biology, in his phrase, would rather be "slow and foggy" than "fast and dead," and he urges people to lean on this route during the present field decline rather than slide into lattice lock, his term for water fully stiffened by deuterium.

He sees the same breaker at work in the whole body during sleep. A brainstem loaded with deuterium has, in his account, already dropped into fermentation, and oxygen at full pressure would arc across its cristae, so the brain turns down its drive to breathe and lets oxygen saturation dip. The brain, he says, would rather run short of oxygen and stay alive than be fully oxygenated and "charred."

A place or a season can hold someone there, which he calls a "Marcus inversion well," and body fat and seasonal timing can soften its walls. For the same reason, he says, no diet can fix the problem. Food supplies fuel, not the magnetic reference that shapes the cristae. Extra fuel jams an inverted chain further, and a prolonged "keto flu" signals a light-and-field problem, not a macronutrient one.

sections.heading: The Warburg shift and the biological SCRAM
sections.body:
Otto Warburg observed cells fermenting sugar even when oxygen is present. Kruse treats this as an ancient survival mode. As the field falls, cells deliberately lower their voltage and retreat to glycolysis (sugar fermentation) to shield their DNA, making deuterium-depleted water in the cell fluid and cooling themselves. Building on Warburg, he says such cells fall from about −70 millivolts to −15 to −30 millivolts. A gate in the inner membrane then lets deuterium-rich water flood the core of the mitochondrion and slow the ATP synthase motor. So, for Kruse, the Warburg question is about spin, not chemistry.

Missing morning sunlight is enough, he says, to start the slide. Without it mitochondria step down from the Krebs cycle (their main fuel-burning loop) to sugar fermentation even with oxygen present, and the iron in heme proteins flips from its ferrous to its ferric form, a "paramagnetic flip" that disrupts energy production.

Speed, not volume, explains the turn to sugar in his account. Glucose is burned quickly but yields less metabolic water than burning fat, so a cell damaged by deuterium, having lost its fat-burning machinery, uses glucose for a fast "flash-wash" out of trouble. Normally, he adds, light runs two clean-up programs: UV drives the suicide of damaged cells and near-infrared drives their self-recycling. When both fail, a damaged cell can neither repair nor die, and fermentation is what remains.

He calls the retreat adiabatic: once inversion has begun, the cell liquidates ordered structure (his Landauer liquidation) and falls into the Warburg shift rather than burn DNA with a free-radical storm. Field loss also triggers what he calls a "biological SCRAM," the nuclear-reactor term for an emergency shutdown.

In practice, Kruse says the way out is to remove what pushed the cell in rather than force more fuel, oxygen or single-band red light through the jam: restore morning sunlight with its UV brakes, grounding and a stable local field, and keep wireless transmitters away from sleep. No diet alone fixes it. Forcing extra oxygen or spinning ATP synthase harder across inverted Complexes I–III, he says, "cooks" the engine.

articles.title: Pin first: magnetism, gravity and "spaceflight sickness without the rocket"
articles.summary: Kruse ranks magnetism ahead of light and water and says modern indoor life behaves like spaceflight, so magnetic pinning must come before changes to diet or exercise.
keyPoints: Kruse ranks magnetism first, then light, then water, and says all three must be tuned together.
In his model an unpinned body cannot use sunlight well, because its water and NAD⁺ become loaded with deuterium.
He argues modern life recreates orbit on the ground, leaving the same gene locks that spaceflight leaves on astronauts.
Pinning works at two scales, he says: Earth's core field and the local rock beneath you.
His order is to leave the wireless soup and ground first, add morning light second, and change exercise or diet only third.

sections.body: "Pinned" is Kruse's word for living under a stable, mostly horizontal local magnetic field, ideally over volcanic rock such as basalt, while grounded and sunlit. He now ranks magnetism first, then light, then water, and says all three are needed together. Because he sees much of modern ill health as a form of spaceflight sickness, his rule is to pin first and only then change diet or exercise.

sections.heading: Why magnetism comes first
sections.body:
In Kruse's model magnetism is the "father" of the body's direct current, because it controls the spin of electrons and so the state of oxygen. Sunlight, he says, does little for a person without Earth's magnetic flux around them. Once oxygen has flipped to its reactive singlet form and NAD⁺ (the cell's main electron carrier) is loaded with deuterium, a state he calls "NADD+," metabolism goes blind to light. When the field is highly dynamic, he ranks magnetism ahead of light — even grounding on an agonic line ahead of sunrise — because light's rules change with the field. Birds, he adds, sense the field in the eye; mammals, bound to the ground, sense it at Complexes I–III.

That creates a catch-22, he says. Without pinning, body water becomes deuterated and the cell can no longer use the very sunlight that would rescue it. He calls this "near-infrared deficiency": an unpinned person can be short of usable red and infrared light even while lying naked in the sun.

He sums up the roles this way: the field tells life *why* to move, morning light tells it *when*, and barefoot grounding near an agonic line (where compass north equals true north) tells it *where*.

He also ties the magnetic leg to three spinning flows inside the body: spinal fluid, blood and the ATP synthase motor. Strong sunlight drives all three, and deuterium-poor water made by cytochrome c oxidase keeps them running smoothly, which is why he insists that light, water and magnetism be tuned together and never one at a time.

sections.heading: Gravity and the other forces
sections.body:
Kruse adds gravity to the picture. He cites a Nature Communications paper, "Gravitational and mechanical forces shape mitochondrial translation," which found that leaving Earth's gravity lowers mitochondrial gene activity with no chemical change. In his reading, gravity is a physical press that keeps the cristae folded and the iron–sulfur clusters close enough for electrons to tunnel between them. In microgravity the press is released, the gaps widen and electrons back up.

He treats gravity, electromagnetism and the weak force as separate anchors that cannot stand in for one another. Gravity is the press, electromagnetism the governor of spin and tunneling, and the weak force the source of life's one-handed (chiral) molecules. The spine has a part in this. The notochord, the rod that forms the embryo's first axis, is in his model the nervous system's "plumb line," held true by gravity and Earth's field. The thalamus, he says, fixes its own position against that axis to keep its 40 Hz timing rhythm; in orbit the axis floats and the thalamus "overclocks" trying to resync. Walking on two small feet shrank our contact with the earth, leaving humans needing to make some of their own "vibrational ground." Singing, laughing and chanting, he says, are the cables that connect head to feet and keep that 40 Hz clock running.

sections.heading: Spaceflight sickness without the rocket
sections.body:
He reads NASA's Twins Study and long space-station missions as showing that spaceflight leaves chemical locks on DNA. These silence the genes for the entry and exit gates of the electron chain (NDUFS1, SDHA and COX4I1) for more than 14 weeks after return, which he calls a "14-week epigenetic lockout."

Kruse argues that modern life recreates orbit on the ground. Insulation from the earth, high-rise living, frequent flying and dense wireless exposure (wireless "soup," which he calls a "hyper-local magnetic excursion") strip away the planet's anchors. The result is "spaceflight sickness without the rocket." People in this state carry the same gene locks, he says, so pushing them into Zone 2 or high-intensity training drives electrons into a blocked chain, making singlet oxygen and damaging the membrane. Supplement stacks given to such a cell, in his phrase, "feed the fire."

In his model the brain shows the damage first. It is about 2% of body mass yet takes 15–20% of the heart's output, and its spinal fluid is pushed mainly by the heart's pulse. When the planet's anchor weakens, he says, the heart's spiral flow loses coherence and the brain develops, here on Earth, the picture astronauts get in orbit: enlarged fluid spaces, swollen sheaths around the optic nerves and flattened eyeballs.

He explains this through what he calls the body's "deuterium centrifuge." On Earth, gravity and the heart's pressure help pull heavy water down and out, and the brain's sleep-time cleaning current is partly gravity-assisted, washing heavy isotopes toward the vagus nerve and on to the gut. In microgravity the centrifuge stops: fluid shifts toward the head, the fourth ventricle stagnates, and heavy water pools in the ventricle floor and the optic nerve sheaths. On the ground he finds the same pieces: a sedentary life is microgravity for the lymphatic system, and nnEMF and blue light act on melanin as cosmic radiation does.

sections.heading: Two scales of pinning
sections.body:
Pinning works at two scales in Kruse's model: the global field from Earth's core (the geodynamo) and the local field of the ground beneath you. While the core field was steady, local rock hardly mattered. As it weakens, local conditions decide who stays well. Everyone's pinning is individual, he says, so the first step is to pin where you already live and to consider moving only if that proves impossible.

Local rock can also work against the global field. Where volcanic rock froze with reversed magnetism, as he describes at Kilauea in Hawaii, the two fields cancel and the field felt by the body approaches zero. The restoring pull on the body's protons then vanishes. In his words the magnetic pin is pulled, which is why living beside a volcano is no guarantee of being pinned.

He offers the Hunza people of the Karakoram as a model of place over plate: high-altitude sun, cold, quartz-rich ground and glacial meltwater matter more than their plate. He calls accepting that food can't fix a field problem "Personal Quantum Solvency," and taking charge of your own magnetic environment "magnetic sovereignty" — more important, in his telling, than the food you eat or the oxygen you breathe, because melanin, collagen and cholesterol only order electron spins when the body is pinned.

In practice, Kruse's "pin first" order runs in three steps. First, leave the wireless soup, ground strictly and sleep in a bedroom free of man-made fields — and when recovering from a hard hit, put the phone down if someone else can handle calls. Second, rebuild structured water with morning solar infrared in a zip code whose field and sun are still strong. Only third, change exercise or diet toward about −70 millivolts; peptides, packaged fillers and supplement stacks, he warns, dig deeper while that voltage is down. He also advises flying less — jet lag as a short magnetic excursion — staying on your feet, daily singing or chanting as a home-made ground, and checking local rock as well as the global field.

articles.title: Lattice lock
articles.summary: His name for the end state of water collapse: body water stiffens and loads with deuterium, the energy motor jams, and the cell can no longer make its own light water or use sunlight; it can build slowly or strike suddenly.
keyPoints: Kruse calls the end point of water collapse "lattice lock": body water stiffens with deuterium, ATP synthase jams and sunlight can no longer be used.
In his model the lock forms when the body's deuterium exhaust, the bicarbonate loop and vagal drain, is welded shut by modern light and fields.
He frames it as a race between deuterium strikes and the body's repair time, which a weakening field makes harder to win.
He traces the lock through the brainstem, spine, fascia and skin, where stiff water replaces liquid crystal.
His release routines pair carbonated and deuterium-depleted water, grounding at sunrise, vibration, chewing, and heart-rate variability tracking.

sections.body: "Lattice lock" is Kruse's term for the end point of the water collapse at the heart of his model. Body water stiffens and fills with deuterium (heavy hydrogen), ATP synthase (the cell's energy motor) jams, and the cell can no longer make its own deuterium-poor water or use sunlight. He uses it to connect changes as different as stiff fascia, a fading heart rhythm and premature aging.

sections.heading: What locks
sections.body:
Deuterium is hydrogen with an extra neutron, about twice as heavy. Kruse says a single deuterium atom stiffens roughly 96 surrounding water molecules. Heavy deuterons also deform the proton channels of ATP synthase, slowing the motor from its normal 9,000 revolutions per minute toward a stop. ATP output and voltage fall, singlet oxygen (the reactive form) rises, and the cell turns pseudohypoxic: it behaves as if starved of oxygen even though oxygen is present.

At root, he defines the lock through spin. Earth's field normally flips electron spins inside radical pairs so oxygen can reach its working triplet form. If that flip fails, oxygen stays singlet, a "hot potato" of heat rather than a signal. Deuterium is the main scrambler: its nucleus has a spin of 1 rather than hydrogen's ½, so a single atom in the lattice confuses the cell's internal compass and traps it in the singlet, fermenting state.

In his account the membrane's own charge normally keeps deuterium out of the mitochondrion. Once NAD⁺ (the main electron carrier) becomes deuterium-loaded "NADD+" and singlet replaces triplet oxygen, that charge falls, less clean water is made, and the lock tightens.

Muscle, in his account the body's second-largest water store, is a backup sink where deuterium settles when the exhaust backs up. He reads muscle shrinking under this load as a safety governor, and calls the lock a kind of hibernation that shields a system its surroundings can no longer support.

sections.heading: How it develops
sections.body:
Kruse describes the usual path in an unpinned, indoor, wireless-soaked person. Without solar near-infrared, which he calls a "photonic purge," nitric oxide stays stuck on cytochrome c oxidase, electrons back up and oxygen flips to singlet. The water then loses its liquid-crystal order and the protein tracks that let the cell decode light are destroyed, so even full sun can't be read.

He explains it with a mechanic's picture. The bicarbonate loop and the vagus nerve's drainage are the body's exhaust pipe. nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields) and missing UV and infrared light weld that pipe shut, and grounding in a place without a magnetic pull lets back-pressure build. However good the fuel, meaning food, the engine eventually fails. The "carbon buildup" is deuterium silt collecting in the brain, the inner ear and the gut.

Diet adds to the load: he names high-fructose corn syrup, tropical fruit in a northern winter and deuterium-rich drinking water. A person can be grounded and tanned on the outside, he warns, and still be locked inside.

Lattice lock usually builds over years, but Kruse says it can strike at once in someone already loaded, when exercise or an immune surge suddenly asks the membrane to move electrons and protons faster than a stiffened lattice can. The system then arcs like an overloaded insulator.

sections.heading: A race against the clock
sections.body:
Kruse also frames the lock as a timing problem. He borrows T2 from MRI physics: how long the body's internal compass holds its phase before noise scrambles it. He sets it against how often a deuterium atom strikes, which he calls a "speed bump." On ordinary water at about 155 parts per million (ppm) he puts a strike every 4.3 seconds against a T2 of about 6 seconds, so the next hit lands before the last one is cleared and the cell's coherent signal leaks away as heat and faint light.

A weakening field makes it worse, stretching T2 past 7 seconds; this is why he expects lattice lock to become common as the decline goes on. At 92.5 ppm, strikes come only every 7.2 seconds, which is why he calls 92.5 ppm his minimum effective dose. Hypertonic 3% salt and grounding add torque and pull T2 back to 5–6 seconds. Win back a buffer of a second or two, he says, and the signal re-pins. In his phrase, buying low-deuterium water is buying "coherence time."

sections.heading: Brainstem and spine
sections.body:
Kruse says the body normally filters deuterium at the floor of the fourth ventricle, a fluid space in the brainstem. When a weak field or heavy wireless exposure makes that filter fail, heavy water backs up in his "sphenoid Venturi," the drain point behind the nose, and blocks the flow of spinal fluid and the vagus nerve's drainage. Chewing, he says, keeps this region moving, since every bite sends a small piezoelectric pulse through the skull base.

He gives the spinal discs a job too. Their jelly-like cores are remnants of the notochord, the embryo's first axis, and in his model they are grounding sinks at the bottom of an exhaust line running down from the brain. Standing barefoot on the earth completes the circuit, so deuterium-heavy water drawn out of the brain during sleep can discharge downward.

sections.heading: Connective tissue and skin
sections.body:
Fascia that looks "dry," Kruse says, has not lost its water; its water has changed from a 160 liquid crystal to a stiff, deuterium-heavy 78 gel. Deuterium's stiffer bonds lock hyaluronic acid, the slippery gel between tissue layers, so layers grind instead of glide, and in joints heavy fluid works like sand in the gears.

In the skin, Kruse says, the first strong spring sun flushes out winter's dammed-up deuterium. With the vagal drain clogged, deuterium collects in covered skin, cannot shed UV energy quickly, and the energy builds into heat and itching; summer infrared then rebuilds structured water. Aging overall, he concludes, is lost synchrony between mitochondria and the environment rather than simple wear.

sections.heading: Reading the lock
sections.body:
Kruse uses heart-rate variability (HRV, the beat-to-beat variation in heart timing) as the readout. Rigid, flat HRV signals complete lock; flexible HRV, especially in deep sleep, is his gauge of progress. His warning signs run from a constantly blocked nose, to fatigue and memory lapses, to low HRV. A lost sun-sneeze reflex, or trouble tolerating carbonated water, shows how deep the lock goes.

In practice, Kruse pairs lattice lock with release routines. The Volcano Protocol combines carbonated water with deuterium-depleted water to build a CO₂–bicarbonate loop that draws deuterium out, adds a strong water jet and a 40 Hz tuning fork on the back to shake deuterium loose from the spine, and grounding at sunrise in a magnetically pinned place. He adds hypnosis as a "de-frag" session and thorough chewing. He says to build sun tolerance through the season rather than hide from it, and puts clearing the exhaust ahead of hard training. In a weakening field he treats 92.5 ppm deuterium-depleted water as the floor, paired with 3% salt and grounding. Throughout, he tracks HRV in deep sleep, and he says no one can honestly promise a timeline.

articles.title: The "Human GPS": the skull's three axes
articles.summary: Kruse maps the head and trunk as a three-axis "Human GPS": the sphenoid bone as the clock-setting switchboard, the notochord line from skull base to sacrum as the drain, and the heart's twist as the spin, all tuned by light, 40 Hz vibration and a faint timing signal from space.
keyPoints: Kruse describes a "Human GPS" built into the skeleton, with three axes: the sphenoid clock, the notochord drain line and the heart's twist.
In his model the sphenoid acts as a "symmetry selector," choosing light-based physics under sunlight and heavy, deuterium-loaded physics under man-made light and fields.
He says the human aqueduct's twist spins spinal fluid into a "super-fractionator" that flings heavy hydrogen out, which he links to becoming human.
All three axes, he argues, keep time to a faint hydrogen signal from space that the power grid and 5G now drown out.
His advice follows the axes: sunrise light, 40 Hz vibration, chewing, DHA and cholesterol from food, staying upright and grounding.

sections.body: Kruse describes a navigation system built into the human skeleton, which he calls the "Human GPS." In his model it has three axes. The X-axis is the circadian compass housed in the sphenoid bone and the brain's master clock. The Y-axis is a vertical line running from the skull base down the spine, carrying fluid past the fourth ventricle and into the vagus nerve's drain. The Z-axis is the twisting vortex of the heart. He presents this map as the way people must understand their bodies to cope with the present shift in Earth's magnetic field.

sections.heading: Why he calls it a "Lagrangian"
sections.body:
In physics a Lagrangian is a single expression that sets energy of motion against stored energy; the whole Standard Model is written this way. Kruse stresses that the same equation yields different physics depending on which symmetry governs it, and that nature chooses its symmetries first and the forces follow.

He places the body's own "Lagrangian" where the sphenoid meets the notochord line at the clivus, the sloping bone of the skull base. This junction, in his account, converts sunlight into currents made by pressure, bending and heat in bone, into motion, and into self-sustaining waves, forms of power a magnetic field can steer.

The sphenoid, he says, acts as a "symmetry selector." Under sunlight and 40 Hz vibration it picks the light-based symmetry, and the pump that sorts heavy hydrogen keeps working. Under nnEMF (his term for man-made wireless and electrical fields) and artificial light it reads the environment as a heavy, high-gravity state he likens to the confinement of quarks, and deuterium (heavy hydrogen) piles up in the spinal fluid. Much of modern ill health, in his view, is the visible result of that environmental choice of symmetry.

sections.heading: The X-axis: the sphenoid switchboard
sections.body:
Kruse calls the sphenoid, the bat-shaped bone behind the eyes, the keystone that anchors the head's sensors. It cradles the pituitary gland and carries the optic and trigeminal nerves, which makes it, in his model, the hardware for both the brain's 40 Hz rhythm and the 380 nm violet signal of sunrise. Light reaching the bone charges its piezoelectric framework (bone that makes current when stressed) and so gives the pituitary its timing. Ultraviolet and near-infrared light set the clock by day, and the fading light of sunset trips the melatonin switch.

The arteries around the sphenoid form a "thermal manifold" that warms and thins blood water toward his structured "160" state (the high charge-holding state of cell water he contrasts with ordinary "78" water) before it enters the brain.

The thalamus, the relay and pacing center just above, completes this axis. Kruse wants it loaded with cholesterol and DHA, the long omega-3 fat, which in his model turn it into an induction coil that wraps the fluid chambers in a magnetic sheath, so the swirl of spinal fluid is steadied by Earth's field instead of turning turbulent.

Blue light and nnEMF jam the X-axis, and so does a weakening field once the swirl of spinal fluid through the cerebral aqueduct, the narrow channel between the third and fourth ventricles, loses its speed. A sphenoid knocked out of alignment, he adds, kinks the cranial nerves that pass through its openings, the vagus among them, so the brain can no longer sense how much deuterium it carries. Metabolism then stutters and the body's frame begins to sag.

sections.heading: The Y-axis: the notochord line
sections.body:
The notochord is the rod that defines the embryo's head-to-tail axis. Kruse traces how the clivus forms around its upper end, with the notochord signalling the surrounding tissue to lay down the cartilage of the skull base. Its leftovers in adults are the jelly-like cores of the spinal discs. He says these cores are the most water-rich tissue in the body, built to hold deuterium-depleted water as a liquid crystal at his 160 value. That makes the column a vertical waveguide along which protons can tunnel from brain to sacrum.

A 40 Hz tone, he says, sets the whole system ringing: the sphenoid, the temples and the disc cores. The vibration loosens deuterium and raises what he calls the thalamus's "antenna gain" for the Schumann resonance, Earth's natural electromagnetic hum.

Posture is part of the design. In apes, Kruse says, the aqueduct runs fairly straight. Walking upright and a shrinking braincase gave the human aqueduct a particular pitch and twist, so fluid passing through it spins as a double helix that he calls a "super-fractionator," flinging heavy hydrogen out of the stream. Upright posture is the gravity assist that lets this nozzle reach the speed needed for the Venturi effect (fluid speeding up as a channel narrows). In his account this is what lets human mitochondria run the ATP motor near 9,000 revolutions per minute where a chimpanzee's cannot, and he says it made us human. Short of DHA and cholesterol, or with a sphenoid left still by too little chewing, a person drops back into a heavier "primate" isotopic state and grows disconnected from other people. The floor of the fourth ventricle and the inner ear are, in his model, the body's gravity sensors. Deuterium makes the fluid of the inner ear's balance canals heavier and thicker, so it trails behind each turn of the head, and he links this to unsteadiness and clumsiness.

The Y-axis also has a shortcut. Citing recent anatomy work, Kruse says heavy isotopes can drain from near the trigeminal nerve's main relay straight into nearby veins, and that vibration opens this drain. He calls the trigeminal and vagal routes a "dual exhaust" that works as a buddy system.

sections.heading: The Z-axis and the timing belt
sections.body: The third axis is the heart. Kruse describes the heart's gravity well and spiral flow, together with the vortex in the fourth ventricle, as the spinners that throw deuterium out into the blood and spinal fluid, keeping the mitochondrial interior stocked with light hydrogen. All three axes, he says, keep time to a faint signal from space. He reads a reported "21 Hz/cm" fingerprint as probably a harmonic of the 21-centimeter line, the radio signature of neutral hydrogen across the galaxy, and calls it the system's "timing belt" and "master metronome." As the solar system leaves the galactic hydrogen cloud that once surrounded it, this background signal fades, and the 60 Hz of the power grid and 5G drown it out like a whisper next to a jet engine, which is why he thinks nnEMF does so much harm now.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Kruse's advice follows the axes. Get sunrise and daytime ultraviolet and near-infrared light on the eyes to set the X-axis, and keep blue light and wireless fields out of the evening. Ring the sphenoid and spine with 40 Hz, through his tuning-fork routine or a hummed low "M," and keep the sphenoid moving by chewing, as in his “Mastic gum and palate reset” practice. Keep enough DHA and cholesterol from food to load the thalamus, stay upright and on your feet, and ground so the vertical axis has somewhere to discharge.

articles.title: The brain's exhaust valves: circumventricular organs, the ventricle cyclone and the bird's pecten
articles.summary: Kruse says the brain vents heavy water by day through spots that lack a blood–brain barrier, sorts it in fluid chambers shaped like a cyclone separator, and points to the bird eye's pecten as the same design taken to an extreme.
keyPoints: Kruse says the brain vents heavy water by day through circumventricular organs, the few spots with no blood–brain barrier.
In his model the ventricles are shaped like a cyclone separator, spinning heavy fractions out of the fluid with gravity's help.
He sees the bird eye's pecten as the same design taken to an extreme: antenna, local hormone gland and deuterium exhaust.
He argues birds show that light and heavy-hydrogen removal, not insulin and leptin, sit at the core of metabolism.
His practical lessons are talking, singing and rhythmic breathing, daylight in the eyes, staying upright and moving, and salt-water grounding.

sections.body: Kruse argues the brain does not wait for sleep to get rid of heavy water. In his model it vents deuterium (heavy hydrogen) through built-in relief valves during the day and sorts it in fluid chambers whose shape does the work. Birds, he says, show the same design in its most extreme form, in a structure inside the eye.

sections.heading: Relief valves in the barrier
sections.body:
The blood–brain barrier walls the brain off from the blood. Kruse sees it as a shield that keeps isotopic interference away from the brain's iron-based (Fe²⁺) core. The circumventricular organs, or CVOs, are the few places where that barrier is naturally missing, among them the subfornical organ, the area postrema and the median eminence. He calls them the brain's "hydraulic masterstroke," the relief valves of the shield — and also open doors: high-atomic-mass material that should never reach the hypothalamus or thalamus can enter here, and he warns that wireless earbuds and phones next to the head make that path worse. Clustered around the third and fourth ventricles, the CVOs let the brain dump the heavy water it makes while Complex IV, the last enzyme of the energy chain, is working flat out by day (he speaks of it "redlining" at 355%), without waiting for the glymphatic clean-out of sleep. The faint light the brain gives off during the day, its ultra-weak photon emission, is in his account the feedback that lets the conscious brain judge how much to vent. The inner ear adds another open path: a melanin sheet in the cochlea, tied to the endolymphatic sac, sits without a blood–brain barrier, so pulsed RF there, he says, can uncouple the head's GPS antenna.

He lists the sensors he thinks read the isotopic "heaviness" of the blood. They include tanycytes, the gatekeeper cells lining the third ventricle; heat- and sodium-sensing channels (TRPV1 and Nax) in the subfornical organ and its neighbor the OVLT; the tightly packed cells lining small vessels, which feel how thick the blood is and how strongly its particles repel one another; and glucose-sensing neurons that call for glucagon. When the load rises, he says, the body raises its metabolic "RPM": birds sing or migrate, and people talk or fall into rhythmic breathing.

These organs are ancient. Kruse notes that every vertebrate has CVOs, with the pineal and the hormone-releasing back lobe of the pituitary the most conserved. In birds the pineal still senses light directly, while the mammalian one only secretes. Birds also have extra CVOs that mammals lack, including a lateral septal organ and a lumbosacral organ in the lower spine that helps with balance.

sections.heading: Shape is the separator
sections.body:
Kruse believes the ventricles, the brain's fluid chambers, are shaped to act as a cyclone separator, the kind of device industry uses to spin heavy particles out of a moving stream. For that reason he says their shape is everything. A chamber that is too narrow cannot form a vortex, so deuterium settles out in still, layered flow and pressure climbs. One that is too wide swells like a backed-up sewer. The shape, in his model, mirrors the magnetic map the brain's mitochondria live in.

Gravity holds the separator steady. Without it, he says, the fourth ventricle can no longer keep heavy and light fractions apart, and fluid backs up into the sheath around the optic nerve and presses on the eye, which he gives as the cause of the eye changes astronauts develop in orbit. He assigns the exits of that chamber by isotope: the midline foramen of Magendie for light hydrogen and the lateral foramina of Luschka for deuterium, so a weak vortex dumps heavy water onto the floor's chemoreceptor zone and brings on nausea — his sign that the head's centrifuge has stalled.

sections.heading: The bird's pecten
sections.body:
The pecten oculi is a pleated, comb-like structure that projects into the bird eye, packed with blood vessels and pigment. Kruse says theropod dinosaurs and birds solved a puzzle for him, an idea he says came to him while standing before Michelangelo's David in Florence. The pecten has 14 to 15 folds (he cites the Baladi duck) capped by a bridge of melanin, and in his model it works as a topological antenna that traps biophotons and harvests both sunlight and magnetic flux. That, he argues, is how migrating birds can fly for long stretches without food or sleep. Sleep, to him, is mainly housekeeping that clears thermal noise, and the dielectric shield the pecten builds makes much of that unnecessary.

It also stands in for a gland. Birds lack the intermediate lobe of the pituitary, the part that makes alpha-MSH, the melanocortin hormone that in mammals drives pigment and energy use. Kruse says the melanocyte-rich, vascular pecten takes over that job locally, so together with the hypothalamus it lets the bird set its metabolism straight from the light entering its eye, without relying on leptin from fat or a slow central signal. It keeps the temperature and acidity of the vitreous, the gel filling the eye, steady so its water stays coherent. He calls it a "coherence pump" that lets birds "dissipate mass directly into time."

Its third job is exhaust. The bird's inner retina is thick, has no blood vessels and runs short of oxygen. The pecten pumps glucose in and lactate out, and in Kruse's model it is also the main exit for the deuterium that the retina's fast sugar-burning makes, sending it through the blood to the liver. As the eye flicks during saccades the pecten undulates, and he calls this a mechanical "Maxwell's demon" that stirs the vitreous toward the drain. Birds can therefore shed deuterium through their eyes and even shrink their guts on long flights; he links this to the Arctic tern, which he wrote about in his 2013 book, and to the godwit. Seabirds, he adds, ground their oxidative "exhaust" in salt water, which spares them the charge build-up he blames for false oxygen starvation and muscle fatigue.

sections.heading: Built for sugar
sections.body: Kruse says birds are built to ignore insulin by design. He describes them as having lost GLUT4, the insulin-driven sugar gate, and the omentin gene, which he dates to oxygen drops around 320 million years ago. They have a liver glucagon receptor that is always switched on (reported in May 2025), five to ten times more of the glucagon-making alpha cells, and blood sugar that can run up to 700 mg/dL to feed the oxygen-starved retina through the pecten. Amacrine cells in the retina even make glucagon locally. To Kruse this shows that insulin and leptin are not the core of the story; light and the removal of heavy hydrogen are.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Kruse's lessons for people follow from the design. Keep the daytime vents working by talking, singing, humming and breathing in rhythm, his “Vagal toning with voice and sound” practice. Let real daylight into the eyes, since in his model light entering the eye is what steers metabolism. Stay upright and moving so gravity helps the fluid chambers spin, and use shoreline salt water to ground.

articles.title: Sunrise: dawn UV-A and the master clock
articles.summary: Kruse says dawn light — UV-A near 380 nm plus red and near-infrared, taken in through bare eyes and skin — is the master signal that sets the body's clocks and readies its energy machinery for the day.
keyPoints: Kruse says first light at sunrise, UV-A near 380 nm plus red and near-infrared, is the master signal that sets every body clock.
In his model neuropsin in eyes and skin reads that UV-A, sets the daily NAD⁺ rhythm and tells mTOR which mode to run.
He says sunrise renews heme and melanin and drives the hormone cascade from POMC to alpha-MSH and ACTH.
He argues the body reads daylight as an ordered sentence, and mitochondrial energy output is gated by the clock that sunrise opens.
His routine is 30–45 minutes outside at sunrise, nothing over the eyes, skin uncovered and feet grounded.

sections.body: Kruse argues that the most important light of the day is the first light at sunrise. In his model its UV-A (the gentle ultraviolet just beyond visible violet, which he pins near 380 nanometres), together with the red and near-infrared that dominate the low sun, is the master signal that tells every clock in the body what time it is. Because he treats mitochondria, the cell's power plants, as light-driven devices, missing sunrise means starting the day with the body's wiring out of step.

sections.heading: How light reaches the clock
sections.body:
Kruse says most of light's effect on the body has nothing to do with seeing. Citing the ophthalmologist Fritz Hollwich's 1948 work on the "energetic portion" of the visual pathway, along with Hufeland, Paracelsus and Franz Halberg's early circadian research, he describes an "optico-magnetic" route: light entering the eyes and skin steers the hypothalamus and pituitary, the brain's hormone control centre. The receivers are not the cells used for vision but other light-sensitive materials — neuropsin, melanopsin, melanin, cholesterol, water, heme and collagen.

Speed is part of his case. When a photon strikes retinal, the light-catching molecule inside an opsin, it changes shape in about 200 femtoseconds (millionths of a billionth of a second), which he reckons is some ten million times quicker than a nerve impulse. Flavins answer blue light and the energy chain's cytochromes answer red and near-infrared just as directly, so in his telling light has already altered the body's chemistry before nerves, hormones or metabolism have had time to respond.

Neuropsin (also called OPN5) is the one he puts first. It is a UV-A sensor in the eye and skin — in cornea and skin he treats it as the non-visual filter for the PER2 clock path — and in his account 380 nm light striking it, paired with near-infrared so melanin can form, sets the daily rhythm of NAD⁺, the molecule cells use to carry electrons and to run repair enzymes such as SIRT1. He also calls NAD⁺ a fluorophore tuned near 340 nm UV-A: that front-end light, with midday UV-B braking between Complexes III and IV, clears electron pile-ups before they become a Marcus crash. He calls 380 nm the "mTOR switch" because it tells mTOR, the cell's build-or-clean-up regulator, which mode to be in.

UV-A has a second target in the skin. Acting on tryptophan, an amino acid, it makes a compound called FICZ that switches on the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), which Kruse treats as another light antenna. Blue light and wireless radiation, he says, disorder the water around these molecules and blur that signal.

Kruse describes neuropsin as a "dual-axis transistor": it reads sunlight on one axis and Earth's magnetic field on the other. When the two agree — his "Zeeman handshake" — oxygen stays in its stable, safe form (triplet oxygen) and metabolism flows toward repair. When the field is disturbed or the light is artificial, he says the handshake fails and the same chemistry tips toward histamine, inflammation and singlet oxygen, oxygen's reactive and damaging form.

sections.heading: What sunrise renews
sections.body:
In his model, sunrise UV-A "renovates" heme (the iron-holding core of hemoglobin and of the energy chain's cytochromes) and melanin. The mild stress of UV-A switches on POMC, a hormone precursor the body cuts into alpha-MSH, the signal that makes melanin; mitochondria make melatonin at the same time to buffer that stress. Because the first step of heme production happens inside mitochondria and depends on UV, he ties how well the body builds its blood pigment to full-spectrum sun. The same light, he adds, gives hair its colour.

Kruse calls hormones "light ferry boats": carriers of magnetic and photonic information, not just chemical messengers. Watching the sunrise while grounded, he says, switches on the MITF–AMPAR pathway (the circuit that keeps a person pigmented) and builds an "internal tan" of biophotons, the faint light cells give off. That light helps cut POMC into ACTH, the pituitary hormone that drives the adrenal glands, and alpha-MSH. ACTH then carries the signal to the adrenal cortex. With enough sun, he argues, the message arrives so cleanly that the adrenals need to make less bulk cortisol.

Skin, he adds, can do much of this even with the eyes in darkness. Skin and brain grow from the same embryonic layer, the neuroectoderm, and share the POMC and MITF wiring, so he calls skin an "unfolded" brain and a body-sized solar panel. On his photorepair slide, UV-A reaching neuropsin in the skin refills NAD⁺ and resets the core clock genes, while 600–1000 nm infrared switches on AMPK, the cell's fuel gauge, and orders the water inside cells. Hormones released from sunlit skin then tell the brain the sun is up, which he says lets an over-alert brain stop straining to "listen harder."

Kruse also says the body reads sunlight as a sentence, in order. The blue pre-dawn hour is the preface that anchors the clock, the amber sunrise is the opening line, and dusk is the closing chapter that cues night-time melatonin and repair. A lone orange LED switched on at a random hour carries none of that meaning. Each sunrise, in his telling, reboots the whole system and reminds it that the sun is the one reference with no alternative; he puts the lifetime need at roughly 25,000 sunrises, about seventy years of mornings. He points to Egypt and the Maya at Tikal as cultures that organised their days around this sequence.

The first horizon light, he says, also triggers the cortisol awakening response (the natural morning rise in cortisol) and the glucagon gene network. Together these start the pancreas's roughly two-litre daily bicarbonate flush, which in his model sweeps deuterium (heavy hydrogen) out through the gut. Morning sun also lets the longevity gene FOXO3 apply its brakes on cell division, which he says protects the genome.

Mitochondria keep time too. Kruse cites Glen Jeffery's finding that ATP output runs about 40% higher in the morning, the energy-chain complexes peak in the afternoon, and cells lean on glycolysis (splitting sugar without oxygen) at night. To him this shows the energy machinery is gated by the clock, and sunrise is when the gate opens. The same morning light, he says, calms adrenaline, re-tightens collagen through nitric oxide and powers the liver's output of albumin, the blood protein that holds water inside vessels; people who block or skip morning light end up, in his account, with flattened cortisol rhythms and leaky vessels.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Sunrise light on bare eyes and skin” routine is to be outside as the sun clears the horizon, using the first 60–90 minutes and staying 30–45 minutes. Nothing should sit between your eyes and the sun: no sunglasses, contacts, glasses or window glass. Uncover as much skin as you reasonably can and stand barefoot on surf, wet sand, dewy grass or basalt. He takes a well-formed stool (Bristol type 4) as the sign that the morning bicarbonate flush is working.

articles.title: Midday UV-B and vitamin D
articles.summary: In Kruse's model, UV-B and the vitamin D it makes in skin are part of a coded light-and-magnetic-field system with a built-in safety cutoff that pills bypass, and the local field, latitude and season limit how much vitamin D sunlight can make.
keyPoints: Kruse says midday UV-B and skin-made vitamin D act as a safety brake on the mitochondrial energy chain, not a nutrient to top up.
In his model sun-made vitamin D has a built-in cutoff, and the local magnetic field decides how much D3 the skin can make.
He says latitude, season, skin cholesterol and deuterium load all limit what sunlight can produce.
He argues a pill delivers "the ink without the book": the blood marker rises while the light-driven steps never happen.
His routine is torso and back in solar-noon sun, no sunscreen or eyewear, building up gradually, grounded, and avoiding oral D3.
