sections.body: Kruse rejects the idea that vitamin D is just a nutrient to top up. In his view UV-B, the shorter and stronger ultraviolet of the midday sun, and the vitamin D it makes in skin form a self-regulating light system tied to the body clock and to the local magnetic field. That is why he wants vitamin D made in the skin, not swallowed.

sections.heading: UV-B as a safety brake
sections.body:
Kruse treats UV-B and UV-A as a pair of brakes on the mitochondrial energy chain. Vitamin D's receptor, which he places on the inner mitochondrial membrane, slows electron flow between Complexes III and IV, while UV-A releases nitric oxide, which briefly slows Complex IV. Together, he says, they keep the chain out of "Marcus inversion" — his term for electron flow that stalls when it is pushed too hard — whenever Earth's field is unstable.

That is why he calls UV-B "term life insurance" for anyone who is not "pinned" (living grounded and sunlit under a stable local magnetic field), and why he says it should not be feared. Citing Slominski, Holick and Reiter (2026), he treats vitamin D and the circadian clock as one coupled loop. Mitochondria, he adds, make melatonin in daytime using UV, so vitamin D and melatonin are twin products of the sun rather than day-and-night opposites.

He illustrates the brake with the elephant, whose unarmoured skin makes plenty of vitamin D; its receptor works like a clutch that keeps a large brain from overheating under the midday sun.

sections.heading: The built-in cutoff
sections.body:
UV-B turns a cholesterol precursor in the skin into vitamin D, but Kruse notes that only about a quarter of the yield becomes vitamin D3; the rest becomes lumisterol and tachysterol. He calls this a self-limiting "thermostat" that makes it impossible to overdose on sun-made vitamin D. In his account the UV-B hit creates a radical pair, two fragments each holding one unpaired electron. If their spins point opposite ways they recombine into D3; if they point the same way they break down into the cutoff products. The local magnetic field tips that balance.

Because the field chooses the path, he says the magnetism where you live caps how much vitamin D you can make. That is his explanation for levels that stay flat in California despite plenty of sun, and for a reader's stalled level in Florida, which sits close to the South Atlantic Anomaly, a large weak patch in Earth's field where, he says, tissue cannot complete the light-driven repair that lets levels climb.

The form of skin cholesterol matters too. In summer, sulfur-rich cholesterol carried in HDL is the "antenna" tuned to UV-B. Years of blue light and nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring) can freeze skin cholesterol in its electron-poor LDL form, his "Mismatch Freeze," so even naked equatorial sun finds nothing to work with. A cell loaded with deuterium (heavy hydrogen), he adds, lacks the energy to make or activate vitamin D at all, and the liver and kidneys can only turn it into its active form when they are themselves low in deuterium. In his reading, that is how light on the skin reaches the isotope balance of organs that never see daylight.

Latitude and season set limits as well. Above about 37°, Kruse says, skin makes little vitamin D for two to eight months of the year, and in winter the low sun stops it whatever a person's ancestry. Darker skin needs more UV to make the same amount, which he says is why the stronger UV of altitude helps melanin-rich people. In a mid-latitude summer, regular time outdoors supplies enough UV-B.

sections.heading: More sun is not always better
sections.body: Strong UV without grounding and infrared can itself stall the energy chain, so Kruse reads a sunburn as proof the person was not pinned enough, and calls burning on purpose foolish. Citing Fosbury's maps of US deaths, he notes that death rates peak one to three weeks after the winter solstice and bottom out after the summer solstice; he blames low light combined with an unstable field.

sections.heading: Why the sun feels good
sections.body:
Strong UV on skin cells, in Kruse's account, switches on POMC, a hormone precursor, right in the skin. POMC is cut into alpha-MSH, the tanning signal, and beta-endorphin, the body's own opioid, which reaches the brain's reward centres and releases dopamine. Sun is meant to feel rewarding, he says, and a life without it lowers beta-endorphin, bringing flatter mood and more pain.

He ties thinking to the same arc. The brain's sharpest window, in his view, mirrors solar noon. People with a steady lifelong history of daytime light, he says, think faster and age more slowly mentally, while light at night lowers dopamine, melatonin and GABA, the brain's main calming messenger.

sections.heading: Sunlight as a coded signal
sections.body: Kruse describes the sun as a pulsed, filtered, coded power supply rather than raw energy. When oxygen rose in Earth's early atmosphere, the ozone layer that formed began carving a pattern into sunlight. The dark Fraunhofer lines in the solar spectrum act, in his telling, like a barcode, and ozone casts a "shadow" across the yellow-orange. He calls this pattern a "photonic grammar" and says it is what lets the vitamin D receptor work as a metabolic brake. Melanin, in his model, is the software that reads the code.

sections.heading: Why pills fall short
sections.body:
An oral pill delivers pure D3 with none of the cutoff products and none of the light-run steps; in his phrase, it gives the body "the ink without the book." Kruse cites an observational study of more than 5,000 older adults that linked routine supplementation in people with normal levels to slightly faster slipping in thinking skills. In his reading the extra vitamin D acts as an "atomic impurity" in an ungrounded brain under artificial light, and he says supplemental vitamin D carries deuterium into the head.

He reads the flat results of two large supplement trials, VITAL and ViDA, the same way: a pill cannot repair a shortfall that is physical rather than chemical. Sun on skin, he says, drives a current and lifts the cell's water toward its structured state (his "160"). A pill raises 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the blood marker doctors test, while delivering no photons and none of the infrared that thins the blood, so the lab value looks fine while the body stays locked up; he likens it to photoshopping a bank balance. He treats a low blood level as a dashboard gauge reporting high deuterium and weak magnetic drive, which a pill only paints over.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Midday sun and UV-B, unfiltered” routine: near solar noon, when your shadow is shorter than you, expose your torso and back, with no sunscreen, sunglasses, contacts or glasses. Build up gradually and move to shade at the first warmth on the skin. Give UV-B priority if you are not pinned and around the winter solstice, and stay grounded while you do it. Oral vitamin D3, especially when levels are already normal, is on his list of pills to avoid.

articles.title: The four-phase sun day and the "solar callus"
articles.summary: Kruse's account of how a person, especially one from a northern maternal lineage, builds tolerance to strong sun by stepping through the day's wavelengths from sunrise to sunset, and why place and altitude change the pace.
keyPoints: Kruse says a "solar callus," skin that tans rather than burns, is built gradually through daily sun rather than inherited.
In his model northern maternal lineages have "leaky" mitochondria that need slow arrival and grounding to re-couple in the tropics.
He says the day's light should be taken in order: red and infrared at sunrise, UV-A mid-morning, brief UV-B at noon, infrared at sunset.
He reads early-season skin reactions as deuterium stored over winter, so build-up must be slow and burning avoided.
He says sunscreen, sunglasses and contacts block the melanin signal, while altitude and place change how fast the callus forms.

sections.body: Kruse uses "solar callus" for skin and tissue that have adapted to strong sun, so they tan rather than burn. He argues the callus is built gradually, not inherited, and that how it is built matters most for someone whose ancestors evolved far from the equator and who moves to the tropics, as he did when he moved to El Salvador.

sections.heading: Lineage and pace
sections.body:
He explains this through haplogroups, the maternal lineages traced through mitochondrial DNA. His own, H, is northern European, and he describes its mitochondria as naturally "leaky": built to shed heat rather than to couple tightly to energy production. Plunged suddenly into tropical UV, he says, such mitochondria lose their coherence. An H-lineage person who flies straight from northern Europe to San Salvador is, in his view, in a very different position from one who arrives slowly.

Mitochondrial DNA does not change, and a northern lineage does not become a tropical one. But Kruse says epigenetic flexibility plus local grounding — bare feet on basalt or wet black volcanic sand, which he says carry a strong horizontal magnetic field — lets the person "re-couple." The mitochondria become better insulated, leak less, and keep the blood and spinal-fluid flows that clear deuterium (heavy hydrogen) working. He calls this a re-coupled relocation. At high latitudes, by contrast, he notes that no one can hold a tan all twelve months, so a year-round natural callus is out of reach there.

sections.heading: Place and altitude
sections.body: Where you stand also changes how fast the callus forms. A reader in Australia noticed he tanned far faster at sea level than at home, about 700 metres up. Kruse's explanation is that at altitude the magnetic field is weaker and noisier, closer to the radiation belts, so MITF, the master switch of pigment cells, stays in a repair-and-survive mode, spending its effort quenching damage instead of laying down pigment. At sea level the thicker atmosphere and stronger field give the melanin-making pathway the steady conditions it needs to switch into building mode, and the tan comes quickly. A tan, he adds, reports only on the skin, not on the state inside the body.

sections.heading: Four phases of light
sections.body:
He built his own callus by treating each day as a training program through the solar spectrum, in order. Sunrise red and near-infrared expand structured water in tissue (water ordered into a charge-holding gel layer) and prepare cells to handle the UV that comes later. Mid-morning UV-A on bare eyes signals the brain, through the POMC hormone pathway, to lay down melanin, which he treats as the skin's spin filter. A brief midday UV-B dose makes vitamin D and sulfur-rich cholesterol and, together with the new melanin, completes the callus. The last daylight hour's red and infrared then repair the day's oxidative damage and prepare the body to make melatonin. In his model the infrared at both ends prepares and repairs the tissue around the UV-heavy middle.

He finds support for those infrared bookends in Chossat's 1843 starvation experiments, as retold by Herbert Shelton. Animals close to death from hunger revived with outside heat alone, and died if the heat was taken away before their food was digested. Kruse reads this as infrared re-expanding structured water and restarting the ATP motor without food, which for him makes food a battery extender rather than the main power supply.

sections.heading: Why the build-up must be slow
sections.body:
Kruse uses the same model to explain why the first strong sun of spring can bring an itchy, burning rash that fades as summer goes on. Over a dark, sedentary winter, he says, deuterium collects in skin that stays covered, such as the chest and arms. When intense UV strikes skin loaded with heavy water and metals, deuterium cannot vibrate or tunnel fast enough to shed the energy, so it piles up as a local heat spike, and the rash is the immune system clearing what the UV has just "cooked." As summer UV clears the surface and the body's fluid flows speed up, the skin "hardens."

Someone whose tissues are loaded while their blood is clean, he adds, will feel up and down in the first weeks of long sun days, so an erratic early response is expected. For very sensitive people he stages the light: infrared first, and UV-A only once the melanin shield and the insulating sheaths around nerves have been rebuilt, since UV-A switched on too early overwhelms the system. His gates for moving on are a flashlight shone on the teeth, which he reads for clarity, and a crisp pupil reflex.

sections.heading: Redness and filters
sections.body: Redness, Kruse says, means the membrane's electrical containment has broken down, so his rule is never to burn. Sunscreen blocks the UV-B and UV-A needed for vitamin D and melanin, and in his telling also blocks the magnetic job of skin melanin and cholesterol so oxygen tips toward its reactive form. Sunglasses make the brain read cloud or darkness, so the melanin signal never starts and the person burns quickly at midday; contacts interfere in the same way. He names DHA from wild seafood as the fat that turns sunlight into current in tissue, and says saffron speeds the callus: its carotenoids crocin and crocetin, its aroma compound safranal and the flavonol kaempferol.

sections.heading: Skin colour as a readout
sections.body: In Kruse's view pale skin is not a sign of health but an atrophied organ, made pale by sunscreen, sunglasses, indoor life or drugs. Near-infrared sun draws blood to the skin and boosts red-cell production, and strong UV keeps blood oxygen in its stable form, turning blood deep red. Sun-flushed skin is, for him, a visible readout of redox health that other species also use to choose mates (he cites gelada baboons and birds). He retells accounts, which he credits to Lavoisier, of ship surgeons near the equator mistaking bright-scarlet venous blood for arterial blood.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His four-phase sun day: at sunrise, 30–45 minutes of red and near-infrared on bare eyes and as much skin as possible, feet on basalt or wet black sand; mid-morning (about 8:30–11:00), 15–25 minutes of UV-A on eyes and skin while moving, with no eyewear; at midday, when your shadow is shorter than you, 3–10 minutes of UV-B on torso and back while grounded, starting at 3 minutes and adding a minute every few days as you tan, and moving to shade at the first warmth. In the last daylight hour, spend 20–30 minutes outside with bare skin and no sunglasses to wind down (his “Sunset light” practice). Keep artificial night light and out-of-season food out of the picture, and if you are relocating to the tropics, arrive gradually.

articles.title: Red and near-infrared: the sun first
articles.summary: Kruse values red and near-infrared light highly — it rebuilds cell water, restarts the energy chain and lowers blood sugar — but says it cannot fix an unpinned body on its own, and that the sun is its only complete source.
keyPoints: Kruse says red and near-infrared, about 43% of sunlight, rebuild cell water, free Complex IV and spin ATP synthase on light hydrogen.
In his model it works best at dawn, needs a full NAD⁺ pool, and pairs with UV-A in a push-pull over nitric oxide.
He says modern LED-lit life leaves people short of near-infrared, an "electronic winter" at the level of the cell.
He argues near-infrared "lubricates rather than drives": without a stable magnetic field and UV, it can deepen the jam.
His guidance puts the sun first, treats panels as secondary, and avoids pairing methylene blue with red light unless grounded.

sections.body: Red and near-infrared light (NIR, invisible light just past red, roughly 600–1000 nm) hold a central place in Kruse's model. About 43% of sunlight falls in this band, he says, and it reaches deep into the body to power mitochondria. But he insists it is only one part of what sunlight provides, and that it only works fully in a body that is "pinned": grounded and sunlit under a stable local magnetic field.

sections.heading: What red and infrared do
sections.body:
Building on Peter Mitchell's account of how mitochondria make energy, Kruse calls red light the sun's "command channel" for light hydrogen (ordinary hydrogen, as opposed to heavy deuterium). Red light, he says, penetrates the abdomen to the liver's mitochondria and spins ATP synthase, the rotary motor that makes the cell's energy currency, at full efficiency on light hydrogen. The liver then needs less food fuel and keeps deuterium out; he calls this the "43% red light engine."

He puts the energy barrier for smooth electron and proton flow down the energy chain at about 0.66 electron-volts. He places photons of that energy near 1878 nm, past the usual near-infrared band, and traces them to the negative hydrogen ion in the sun's atmosphere, which he says pours out a continuous infrared stream there. In his view the stream only becomes biologically useful once it has passed through Earth's magnetic shield and reached the body's water.

That energy, he says, accelerates the hand-off of electrons from NADH, the loaded form of the carrier NAD⁺, into the energy chain, turning it back into NAD⁺. When the chain stalls, NAD⁺ falls. The size of the NAD⁺ pool also decides what red light does: when it is low, 670 nm light has nowhere to land and ends up as heat, a "nanoscopic sunburn," while a large pool lets the same pulse become the membrane's electric field.

NIR's best-known job in his model is at Complex IV, the last step of the energy chain, where oxygen is turned into water. Nitric oxide can sit on Complex IV's copper–iron centre and block it. Morning NIR breaks that bond, his "photonic purge," so oxygen can enter. Without it, he says, electrons pile up, oxygen flips into its reactive singlet form, and the cell can no longer make its own deuterium-depleted water. Until Complex IV is running and the cell's water has changed, he says, no supplement works.

He pairs this with UV-A in a push-pull. UV-A frees the nitric oxide stored in skin and blood, relaxing vessel walls and making them slick; he notes the body's nitric oxide falls by about 65% between the twenties and the sixties. But that same nitric oxide competes with oxygen at Complex IV, so near-infrared is needed to lift it off again, restoring ATP and the metabolic water that keeps elastin, the springy protein of artery walls, hydrated. Without enough infrared, he says, elastin dries and calcium binds to its fibres.

Order matters. Kruse says red and near-infrared first rebuild exclusion-zone water, the ordered, charge-holding layer water forms beside surfaces, and only once that layer is restored can UV drive the orderly spin changes the energy chain depends on. That is why he puts red and infrared at both ends of the sun day.

Timing matters as well. Citing Glen Jeffery's work, Kruse says 670 nm light lifted mitochondrial output only early in the day and did nothing in the afternoon, when cells are already at full load. He treats mitochondria as clocks that need a dawn reset pulse, so red light from a device late in the day is lost as heat. In nature, infrared peaks relative to UV at dawn and dusk, when he says it thins the water in blood and spinal fluid; window glass filters it, so people indoors miss those transitions.

Red light also acts on blood sugar. Citing work with 670 nm light, he says blood glucose fell by 27% with no insulin, while blue light pushes glucose up as the system stalls to avoid overheating. Lowering blood sugar, in his view, means fixing the light and clearing deuterium.

sections.heading: The near-infrared shortfall
sections.body: Kruse describes a modern lack of 600–1000 nm light. An ancestor sitting by a wood fire, in the sun and grounded to a strong local field, was bathed in it. Modern people live under LEDs that emit almost none, and the phase-out of incandescent bulbs removed the last indoor source. He calls the result an "electronic winter": having traded the sun's water-thinning infrared for cold blue light, people are chilled at the level of the cell whatever the thermostat says.

sections.heading: Why NIR alone is not enough
sections.body:
Yet Kruse says NIR "lubricates rather than drives." It thins the water around ATP synthase and speeds Complex IV, but it does nothing to align electron spins, the job his model gives to the magnetic field. If Complexes I–III upstream are already in Marcus inversion from a weak field or nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring), spinning ATP synthase harder only pulls more electrons through the crash; he likens it to sending more cars onto a NASCAR pile-up. Relying on red or near-infrared alone breaks nature's rules in his view: UV-A releases nitric oxide that briefly brakes the synthase, and UV-B via the vitamin D receptor slows the hand-off between Complexes III and IV — the pair that keeps an inverted chain from dumping destructive free radicals.

Devices have further limits. Most panels emit a few narrow bands that stop at 850 or 940 nm, well short of the 1878 nm band; their light is far more uniform than sunlight's broad, scrambled mix; and even "flicker-free" drivers add electrical noise that the cell must spend energy sorting. A costly panel, he says, can leave someone merely better lit while their deuterium load stays put.

For people who are unpinned he goes further. When oxygen is in its singlet state and NAD⁺ is loaded with deuterium, he says metabolism becomes blind to light, so magnetism matters more than light, a catch-22 he calls rare in human history. Such a person can lack near-infrared while standing naked in the sun. The precondition for using light is what he calls a "paramagnetic lock": membranes, cholesterol rafts and structured water acting together as an ordered antenna that keeps oxygen in its stable form.

He also warns against a popular combination. Methylene blue shuttles electrons past Complexes I and III, and 670 or 830 nm light excites Complex IV; in an ungrounded person living under wireless and blue light, he likens the pairing to a turbocharger on a short-circuiting transformer.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Sun first, red-light panels second” guidance puts the sun first: get red and infrared from sunrise and daylight together with UV-A and UV-B, and if you have hours of sun, a panel is redundant. Don't rely on single-wavelength devices, which he says can harm; where he does use panels, they are 660 and 850 nm, and never as a substitute for the UV brakes. He prefers grounding plus full solar light to panels, and says not to combine methylene blue with red light unless grounded and away from wireless and blue light.

articles.title: Melanin: the body's solar semiconductor
articles.summary: Kruse treats melanin as a light-driven semiconductor, spin filter and metal and deuterium trap, wired to the brain through a two-way skin–brain loop, that daily UV-A, a stable magnetic field and well-hydrated cells must renew.
keyPoints: Kruse calls melanin a biological semiconductor that splits water with light, feeding cells a current that does not depend on food.
In his model it filters electron spin in skin and arteries, traps metals and deuterium, absorbs radiation, and can migrate when voltage and sun allow.
He says a two-way skin–brain loop through MITF and AMPA receptors lets sunlit skin tell the brain the sun is up.
He argues sunglasses, sunscreen, hats, tattoos, hair dye and lotions block or smother the signals melanin needs to charge.
His main lever is regular unfiltered sun, sunrise UV-A, grounding, and at most tallow or coconut oil on the skin.

sections.body: For Kruse, melanin is far more than skin pigment. Found in skin, eyes, brain, the nerves around the heart, fat and fascia, it is in his model a "biological quantum semiconductor," a material that turns light into electrical current, and a vault for metals. Keeping it renewed with daily sunlight is central to his approach.

sections.heading: What melanin does
sections.body:
Kruse compares melanin to chlorophyll. It absorbs a broad range of light, especially UV and visible, and uses it to split water into hydrogen, oxygen and free electrons. That continual splitting feeds a "wireless" current into cells that does not depend on food. Working with structured water (water ordered into a charge-holding layer), he says, melanin also sorts light hydrogen from deuterium, its heavy form.

That sorting has a cost. Splitting deuterium-heavy water takes eight to ten times more energy, so an overloaded melanin stalls, bleaches or browns. He calls melanin a sacrificial sink: it soaks up deuterium so the heavy hydrogen never reaches the mitochondrial motor, and it wears out doing so. Its one-handed (chiral) structure also lets it pass on only electrons with the right spin and soak up almost any frequency of electromagnetic noise before it reaches mitochondria.

Melanin is also a trap, a buffer and a radiation sink. It grabs free iron and copper, which in his account stops iron-driven radical chemistry and singlet-oxygen formation at the source. It buffers protons, magnesium and calcium like a capacitor. He reads high heavy-metal levels as a sign that a person's internal melanin is failing, which makes them a sun and grounding problem. He stresses that melanin absorbs huge amounts of electromagnetic energy, which is why he wants people outdoors in strong sun, "like a rotisserie chicken," especially in the tropics, to keep that shield charged.

Neural-crest melanin also lines arteries on an elastin and fibrillin scaffold, where he says it keeps deuterium in the blood rather than the cell. When that filter fails — too little sun or grounding, too much blue light — calcium settles in vessel walls and teeth yellow. Eumelanin versus pheomelanin is largely sulfur chemistry set by triplet oxygen; under a weak field or the South Atlantic Anomaly, people can lose the ability to melanate even in equatorial sun. Adult neural-crest cells still migrate along collagen and elastin, so melanin can move — explorers lighten in the Arctic and darken at the equator, and an ungrounded plane flight can shed a tan in hours. Interior mitochondria "tan" when membrane voltage is high enough for cells' own UV glow to drive POMC.

Holding metals is how melanin turns information into chemistry. When it absorbs a biophoton (the faint light cells give off) or a particular radio frequency, Kruse says, it changes shape, squeezing or loosening the metal it holds and so reshaping the enzyme attached to it: light becomes metabolism with no gene in between. When a reader worried about low copper, his answer was that melanin controls the metals, and sun and grounding restore the controller.

sections.heading: The interior tan
sections.body: In the brain, Kruse calls neuromelanin bound to iron in the substantia nigra a solid-state battery that holds local fields steady so oxygen keeps its stable spin; nnEMF, blue light or dehydration deform it. Melanin in dark places like this and the inner ear harvests the faint light mitochondria give off. A skin tan shows only the outer shield; this "interior tan" matters more, and a deep skin tan can hide a "browned" interior.

sections.heading: Renewal, and how melanin "rusts"
sections.body:
Melanin must be renewed. Without 380 nm UV-A reaching neuropsin and without strong pinning (grounded and sunlit under a stable local field), the POMC pathway that yields alpha-MSH shuts down. The ageing polymer soaks up toxins and deuterium, its iron "rusts," and debris settles as lipofuscin, his "rusted melanin." Melanin can only shed UV safely when wet with the deuterium-depleted water Complex IV makes.

With UV-A and well-oxygenated blood, tyrosine becomes melanin; without them the pathway slides back toward tyrosine and phenylalanine, and stored melanin breaks down into catecholamines used as emergency "dopants." He reads low vitamin D and greying hair as the same circuit failing — and color can return when pinning returns, so pigment loss is not a one-way clock.

sections.heading: The skin–brain loop
sections.body:
Kruse's newest piece is what he calls the transdermal MITF–AMPAR loop. He points to research showing that human pigment cells carry working AMPA receptors, the fast receivers for glutamate, the brain's main "go" signal, and that blocking them sharply lowers MITF. He reads this as proof that the glutamate system running the brain also sets the charge of the melanin "battery," in skin and inside the head alike.

The loop also explains, in his view, what happens when light goes missing. The faint light mitochondria give off under load is meant to strike melanin, with AMPA receptors acting as its antennae. When that signal fails, through light starvation or wireless noise, the brain adds AMPA receptors to "listen harder" and slides into a noisy, over-excited state with foggy thinking. Sun on skin reverses this: hormones released through POMC tell the brain the sun is up, and receptor numbers can fall.

sections.heading: What blocks the signal
sections.body:
Blocking daylight, in his model, cuts the eye-to-skin signal that builds melanin. Sunglasses make the brain read darkness, so pigment is never ordered and the person burns at midday; contacts, sunscreen, face-shading hats and daytime blue blockers do the same. He treats sunscreen as a tarp over the skin's solar panel: it blocks melanin and cholesterol, tipping oxygen toward reactive singlet. Skin and brain share the neuroectoderm, so the tarp underfeeds the brain — worse at high latitude indoors. Tattoos, in the same spin story, ruin the chirality of that solar-semiconductor surface.

Hair, for Kruse, belongs to the same antenna: a melanin-filled light guide, not dead keratin. Dyeing or bleaching, he says, "shaves the antenna."

sections.heading: Melanin and the magnetic field
sections.body: Melanin, like oxygen, is paramagnetic, so in Kruse's model making it inside the body depends on Earth's field; when the field weakens, internal melanin fails first. He tells people to live where they can make melanin, naming places with an erratic compass, such as Hawaii and New Zealand, as hard on it.

sections.heading: Skin water and lotions
sections.body: Kruse treats dry skin as a light-clock failure, not a shortage of drinking water. Light at night disrupts the POMC signal, and the sweat glands stop building a film of structured, deuterium-depleted water on the skin. Skin, he says, is hydrated from the inside, by mitochondria making water. Lotions make matters worse: petroleum and silicone bases collapse skin water from its structured state (his "160") to ordinary water (his "78"), hidden UV filters breed singlet oxygen under LEDs, and any synthetic coat smothers the oxidising film the skin makes at its surface.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Midday sun and UV-B, unfiltered” routine is the main lever: regular unfiltered sun, with sunrise UV-A for renewal, and no sunscreen, sunglasses, contacts or blue blockers in daylight. For dry skin he uses morning sun, cold and grounding rather than lotion; after a shower he allows at most tallow or coconut oil, and never petroleum, silicone or UV-filter products. He sums the daily posture as "make like the Sphinx and eat like a great white shark": ground at sunrise, face the sun, and keep the plate on clean seafood rather than packaged fillers.

articles.title: Blue light, LEDs and screens
articles.summary: Kruse blames blue-dominant indoor light and screens, stripped of red and infrared, for damage to the body clock, eyes and metabolism, and calls screen life "reality subtraction."
keyPoints: Kruse says LEDs and screens deliver blue light stripped of red and infrared, and in his view disturb the body more than food does.
In his model indoor blue light without magnetic "pinning" raises blood sugar and insulin and pushes deuterium into tissue.
He says wrong-way light makes singlet oxygen that damages the clock's physical hardware, starting with the eye.
He wants blue gone after sunset but never blocked in daylight, where blockers act on the clock "like a drug."
He calls screen life "reality subtraction" and says to swap in incandescent bulbs and keep screens away from workouts and bedrooms.

sections.body: Kruse argues that modern indoor light is one of the biggest forces pulling the body out of order — in his view a bigger one than food. LEDs and screens deliver a spike of blue light with almost none of the red and infrared that come with natural light, and people take it in indoors, away from both the sun and the ground.

sections.heading: How lighting changed
sections.body:
He dates a turning point to efficient blue LEDs, whose inventors (Akasaki, Amano and Nakamura) won the 2014 physics Nobel. Built to emit only visible light, LEDs strip out the red and infrared that sunlight, firelight and incandescent bulbs supply — the longer wavelengths that, in Kruse's model, penetrate the body and power mitochondria. Phasing out incandescent bulbs removed the last indoor source of infrared and left a blue spike he says can drive the dopamine pathway once melanin breaks down and the blood–brain barrier is leaky. He likens running a brain on LEDs to powering a quantum computer from a flickering 5-volt supply instead of the sun's broad, steady battery. On stages and in conference halls he wants red light, not blue-heavy LED blasts.

Sunlight, he adds, comes from countless atoms and transitions at once, which makes it the most varied and least polarized light there is. Any lamp is a far smaller set of sources, which is why by day he sends people outdoors rather than to sun-imitating lamps.

sections.heading: What it does to the body
sections.body:
Indoor spaces, Kruse says, are both blue-dominant and "devoid of magnetic effects." That combination forces a spin change in the mitochondrial energy chain (intersystem crossing) that drives insulin spikes and dulls the body's response to insulin; he holds that light and missing magnetic "pinning" raise blood sugar and insulin more than any food. A burst of red light while grounded, he adds, can blunt a glucose and insulin spike.

Night-time blue is the worst case for blood sugar. In his account it strikes melanopsin in the lower retina, scrambles the hypothalamus's clock and throttles hypocretin, the brain's alertness signal, which he treats as a brake on heavy mass. Deuterium (heavy hydrogen) then floods tissue and cells call for more glucose.

Bad light, Kruse says, also changes where deuterium sits. In the blood it is fairly harmless and mobile, and the pancreas can pass it to the bicarbonate system to be cleared through the gut. Blue-heavy, infrared-poor, pulsing light breaks the daily rhythm and lets it seep into tissue and spinal fluid, where it lodges in the ordered water around proteins and slows their motion. Sensing that heavy floor, the hypothalamus locks into a lasting cell danger response (a defensive shutdown mode), felt as anxiety or headache.

Wrong-way light also makes singlet oxygen, an energised form of oxygen that bypasses the body's normal safety controls. Kruse calls it a "molecular buzzsaw": it burns the fatty membrane rafts that anchor PER2, a core clock protein, which he names as the root of every circadian mismatch. In his model the body clock is physical hardware being damaged from inside, not an abstract genetic timer. He adds that most clock control happens after proteins are made, as they fold: proteins take their final shape under forces from light, so incoherent LED light keeps them from reaching it, and strained mitochondria send out GDF15, a distress signal.

Light stripped of sunlight's infrared and UV also blocks the POMC hormone pathway from making its tanning and calming signals. In his telling the skin–brain melanin loop then drifts, the brain adds AMPA receptors (fast receivers for the excitatory messenger glutamate) and nerves turn jumpy, which people feel as racing thoughts and jitters.

The eye takes the first hit. He says nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring), blue light and a weak local field damage melanopsin (the eye's blue-sensing clock receptor), mitochondrial DNA and heme proteins, dry out the retina's melanin and let deuterium into the eye's water. Contact lenses worn around the clock, he adds, trap blue light and EMF right at the eye.

Isolated indoor blue, roughly 400–465 nm, keeps the energy chain stuck on the singlet-oxygen path and browns the brain's neuromelanin, the pigment he treats as its light processor.

sections.heading: When to block blue — and when not to
sections.body:
After sunset, blue light should be gone. But Kruse is equally firm that blue blockers of any tint, red or yellow included, should never be worn in daylight. There, he says, they act on the clock "like a drug": they change the body's own feedback loops in the same way a supplement or medication does, and they block the daylight signals that build melanin.

The hour before sunrise matters too. Habitually switching on artificial light before dawn, he says, keeps Complex IV from being primed by the day's first natural light, so the cell never makes the water that hydrates melanin and runs the whole day in a fermentation-style, low-efficiency mode.

sections.heading: Screens and "reality subtraction"
sections.body:
Kruse calls social media and AI feeds "reality subtraction": algorithms that replace direct perception of the real world with a profit-driven version, exploiting dopamine while users sit ungrounded under blue light. The weaker the magnetic field a person senses, he says, the more marketing and manipulation get through. Wild animals simply stay locked to the planet's rhythms; the human frontal lobe lets us plan ahead but also lets us ignore the present, which makes us, in his view, the one species that chooses to live out of sync.

A phone's blue light is, in his phrase, a "counterfeit timestamp": it tells the body clock it is always noon, so the brain's night-time waste flush never gets going. Fast scrolling adds strobing spikes of blue light down the optic nerve. In healthy brain fluid they would pass cleanly, he says, but in deuterium-heavy spinal fluid they scatter into noise that the brain's vomiting centre reads as a toxin, bringing on nausea and headache.

Screens also spoil exercise. In his account blue light from TV leaves the clock genes and DNA weighed down, and training on top of that only multiplies the strain, so going straight from the television to a workout makes exercise partly toxic.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Evening light: incandescent, red, dark” rules: swap LED and fluorescent bulbs for incandescent; after sunset, use red incandescent bulbs or glasses that block 100% of blue; never wear blue blockers in daylight; avoid switching on artificial light before sunrise; and by day, open a window rather than buy sun-imitating lamps. His “Cut screen time” rules: cut screen and wireless time, don't go straight from TV or screens into a workout, and keep devices out of the bedroom.

articles.title: Elephants, rhinos and why big brains grew
articles.summary: Kruse argues big brains grew from how a species handled sunlight and vibration rather than from lucky genes: the thin-skinned elephant and the hairless human invested in light capture and time, the armored rhino in mass, and indoor life is now shrinking the human brain.
keyPoints: Kruse says big brains grow when a species captures enough sunlight through its skin and keeps its body water clear, not from lucky genes.
In his model the thin-skinned elephant bet on light and time, while the armored rhino bet on mass and blocked solar input.
He frames evolution as "Symmetry Selection," with each species settling into the state that keeps its physical Action lowest.
He calls large brains a vibrational achievement, built from coupling sound and light in body water.
He reads the human brain's shrinking as the cost of indoor life, and wants bare skin in sunlight plus daily humming, laughing and chanting.

sections.body: Kruse argues that big brains are not a genetic jackpot. In his model a brain grows large when a species finds a way to capture enough sunlight, and to keep its body water clear enough, to power it. He uses the elephant and the rhinoceros, two large animals that lived under the same sun and ended up with very different brains, as his main test case.

sections.heading: Same sun, different bets
sections.body:
Rhinos, elephants, gorillas and humans all evolved on the same high-UV savanna. What decided whether each invested in armor and bulk or in brains, Kruse says, was the coupling between skin and brain that he calls the transdermal MITF–AMPAR loop: the circuit linking the pigment switch in skin (MITF) to the brain's fast glutamate receptors (AMPA receptors). He calls the result a "Solar Panel Efficiency" law of evolution. The rhino's armored hide and keratin horn form an "Ohmic shield," a resistor that blocks solar input, so it stays a low-complexity tank. The elephant's thin, blood-rich skin and its sensitive trunk harvest enough light to run the trunk's roughly 100,000 muscles and a large brain.

Hair tells the same story. Gorillas, he says, kept their coats, choosing a stable body temperature over capturing light, so their brains were capped at what digestion alone could supply. Humans, a change he ties to the fusion that formed our chromosome 2, shed most of their hair and turned the whole skin into a neuroectodermal semiconductor (light-handling tissue from the same embryonic layer as the brain) that "remote-starts" the brain's mitochondria.

He adds a twist on what the big brain is for. Humans, in his account, also lost the external magnetic hardware other animals keep, such as long hair, horns and large canine teeth, and needed a bigger neocortex to process the "noise" of an isotopic exhaust that no longer clears as well. He calls the rhino "hardware-dominant" and the elephant "software-dominant," with humans in between: hair, but no tusks or horns.

sections.heading: Mass or time
sections.body:
Kruse frames this with the physicist's "Action," the running total of a system's Lagrangian (kinetic minus potential energy) over its lifetime, which nature tends to keep as small as possible. Bulk, as in the rhino and gorilla, is a strategy heavy on kinetic energy: it wastes energy as heat and shortens relative lifespan. Complexity, as in the elephant and human, leans on potential energy and information, and maximizes what he calls UV-to-near-infrared "income." He notes that the Human Genome Project found species' gene "parts lists" strikingly similar, so the difference, in his reading, lies in the strategy: the elephant chose potential energy and time, the rhino kinetic energy and mass, as ways of dealing with the sun, which he nicknames "the Thief."

From there he restates his long-held "Symmetry Selection" idea, which he says he has proposed for 25 years. Evolution, in his view, selects a symmetry group rather than accumulating random mutations, much as a cooling crystal settles into one lattice. An organism "chooses" the symmetry that keeps its Action lowest under the boundary conditions around it, chiefly UV, near-infrared and nnEMF (man-made wireless and electrical fields). Species are stable phases of a "biological Lagrangian," the MITF–AMPAR axis plays the part of the force-carrying particle, and every cell evaluates its surroundings locally, so DNA is not the boss. In a noisy world of wireless fields and LEDs, he says, that symmetry collapses into simpler, higher-entropy states.

sections.heading: The elephant's toolkit
sections.body:
The trunk, Kruse says, is both antenna and actuator. Its 100,000 muscles are coordinated by phase-locking, through spin filtering (CISS) and an infrared water harmonic near 1878 nm, rather than by heat-generating nerve "computation." He agrees that the trunk works as a water-cooled actuator that grounds the animal and samples Earth's field. Bursts of brain growth 20–26 million years ago, during unstable climate, were in his reading not mutations: the rhino added resistance (armor) to block noisy flux while the elephant raised its "optical indexing" (brain) to process it, conserving its melanin hardware as Noether's theorem (the physics rule tying each symmetry to a conserved quantity) would predict. He also claims the elephant's large brain serves as a resistor, letting it drive the trunk without frying its own circuits, and that elephants lack the brain melanin humans carry.

Tusks have a role too. Ivory is collagen plus hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone and teeth, and Kruse says it turns mechanical stress into voltage, matching seismic and infrasound vibration (sound below human hearing) to the trunk's muscles. Through the living pulp it connects to blood and nerves, a point he says he made in a talk at a dental school in 1986. He calls the tusk a "dielectric mirror" that deflects optical noise away from the brain, and agrees that its spiral growth uses twisting forces to separate isotopes.

Pregnancy is calibration time in his account. At 22 months, the elephant's pregnancy is in his view the longest "optical calibration" of any mammal, needed to phase-lock the 30-million-volt-per-meter field of the inner mitochondrial membrane across a 5,000-gram brain. The rhino's 15 months saves seven months but spends the savings on armor rather than on an optical buffer.

sections.heading: Brains built by vibration
sections.body: Kruse adds that large brains are a "vibrational achievement." The big-brained mammals, he says, all couple sound and light through what he calls a quantum acoustic mirror. Whales and dolphins use sonar in the dense medium of the sea to shake their body water into that mirror. Elephants use infrasound and the rumble of the ground carried up the skeleton's central axis as their own version of a hummed "M." Humans have to hum, laugh and chant on purpose. In his view brains grew large because the water mirror became clear enough for fast signaling by light, not the other way round.

sections.heading: Shrinking again
sections.body: He endorses the idea that the human brain has lost roughly 10% of its volume over the last 10,000 years, and reads it as our own "Neanderthal Event": moving indoors cost people the ultraviolet "clutch" that engages the brain's light machinery. Sunscreen, in the same picture, is a chemical tarp over the skin panel, so the brain that shares its embryonic tissue with skin is left underfed and shrinks further — especially under high-latitude indoor life. Artificial light and electromagnetic interference, he warns, add to that loss.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Because in his model the skin is the solar panel that builds and runs the brain, Kruse wants as much bare skin as possible in real sunlight, not just the eyes, as in his “Midday sun and UV-B, unfiltered” routine, without sunscreen. He warns against building bulk under artificial light at the brain's expense, and asks people to hum, laugh and chant daily to supply the vibration humans no longer get from the ground, while cutting the wireless and indoor light he blames for the shrinking.

articles.title: Deuterium and what to drink
articles.summary: Kruse says healthy mitochondria make their own deuterium-depleted water, that deuterium can only be excreted and should be controlled rather than erased, and that it matters most once magnetic or electrical interference has already damaged the cell's engine.
keyPoints: Kruse says healthy mitochondria make their own deuterium-depleted water at Complex IV, and deuterium can only be excreted, never converted.
In his model deuterium becomes a problem only after magnetic or electrical interference has deformed the cell's engine.
He says a strong, stable magnetic field sorts light hydrogen from deuterium, which matters more than cutting intake.
His water choice is reverse osmosis with UV, copper over plastic, no fluoride, and DDW at 25–105 ppm, never aiming for zero.
He counts pressure from diving or immersion as a broom that clears deuterium, but puts location and light first.

sections.body: Deuterium is hydrogen carrying an extra neutron, which makes it twice as heavy as ordinary hydrogen. Kruse calls clearing it "the real game" for human health, but he argues the body is built to do this itself. The main goal, in his model, is restoring that ability; drinking water with less deuterium is a support, not the fix.

sections.heading: How the body handles deuterium
sections.body:
In Kruse's model, Complex IV — the last step of the mitochondrial energy chain, where oxygen is turned into water — acts as an "isotope mass gate" that makes deuterium-depleted water (DDW). Healthy mitochondria keep their internal water near 90 parts per million (ppm) of deuterium, so only light hydrogen enters ATP synthase, the cell's energy-making motor. Deuterium cannot be converted into anything else; it can only be excreted. Sunlight carries no deuterium, he notes, which is why life built its energy system on light hydrogen.

Deuterium in the blood is normal. Kruse points to a serum table listing it at 12–14 millimoles per litre, two to three times the level of glucose or potassium, and treats it there as a harmless buffer so long as it stays out of the Krebs and urea cycles inside cells. It travels not as a free ion but inside metabolic water from struggling mitochondria, in glucose and amino acids, and in the bicarbonate buffer. The vagus nerve acts as gatekeeper, firing when it senses the electrical charge of the blood drop, and the pancreas, with its rich blood supply, gathers the heavy load and empties it into the upper gut in its bicarbonate juice. Kruse stresses that deuterium becomes a problem only after the cell's "engine" has been deformed by magnetic or electrical interference: a weak or unstable local field, nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring), or artificial light. When the field holding the mitochondrial membrane together collapses, deuterium floods in and jams the motor. A strong, stable horizontal field, by contrast, sorts light hydrogen from deuterium, because their nuclei respond differently to magnetism: ordinary hydrogen's nucleus is a magnet about 3.25 times stronger than deuterium's, so a field can steer the one far more than the other. That, he says, is why coconuts and bananas carry no penalty in El Salvador that they would in Boston. Cutting deuterium intake is always wise, in his view, but sorting it well matters more.

Sorting has limits, though. Someone who grounds but keeps drinking ordinary water of about 155 ppm in a poor-field area, he says, will tan on the outside yet still lock up the inside, because deuterium keeps arriving through the gut.

sections.heading: Water in nature
sections.body:
Light water evaporates first, so heavy water rains out early as weather moves toward the poles, and high-latitude water and food are naturally low in deuterium. Kruse accepts this as the explanation for long-lived Siberians. Yet he says northerners who live indoors under artificial light load up anyway, because a weaker shield and indoor life stop them sorting it. Warm, stagnant seas and desert surface water grow richer in deuterium as light water evaporates.

Big river floodplains gather heavy water too. The Mississippi's draws runoff from vast basins, and he says rain over regions where the compass points far from true north is heavier still, so local water and food carry more deuterium. Each source, he adds, has to be judged by its own hydrology. Deep "primary water," which the geologist Stephan Riess held forms new deep in the earth, has never evaporated and is naturally low in deuterium.

sections.heading: What to drink
sections.body:
Kruse's choice is reverse-osmosis water with a UV stage. He warns against hard, metal-laden well water, especially for people working in heat around farm chemicals. He ranks fluoride worse than iodine in an unstable field: it mimics deuterium, collapses structured water (water ordered into a charge-holding layer) and blinds the body's light sensors. Clean local spring water drunk in the sun is his source of minerals, and deep primary water from volcanic fissures or ancient artesian wells beats surface water.

For DDW he gives a range of 25–105 ppm, against about 150 ppm for tap water, and says how much a person needs is individual — as is whether to drink it daily or in cycles. It works quickly, he says, only when the body's own clearance routes are working. Feeling worse at first is expected in a deuterium-loaded body. He makes his own DDW by running a small current through zinc and copper electrodes in a decanter, which he says copies how mitochondria do it. He warns that commercial hydrogen water, made by splitting ordinary water, carries that water's deuterium with it.

He does not aim for zero. A vortex, in his model, needs a little heavy mass as ballast to catch and hold its spin, and water of pure light hydrogen would let ATP synthase spin out and lose its rhythm. The goal is to control deuterium, not erase it.

sections.heading: Pipes and structure
sections.body:
Plumbing matters too. Copper pipes, he says, give water free electrons and expand its structured layer, while plastic strips its charge — his "plastic static trap" — and weakens the gut microbes' ability to sort deuterium. He extends this to copper drinking vessels: water breaks apart faster on a copper surface, light hydrogen reacts first, and deuterium is held back at the metal's oxide layer, so he says letting water stand in copper for 4–16 hours shifts it toward light hydrogen.

Older cities built vortices into their water systems; at the centre of a water vortex, he says, the lighter, thinner water gathers while heavier water is flung outward. Water cascading down a stepped wall restructures it through the Lenard effect (the charge separation produced when water splashes and breaks).

sections.heading: Pressure as a broom
sections.body: Kruse also counts pressure as a clearing tool. Outside pressure, he says, wrings deuterium out of the thin shells of water that cling to proteins, which is why he suggests everyone may one day need to learn to dive. Deep-diving mammals, he says, use depth this way to lighten their large bodies. He prefers plain pressure, from diving or from immersion at two to three atmospheres on ordinary air, to hyperbaric oxygen, because flooding a body that has slipped into fermentation with extra oxygen feeds disorderly reactive oxygen. As he puts it, oxygen is the fuel and pressure is the broom.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Drinking water: reverse osmosis plus UV” steps: filter by reverse osmosis followed by UV; don't rehydrate on hard well water; avoid fluoride; get minerals from clean spring water in the sun; prefer copper plumbing to plastic. Prefer coconut meat over coconut water as a daily drink (he treats the water as a deuterium load best reserved for blood-like trauma use), and egg yolks over whites for the same isotope reason. His “Deuterium-depleted water targets”: 25–105 ppm in general, made at home or bought, paired with carbonated water and mineral salt (see “Sea salt with DDW ("Jade and Salt")”), and checked by sending a sample to a lab. Diving or other time under water pressure adds a mechanical way to clear it. He treats deuterium as secondary — location and light come first.

articles.title: How deuterium jams the motor
articles.summary: Kruse's account of how deuterium disrupts the cell: it scrambles electron spin, pays a heavy energy "tax" to move, chokes Complex I, makes the ATP synthase motor stutter and stiffens the water around it.
keyPoints: Kruse says deuterium, hydrogen with an extra neutron, disrupts both the quantum and mechanical steps of making energy, with ATP synthase as its main target.
In his model its doubled mass and different spin slow enzymes, scatter spin-sorted electrons and stiffen the water around proteins.
He names Complex I as the most deuterium-sensitive step and reads a high NAD⁺ to NADH ratio as a sign of a deuterium-depleted cell.
He argues the cell's design, from glycolysis to spinning blood and spinal fluid, works to keep deuterium out of the mitochondria.
He pairs deuterium-depleted water with fixing light and location, which he treats as the primary levers.

sections.body: Kruse argues that deuterium (hydrogen with an extra neutron) harms cells not simply by being heavier, but by disrupting both the quantum and the mechanical steps of energy production. Its main target is ATP synthase, the tiny rotary motor in mitochondria that, in his figure, spins about 9,000 times a minute to make ATP, the cell's energy currency.

sections.heading: Why the extra neutron matters
sections.body:
Deuterium is not rare. Kruse puts its level in blood serum at roughly 150 parts per million, more than the calcium, magnesium or potassium doctors routinely measure. That is normal in blood; the trouble starts when it reaches the mitochondria's inner chemistry, where he likens it to a bowling ball hitting a desk fan.

Deuterium has the same charge as ordinary hydrogen but double the mass, and its nucleus has a different spin. Kruse says that spin drifts out of step with the chiral (one-handed) proteins that sort electrons by spin, a process called CISS. He calls deuterium a spin-phase "wrecking ball" that scatters spin-sorted electrons and shifts the outcome of the magnetically sensitive reactions that depend on them.

Every chemical bond vibrates at a minimum energy, its zero-point energy. In Kruse's account deuterium's sits lower, so its bonds need more energy to break and it tunnels (slips through energy barriers by a quantum effect) far less easily. Light hydrogen tunnels almost "tax-free"; deuterium pays a heavy "tax." He says a single deuterium atom locks about 96 surrounding water molecules into a stiffer lattice and drags cell water from its structured, charge-holding state toward ordinary water. Morning infrared, he says, builds exclusion-zone water, the ordered layer water forms beside surfaces, whose walls push deuterium to the edges; nnEMF, blue light or weak spots in Earth's field collapse those walls and let it in.

The slowdown has a name, the kinetic isotope effect: heavier isotopes react more slowly. Kruse says it slows the enzymes of the energy chain and of fat burning two- to sevenfold, weakening the proton gradient that drives the motor and leaking reactive oxygen. Healthy mitochondria normally scrub deuterium by pumping light hydrogen in preference, but a rising load from food overwhelms them.

sections.heading: Complex I takes the first hit
sections.body:
Kruse names Complex I, the entry point of the energy chain, as its most deuterium-sensitive step, and links falling NAD⁺ levels to it. A heavy glucose load forces electrons through this bottleneck. Wireless exposure feeds the jam: citing a 2011 finding that cell-phone fields raise the brain's glucose use, he says nnEMF disorders the water around proteins, the body answers with more blood sugar, and glucose carries deuterium straight to Complex I.

He treats a high ratio of NAD⁺ to NADH, its electron-loaded form, as one of the most reliable signs of a deuterium-depleted cell. In a heavy system NADH carries deuterium where ordinary hydrogen should be, and the enzymes that strip it off slow down. Rebuilding NAD⁺ by the back route, the long kynurenine pathway, is slowed at each step in deuterium-heavy water, yielding a "heavy" NAD⁺ that ferries electrons poorly.

Under that load the cell switches to a side route, the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, which drops electrons further down the chain without pumping protons at that step, so heavy hydrogen is left behind. He calls it "a proton thing, not a food thing." A well-running adult, in his ranking, uses full Complex I, which clear thinking needs; a stressed adult falls back on the shunt. Clearing deuterium and restoring grounding lets the person leave it, and he says the mental haze lifts.

sections.heading: The stuttering motor
sections.body:
On ATP synthase's rotor, a deuteron (a deuterium nucleus) takes a proton's place, binds too tightly and lets go too slowly. The motor stutters, its parts warp, and in his phrase deuterium "strips the gears." ATP output and membrane voltage fall, and the cell drops back to fermentation, the Warburg shift. In his reading, the high blood sugar and insulin that follow are a compensation rather than the root problem: the body floods the jammed engine with fuel, paying what he calls an "entropy tax." In the brain, the same shortage of electrons is misread by reward centres as famine and drives cravings.

The heart and brain feel the shortfall early. In models he cites, a drop of about 5% in ATP efficiency can push heart rate up by as much as 28%. In the brain, the sodium–potassium pump that keeps nerve cells charged uses 20–30% of all its energy; once mitochondria stop making their own water, he says, the pump falters and the brain's alarm centre misfires.

Drawing on Szent-Györgyi, Ling, Prigogine and Becker, he describes ATP synthase as a motor that must stay far from balance. Deuterium pulls it back toward a settled, symmetric state, which for a living system that runs by constantly dissipating energy means death, his "internal rigor mortis." Much of what is called inflammation, he adds, is this lost energy: a slowed motor pushing against thick, low-charge water dumps its effort as trapped heat.

The damage spreads. Deuterium-loaded NAD⁺, which he writes as "NADD+," produces pseudohypoxia: oxygen is present but the cell cannot use it. He says the carbon–deuterium bond also slows the first enzyme of glutathione production by up to tenfold and upsets the last step in making melatonin, so antioxidant protection and night-time repair both falter.

sections.heading: How the body fights back
sections.body:
In Kruse's view the design of complex cells is itself an answer to deuterium. Archaea, one of the two partners that merged to form such cells, tolerated it; bacteria, the ancestors of mitochondria, did not. The merged cell keeps the two apart: the heart's "gravity well" and the swirl of fluid in the brain's fourth ventricle spin deuterium into blood and spinal fluid, which serve as a sink, so the inside of mitochondria stays almost pure light hydrogen.

The ten steps of glycolysis and nine of the Krebs cycle act, he says, as an "isotope centrifuge," harvesting light hydrogen and holding back deuterium before it reaches the motor. Spinning blood and spinal fluid fling deuterium-heavy water outward, where melanin in vessel walls catches it, and joints spin it out by moving. He borrows the power-plant maxim "the solution to pollution is dilution": in any swirling flow the lightest isotope moves fastest, so deuterium is flung aside and diluted. The spinning ATP synthase does the same at the smallest scale, and when the inner mitochondrial membrane holds its full voltage, he says, deuterium cannot get in at all.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: The linked “Deuterium-depleted water targets” protocol calls for deuterium-depleted water in his 25–105 ppm range, paired with carbonated water. He expects people to feel worse at first in a deuterium-loaded body, and treats deuterium as secondary to fixing light and location, since those determine whether the body can sort it. His waking readout: warm in the core but cool on the skin means the membrane is back at full voltage, while waking sweaty or cold and clammy means deuterium is jamming the motors and their output is scattering as heat.

articles.title: Carbon dioxide: breath, sauna and carbonated water
articles.summary: Kruse treats carbon dioxide as a brain protector and deuterium flush, raised by gentle under-breathing, rhythmic CO₂ pulses, sauna and naturally carbonated water.
keyPoints: Kruse sees carbon dioxide as protective, not waste: it shields the brain, releases oxygen into tissues and helps clear deuterium.
In his model CO₂ hands oxygen to tissues through the Bohr effect, so under-breathing can deliver more oxygen than heavy breathing.
He says rhythmic CO₂ pulses wake the brain's waste-clearance system while awake, pumping spinal fluid through tissue.
He pictures the brain's fluid spaces as a motor whose vortex flings deuterium outward and leaves light water at its core.
His practices are Buteyko breathing, CO₂ pulse breathing, traditional sauna and naturally carbonated water with deuterium-depleted water.

sections.body: Most people think of carbon dioxide as waste. Kruse sees it as protective: in his model CO₂ shields the brain from magnetic degradation, releases oxygen into tissues and helps clear deuterium (heavy hydrogen). He argues for holding on to more of it, through breathing, sauna and carbonated water.

sections.heading: Copying the planet
sections.body: Kruse takes Earth's behaviour as his model. During a decline in the magnetic field, he says, volcanoes release CO₂ that dissolves into seawater as a "bicarbonate blanket," changing the water's electrical properties and keeping iodine locked in the sea. He reads rising atmospheric CO₂ (he cites 370 to 426 ppm) and the roughly 5% greening of the planet as Earth's "dielectric booster" — a boost to its charge-holding capacity — as its magnetic shield weakens. His Volcano Protocol copies this response at body scale.

sections.heading: How CO₂ delivers oxygen
sections.body: CO₂, not oxygen, sets the rhythm of breathing. Through the Bohr effect — CO₂ making blood slightly more acidic so hemoglobin lets go of its oxygen — CO₂ is what hands oxygen to tissues. Without enough CO₂ and the nitric oxide made in the sinuses, Kruse says, oxygen stays stuck on hemoglobin: a pulse oximeter reads normal while tissue starves. He calls this the "Deuterium Ghost" and says it shows as dark circles under the eyes and as fatigue, anxiety and brain fog. The less sun a person gets, the better their breathing must be, and he calls mouth-breathing in a high-tech office a "death sentence."

sections.heading: Waking the brain's waste clearance
sections.body:
Kruse cites Dr. Sephira Ryman's team at the University of New Mexico, who alternated room air with CO₂-raised air every 35 seconds for 30 minutes. This woke the glymphatic system — the brain's waste-clearance network that normally runs in deep sleep — while people were awake: vessels opened and closed rhythmically, as in slow-wave sleep, pumping spinal fluid through tissue and flushing out tau and amyloid and, he adds, deuterium. He stresses that the rhythm does the work, and says clearing that debris lets the brain's water restructure.

He reads Kochunov's findings of reduced fluid flow in the brain as a viscosity map. Blood and spinal fluid are thixotropic — they thin as they move — and deuterium's stronger hydrogen bonds thicken them. Where Earth's field is weak, he says, melanin cannot sort deuterium out, so flow slows.

He also points to Russia, which uses CO₂ in its space program — training cosmonauts on carbonated water — and once sold "gazirovka" from street machines. In his reading those machines treated citizens as astronauts on Earth: a street-corner stand-in for missing sun and field, and a cheaper everyday substitute for bottled deuterium-depleted water. He says he spent close to $200,000 translating Russian biophysics papers two decades ago, and that this is why he drinks carbonated water.

sections.heading: The brain's fluid motor
sections.body:
Kruse pictures the brain's fluid spaces as a motor. Tiny beating hairs (motile cilia) on the cells lining the ventricles drive a travelling wave through spinal fluid, much like a stadium wave. Because that fluid is rich in charged salts, he says, the moving wave throws off ribbons of magnetism, with the C-shaped lateral ventricles and the diamond-shaped fourth ventricle acting as the motor's fixed housing. He recalls watching fluid waves in the third ventricle change at sunset during an operation some fifteen years ago, says he spent a decade researching it, and ties the pulsing flow to the timing of the twisting heartbeat.

A vortex, in his view, is the only shape that concentrates energy without heating up. A fast spinal-fluid vortex lowers the pressure at its centre, flings deuterium to the edges and leaves a core of light water where ATP synthase can spin freely. Fluid heavy with deuterium tumbles instead, scattering its energy as the brain fog and inflammation he sees so widely.

Unlike rhinos, which drain passively, humans clear the brain actively, he says: the voice and the jolt of each step help push waste toward the brain's outlet points. Silence, long sitting and artificial light clog those outlets, which he says brings back a metallic taste and mental fog.

sections.heading: Breathing less: Buteyko, Tummo and sleep
sections.body: Buteyko breathing (deliberately breathing less) raises arterial CO₂ to about 40–45 mmHg without lowering oxygen saturation. In Kruse's account this dilates small brain vessels and, through the Bohr shift, sends more oxygen to the brainstem — and, more fundamentally for him, raises magnetic flux so electron spins stay parallel and chiral molecules work. That is why he ranks Buteyko above hard hyperventilation styles that dump CO₂: cold thermogenesis can still fractionate deuterium, but the pairing he prefers is Buteyko with cold, the combo he credits to Russian space practice. In Tummo breathing it is the breath hold, not the active phase, that raises CO₂. Humans breathe at low pressure, he says, so the breath is an under-used exit for deuterium; deep breathing, breath holds and even brass or wind instruments that train the diaphragm for hypoxia can widen it. He says a Buteyko belt slowing breathing during sleep raises CO₂ and magnetic flux in the diaphragm, toning the vagus. A traditional sauna's real benefit, in his view, is its CO₂, not its heat.

sections.heading: Carbonated water and baking soda
sections.body:
Carbonated water with deuterium-depleted water (DDW) is his "gaseous isotope flush": it builds a CO₂–bicarbonate loop that draws deuterium out of spinal fluid and gut. Carbonation also dissolves minerals, making sulfate and magnesium more available; he names San Pellegrino for sulfate and Muszynianka for magnesium. The source rock matters: San Pellegrino flows through dolomite and gypsum and has its CO₂ added at bottling, while Muszynianka is carbonated naturally in volcanic Carpathian rock, and natural CO₂, he says, dissolves more of the rare-earth trace elements he values. Drinking carbonated water in the cold, he adds, strengthens the Bohr effect.

Trouble tolerating carbonated water, he says, signals deeper "lattice lock" (stiff, deuterium-loaded body water). Oral baking soda, his "bicarb hack," copies the roughly two litres of bicarbonate the pancreas releases each day, which in his model flushes deuterium. Citing a 2018 study, he says it signals the spleen through acetylcholine to calm inflammation.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: The linked protocols: drink carbonated water with DDW, favouring naturally carbonated volcanic sources (see “Carbonated water with DDW”); breathe less with Buteyko — a small breath in and out, a 3–5 second nose-pinch hold, then 10 seconds of easy breathing, for 5 minutes — and use a traditional sauna and, if desired, a sleep belt (see “Buteyko under-breathing and sauna CO₂”); alternate room air and CO₂-raised air every 35 seconds for 30 minutes (see “Rhythmic CO₂ pulses (Ryman protocol)”); for a blocked sinus, hum, position the head, do CO₂ breathing and ground in morning sun (see “Sinus-clearing routine”). His Volcano Protocol combines a high-pressure water jet with a 40 Hz tuning fork on the spine, carbonated water, DDW and sauna, and barefoot sunrise on volcanic ground in a pinned Pacific Rim location.

articles.title: Seafood, DHA and careful iodine
articles.summary: Kruse favors wild seafood for DHA and minerals, prefers cold, well-mixed waters such as the Pacific Northwest, accepts antioxidants only within whole marine food, and says iodine is safe only for someone who is pinned.
keyPoints: Kruse calls wild seafood his go-to food because it supplies DHA, magnesium and marine antioxidants in forms the body can use.
In his model DHA is a semiconductor that turns sunlight into current and shields the brain's appetite and energy circuit.
He says where a fish grew matters, ranking cold Pacific Northwest waters above the US East Coast and southern oceans.
He accepts antioxidants such as astaxanthin and vitamin C only as whole food, saying isolated pills scramble membranes and silence useful alarms.
He treats iodine as powerful but conditional: safe for someone who is pinned, risky for someone indoors and unpinned.

sections.body: Wild seafood is Kruse's go-to food. In his model it supplies DHA and magnesium in a form the body can use, along with marine antioxidants bound into whole food. But he attaches conditions, above all to iodine and to where the seafood comes from, that depend on a person's light and magnetic environment.

sections.heading: DHA as a light conductor
sections.body:
DHA is the long omega-3 fat concentrated in the retina and brain. Kruse rejects the textbook view of it as a generic fat for membrane flexibility. Citing Michael Crawford, he treats DHA as a magnetic fat whose semiconductor chain of six double bonds has been conserved for hundreds of millions of years; cholesterol shares that magnetic role, and cardiolipin is the matching fat inside mitochondria that holds Complexes I–IV at the right ångström spacing. Packed into the retina, the brain's master clock and its links to the thalamus, DHA pushes surrounding water into a structured, charge-holding state, so these pathways carry sunlight's signal like fibre optics. How much it helps, he says, depends on how damaged a person's mitochondrial membrane voltage already is — and on whether cardiolipin has been enriched with linoleic chains after the matrix lost its magnetic ground.

DHA is also the raw material for healing signals. Citing Bazan's work, he notes that photoreceptors and neurons lengthen DHA into elovanoids and neuroprotectin D1, messengers that tell inflamed tissue to resolve. When the fat carries deuterium (heavy hydrogen), its bonds vibrate at a different frequency, so these "heal" signals arrive mistuned while the inflammatory signals made from arachidonic acid carry on, his "signal-jamming."

He also calls DHA a Faraday cage (a shield that keeps out stray fields) for the leptin–melanocortin pathway, the brain circuit that reads the fat hormone leptin and sets appetite and energy use. Its fast-moving electrons protect the leptin receptor from oxidative noise, so the brain reads the body's energy stores correctly. Eaten with saturated fat, he says, high-DHA seafood gives the thalamus the shielding it needs to take in magnetic signals.

sections.heading: Why seafood rather than plants
sections.body: Plant protein cannot stand in, in his view. Lentils supply protein but no ready-made DHA and none of the iodine-to-selenium balance of marine food, and treating all animal protein as one category misses that seafood carries electron "instructions" in its DHA. He points to Kerala, where fish is a daily food and the Indian state has the country's highest life expectancy and notably tall young men, crediting small oily fish such as sardines and mackerel.

sections.heading: Where the seafood comes from
sections.body:
That makes the water a fish grew in matter. Kruse says southern-hemisphere seafood has become a concentrated source of deuterium: the water cycle leaves heavier water at those latitudes, and aquaculture, industrial processing and seed-oil contamination of marine food chains add to it. In the Atlantic, he says the slowing of the great overturning current that carries surface water north and sinks it into the deep is leaving deuterium in US East Coast surface water.

His regional ranking follows. The US East Coast is suboptimal. The Gulf is mixed: evaporation adds deuterium, but the Loop Current keeps the water moving. The Pacific Northwest is his preference, because he sees the Pacific's field as steadier and its cold, deep upwelling as lower in deuterium. Oysters show the trade-off: one filters up to 50 gallons of water a day, concentrating whatever is around it, so for people already deuterium-loaded an East Coast oyster's heavy hydrogen may now outweigh its DHA. He says he has switched to Gulf and Pacific oysters.

sections.heading: Antioxidants only as food
sections.body:
Astaxanthin, the red carotenoid in salmon and krill, Kruse accepts only as food, ideally after time barefoot in the surf. Food-form astaxanthin arrives bound to DHA and lines up across the membrane like a wire; isolated or synthetic forms, he says, insert crookedly and scramble the membrane's structure. A long, oil-loving body with water-loving ends, it can span the whole mitochondrial membrane like "structural rebar," acting as a "dielectric sealant" against the shaking wireless fields cause. Its chain of alternating double bonds also quenches high-energy excited states, so he calls it an internal blue-blocker that soaks up the noise mitochondria release before it reaches the nucleus.

Isolated antioxidants also silence a useful alarm. Citing Martin Picard's work, Kruse calls brief bursts of singlet oxygen "mitoception," the cell sensing its own distress, which tell the nucleus and the brain's clock that the local field is compromised and prompt mitochondria to make their own melatonin. Scavenger pills cut that wire. Reactive oxygen, in his view, is a readout of a broken spin filter, not a chemical mess to mop up.

Vitamin C, in his account, is the main guard of brain DHA: when it runs low, DHA oxidises and the brain shifts into an emergency low-oxygen mode. Whole-food vitamin C, together with fat-soluble partners such as vitamin E, protects DHA at the membrane. Extra vitamin C pills often fail to raise levels inside cells, he says, because glutathione normally recycles spent vitamin C; if sulfur metabolism is impaired, the vitamin is used once, breaks down into oxalic acid and leaves. He puts light first: infrared that frees cytochrome c oxidase lowers the oxidative load eating up the vitamin, and he says nothing else works until the cell's water has changed state.

sections.heading: Magnesium
sections.body: Magnesium pills help briefly, Kruse says, but a low-voltage cell cannot hold the mineral. Under nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring) and LEDs the cell's charge flips, it loses its grip on the ion, and the magnesium leaks out, bringing loose bowels or a false calm. He compares it to delivering parts to a factory with no power. His source is wild marine food or local spring water drunk in the sun.

sections.heading: Iodine: powerful but conditional
sections.body:
Citing Küpper and colleagues (2008), Kruse notes that iodide neutralises reactive oxygen up to 500 times faster than vitamin C, and that kelp moves iodide to its surface under stress. He sees iodine as a heavy atom that steadies electron spins in the thyroid, the stomach lining and the brain's fluid. But in people who are indoors, unpinned and out of rhythm, singlet oxygen turns incoming iodide into radicals that damage cardiolipin (the membrane fat that holds the energy chain together) and drop the cell's voltage. Isolated or high-dose iodine, he says, sets off an "uncoupled halide storm."
