Inside the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), a large weak patch in Earth's field over South America and the South Atlantic, he calls iodine use right now "a death sentence."

Mercury, by contrast, does not worry him: the selenium in seafood is, he says, nature's built-in antidote.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Wild seafood, DHA and careful iodine” guidance: eat wild-caught seafood for DHA and magnesium, including small oily fish such as sardines and mackerel, alongside saturated fat, favouring cold Pacific waters over the US East Coast and the southern oceans; take astaxanthin only as food, such as wild sockeye or krill, ideally after barefoot time in the surf; get vitamin C from whole food; limit iodine if you are not pinned (living grounded and sunlit under a stable local field), avoid isolated or high-dose iodine, and take no iodine supplements while living in the SAA.

articles.title: Meal timing and the heme clock
articles.summary: Kruse says when, and under what light, you eat shapes how the body handles sugar more than what you eat, through a heme-based clock that should switch off the liver's night-time sugar output.
keyPoints: Kruse says the timing and lighting of a meal matter more than the food on the plate: light outranks food.
In his model a heme-based clock in the liver should switch off night-time sugar production, and late meals under LEDs break it.
He wants a first meal in the morning after sunrise light, near the cortisol peak, to keep the pancreas's bicarbonate flush running.
He calls eating on a plane the worst case, because the metal fuselage cuts the steadying pull of Earth's field.

sections.body: Kruse argues that the timing and lighting of meals matter more for metabolism than the food on the plate. A steak eaten at 10 p.m. under LEDs, he says, drives night-time glucose output and fat build-up in the liver even at zero carbohydrate, while the same ribeye eaten at solar noon in sunlight does not. His rule is that light outranks food.

sections.heading: The heme clock
sections.body:
In Kruse's account, the liver's night-time brake on sugar production runs on heme, the iron-holding molecule also found in hemoglobin. Heme production inside mitochondria follows the light day: the enzyme that starts it, ALAS1, peaks in the late afternoon, heme itself peaks around dusk, and later in the night the enzyme heme oxygenase-1 turns heme into carbon monoxide. Heme is the key that lets the clock protein Rev-Erbα switch off the liver's glucose-making enzymes overnight, and the carbon monoxide quiets the daytime clock genes.

Because Rev-Erbα must bind heme to work, Kruse calls it a sensor of both mitochondrial health and the local magnetic field. With morning 380 nm light and strong "pinning" (living grounded and sunlit under a stable local field), it rhythmically holds down inflammatory signals such as IL-6 and IL-1β. When its heme "rusts" (oxidises), it fails, inflammation runs unchecked and, he says, the body walls off the damage with adhesions.

Dietary iron, in his view, is only raw material: it sets how strong the heme rhythm is, never its timing. So, against Nick Norwitz and Harvard researchers, he argues that iron from red meat is not what disturbs sugar handling.

sections.heading: What a late meal does
sections.body:
Eating at night under blue-heavy LED light, Kruse says, disrupts melanopsin (the eye's clock receptor) and the retina–clock–liver connection, and flips oxygen into its reactive singlet form. The liver's energy chain stalls and the heat melts its structured water. Without the heme brake, the liver makes sugar and fat through the night and deuterium (heavy hydrogen) pours into the portal vein, his "Sludge Shunt." Eating late also disturbs the spinal-fluid vortex through the gut's vagal nerves and blocks hormone release after dark. He adds that blue-light exposure in newborns disrupts this same heme clock for life.

A late meal also undoes the morning's work. A heavy evening meal under LEDs, he says, silts the engine up again and cancels the deuterium clearing achieved since sunrise. Even a ketogenic diet only pays off for longevity, in his view, when it follows the light: sunset's infrared-rich, blue-fading light flips a melanopsin switch that steers the breakdown of the amino acid tryptophan toward ketones, while the same keto meal eaten under LEDs at 9 p.m. still runs down the sugar-making route. Keto, for him, is a timing loop rather than a food list.

sections.heading: Why breakfast matters
sections.body:
Kruse wants a first meal in the morning, at the peak of the cortisol awakening response. In his model that morning surge raises blood pressure enough to restart the brain's blood and spinal-fluid vortices, and it primes the pancreas to release its roughly two-litre bicarbonate flush, which sweeps deuterium out of the stomach and upper gut. Skipping breakfast stalls the flush, and deuterium pools in the upper gut.

The order still runs light first. Sunrise is the signal that locks the day's rhythm in place, and morning light switches on the Krebs cycle (the mitochondrion's main fuel-burning loop) and the urea cycle so deuterium can be cleared; food belongs after that. He calls breakfast loading the capacitor, and faults the usual approach for eating before light has shaped the system to receive it.

sections.heading: Never on a plane
sections.body: Eating on a plane is the worst case. Inside a metal fuselage at altitude, he says, the steadying pull of Earth's field drops while cosmic radiation and nnEMF from wiring and Wi-Fi rise, so both food and gut tissue lose their magnetic footing. He calls it one of the fastest routes to pseudohypoxia, oxygen present but unusable, in the gut and brainstem.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Eat in daylight, nothing after dark” protocol: eat the main meal near solar noon, ideally outdoors; eat nothing after dark; never eat on a plane; and eat a first meal in the morning, after sunrise light and near the cortisol peak, so the pancreas's bicarbonate flush keeps running.

articles.title: Food: substrate, isotopes and local information
articles.summary: Kruse says food supplies fuel and isotopes but not the magnetic field the cell needs; he favors fat over glucose, low-deuterium plant parts and fresh local food, and rejects any diet as a fix for a location problem.
keyPoints: Kruse says food supplies fuel and isotopes but not the magnetic field the cell needs, so no diet can fix a location problem.
In his model the key questions about food are how much deuterium it carries and the spin state of its electrons.
He ranks animal fat as the most deuterium-depleted fuel and calls glucose a "deuterium bomb," with corn syrup the worst.
He favours leafy greens, saturated fats and wild marine food, and says food should be fresh, local and in season.

sections.body: For Kruse, nutrition is secondary to light and location. Food supplies substrate — electrons and hydrogen to burn — but not the external magnetic reference that, in his model, folds and orients the mitochondria's inner membranes, and it cannot reach the light-run clock that governs fat synthesis. Spaceflight is his proof case: the same carefully measured rations that look ideal on paper fail once magnetic and electric fields and solar plasma change. So no diet can fix what he calls a geometric problem caused by place, light and nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring). Cells, he says, count electrons, not calories.

sections.heading: Food imports spin and isotopes
sections.body:
Kruse reduces diet to one idea: food brings in electron spin states and hydrogen isotopes that either support or disrupt the cell's dynamo. What decides the outcome is how much deuterium (heavy hydrogen) the food carries, the spin of its electrons, whether NAD⁺ ends up loaded with deuterium (his "NADD+"), and whether oxygen stays in its stable triplet form. All of these depend on the field you are standing in, so without a stable local field even the cleanest organic diet ends, in his words, in a singlet-oxygen crash.

That is why he treats more fuel as no answer for a stalled network. A keto flu that never lifts is, in his model, a "Marcus crash." Keto shifts electron input from Complex I to Complex II, which depends on very precise spacing; under magnetic interference the fat-derived electrons pile up and the chain stalls (Marcus inversion — electron flow stalling when pushed too hard). By contrast, if switching to fat brings a felt rise in CO₂ and easier, clearer breathing, he reads that as fat doing its job.

sections.heading: Ranking the fuels
sections.body:
Kruse ranks fuels by their isotopes. Glucose is a "deuterium bomb," because plants pack deuterium into their storage sugars. Burning fat yields deuterium-depleted water and plenty of CO₂, and he calls animal fat the most deuterium-depleted fuel — keto, for him, is a hack of the body's water, not of its macronutrients. Protein is a fuel of desperation. Carbohydrates suit life near the equator under full sun. Fructose drains ATP and halts the cell's clean-water production; he says it evolved as a winter fat-storage switch. Because UV-B slows electron flow, heavy fat and protein under tropical sun fit poorly.

The same logic works inside a single plant. As fruit and tubers ripen, plants park deuterium in their sugars and starches while the leaves stay light, so Kruse calls it an oversight to chase potassium with potatoes, sweet potatoes or coconut water while trying to cut deuterium. His lighter sources are leafy greens, animal fat, avocado, salted nuts and wild marine foods such as squid, octopus, halibut, salmon and clams. Wild ocean fish beat freshwater fish, which he says carry more deuterium from still inland water.

Plant-only and juicing diets often help at first, he says, because people stop eating deuterium-heavy processed oils, wheat and corn, a "system restore" on a crashed computer. But he calls whole-food plant eating a clean, low-torque fuel that in time cannot make enough internal light to keep the system running.

Season changes the engine too. Summer, in his model, leaves metabolism open to deuterium from tropical carbohydrates, while winter cold and fat switch on brown fat, so cells need less insulin.

Saturated fats such as ghee, coconut oil, lard and clarified butter template structured water: citing Abha Sharma and Gerald Pollack, he says they expand the ordered, charge-holding layer of water, with cold ghee producing especially large ones. Seed oils, in his view, harm mainly an ungrounded engine. Egg-yolk choline helps the liver clear deuterium and improves sleep. And salt cannot rescue a deuterium-loaded system.

He also recasts antinutrients, the plant compounds said to block mineral uptake, as largely a deuterium problem. Melanin pulls the deuterium out into the blood, where the glucagon system clears it, so in his view the sun, not avoiding foods, is what neutralises them. Spinach is his cautionary tale: its high oxalate binds iron and calcium, so little of its iron is absorbed compared with the heme iron in meat.

sections.heading: Carbon spin and corn syrup
sections.body:
Isotopes of carbon carry spin too. Carbon-12 has no nuclear spin; carbon-13 does. C3 plants — wheat, rice, trees and most temperate vegetables — prefer carbon-12, giving what Kruse calls a "low-noise" fuel. C4 plants such as maize, sugar cane and sorghum load carbon-13, whose spin adds noise to the electrons food delivers. Because commercial glucose and many supplement bases come from maize, he says they clash with a body tuned to local C3 food.

Corn syrup, in his account, is worse than sugar on three counts. Corn hoards deuterium because it loses little water through its leaves; enzymatic processing in ordinary water enriches it further, since each step uses up light hydrogen first; and the syrup is about a quarter unstructured, deuterium-heavy water with its sugars floating free. Crystalline beet sugar, from a C3 plant, is the lesser harm.

sections.heading: Soil, farming and glyphosate
sections.body: Glyphosate acts, in his model, as a "dopant" — an impurity in a semiconductor — that breaks spin filtering. He also says it pulls magnetic iron out of soil: it props up crops in weak-field land but leaves them deuterium-heavy, and he calls it a melanin inhibitor. He reads the spread of microbial nitrogen fixation on Brazilian soy as a sign that farming inside the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), a large weak patch in Earth's field, has had to turn to microbes. The gut's microbes, he adds, have the same main job: depleting deuterium.

sections.heading: Fresh, local and in season
sections.body:
Food also carries information from where it grew. A freshly picked garden tomato, Kruse says, holds solar infrared, structured water and faint coherent light that the gut reads to set its clock; shipping and display under blue LEDs destroy all three. Hence his long-standing advice to eat within your zip code and in season — a tropical banana in Boston in December is, for him, a quantum error. Weston Price, he argues, mapped local magnetic dynamos, not a food formula.

He adds that deuterium-heavy rain from stalled ocean circulation can turn local food toxic. He redraws John Wesley Powell's 100th meridian, the old line between the humid US East and the arid West, as a boundary of good-quality water that has since moved east. Mississippi-valley water and food, he warns, are more deuterium-heavy than ever, and he says deuterium cuts crop growth by 40%.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Saturated fat as main fuel” protocol: favour ghee, coconut oil, lard and clarified butter; eat egg yolks for choline; keep carbohydrates for equatorial life under full sun, avoid year-round fructose and never use corn syrup; don't make protein a main fuel (no daily protein powder, no carnivore in the tropics); and treat a keto flu that won't lift as a light and magnetic signal, starting with deep cold. His “Eat food from your own zip code” protocol: grow or buy food from where you live, eat in season, get nutrients — potassium included — from local whole food eaten in sunlight rather than pills, avoid maize-derived glucose and supplement bases, and avoid food and water from weak-shield zones such as the SAA.

articles.title: Fat as a capacitor: body fat, fasting and the buffer
articles.summary: Kruse treats body fat as an electrical capacitor and deuterium store that protects heart and brain, so stripping it, or dry fasting without enough of it, backfires; in his view weight gain reflects lost efficiency rather than a calorie surplus.
keyPoints: Kruse calls body fat an "adipose capacitor" that soaks up excess charge and heavy hydrogen to protect the heart and brain.
In his model fat builds up when mitochondria cannot burn the fuel passing through them, so the body parks it as a pressure-relief valve.
He says burning fat yields deuterium-depleted water, which is why he favours saturated fat and cold in a weakening field.
He argues that too little fat, not too much, is the danger, and that stripping fat without fixing light leaves cells "redlined."
He says a dry fast only works with enough body fat, done grounded in morning sun and broken with saturated fat.

sections.body: Kruse turns the usual view of body fat around. In his model fat is an "adipose capacitor," a store that soaks up excess electrical charge and heavy hydrogen to protect the heart and brain, and carrying more of it is a protective response to a struggling energy system rather than the root problem.

sections.heading: Why the body stores fat
sections.body:
Drawing on Enzo Nisoli and Martin Picard's model of fat as a capacitor-like organ, and on Cameron Borg's idea of "energetic resistance," Kruse says fat builds up when mitochondria are stuck in Marcus inversion (electron flow stalling when it is pushed too hard). Under nnEMF (non-native electromagnetic fields from wireless and wiring), blue light and lost grounding, cells cannot burn the fuel passing through them. To avoid a blowout, the body routes the unburned fuel into white fat, which acts as a pressure-relief valve. Nothing raises that resistance, he adds, like deuterium (heavy hydrogen).

Fat also stores deuterium. Visceral fat and fat stored in the liver hold heavy hydrogen away from core organs, and later the fat can be burned for water: citing Kenneth Mellanby's 1942 note in Nature, Kruse says 100 grams of fat yields about 110 grams of metabolic water, twice the yield from the same weight of carbohydrate, and that this water is deuterium-depleted. Babies, he notes, are born fat to build the brain, and fat cells protect the brain by holding deuterium. Extra fat, in his view, may be a "safe mode" that buys time while the environment is put right.

Fat does more than store. It acts as an electrical insulator, a kind of Faraday cage around the gut and heart, and as a reservoir of infrared and faint cell light that gives tissues the inner vibration they need to overcome deuterium's drag. As food chains grow heavier, he predicts, body fat may become a person's last dependable source of light hydrogen, though it only helps if the brain is not already locked up by deuterium.

Fat even senses light. Mammals carry neuropsin (OPN5), the UV-A sensor, in the cornea, skin and fat cells, while birds keep it only deep in the brain and retina. Without 380 nm light reaching fat cells, Kruse says, deuterium backs up into other tissues, the brain included. He frames it as a mammalian bargain: mammals swapped the bird's light-driven energy flow for insulin-sensitive fat storage, which lets them outlast darkness and famine but ties them to a leptin signalling loop that deuterium easily disrupts.

Desert animals show the strategy. Camels, jerboas and desert ants store saturated fat and burn it for their own deuterium-depleted water, rather than relying on surface water that evaporation has made heavy. Their melanin-rich coats, he says, turn sunlight into the electron current that builds that fat. In a weakening magnetic field, he says, "we are all desert mammals," and should shift our baseline fuel toward fat to make the most of this internal light water.

sections.heading: Fats that burn on the spot
sections.body:
Not all fats behave alike. Medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs), especially C8 (caprylic acid), go straight from the gut to the liver and must be burned at once, so they deliver deuterium-depleted water and ketones on demand; long-chain fats can instead be parked in white fat.

Burning fat also routes more electrons through FADH₂, a carrier that enters the energy chain after its deuterium-sensitive first step. That, Kruse says, means fewer protons forced through a deuterium-burdened motor, less leak, heat and reactive oxygen, and intact folds in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is why he calls saturated fat and cold "quantum engineering tools" for a time when Earth's field can no longer steady mitochondria.

sections.heading: The BMI paradox
sections.body:
The danger, in Kruse's model, is low fat mass. Heavier people ride out acute physical stress because their fat buffers the surges, while frail, thin older people have no buffer left. Lean athletes lack the capacitor and can falter suddenly under stress such as heavy EMF exposure, while heavier people survive the first hit. He calls this the "BMI paradox" and puts the danger zone below roughly BMI 20–21.

He expects a weakening field to sort people the same way. Lean, blue-lit, high-carbohydrate people, with no fuel buffer and a deuterium exhaust that depends on the failing field, falter first, while fat-adapted, grounded people keep their internal vortex spinning. Ketosis and cold, which burn fat into internal light, are in his view the ways to keep the brain stimulated from within.

Forcing fat off with calorie restriction or appetite drugs while the light and nnEMF environment stays the same strips the buffer and leaves the cell's voltage "redlined." He warns trainers the same way: shredding tens of pounds before arterial melanin and the blood vortex can hold deuterium dumps heavy water into an unprepared tree. Fix the light signals, clear heavy hydrogen and restore the energy chain, he says, and the body dissolves the capacitor on its own.

Calories, for Kruse, do not explain rising body weight. He points to US national survey data showing calorie intake roughly flat since about 1999 while average weight kept climbing, and reads that as a failure of efficiency, rising deuterium in the food chain plus a disrupted light and magnetic environment, not a surplus of energy. Poverty makes the same point: if weight depended on being able to buy calories, the poor would be thin, yet the poorest groups often carry the most fat. He reads this as field deprivation: cheap LED and fluorescent light, constant screens, dense urban nnEMF, and no time or space for sunrise or bare ground.

sections.heading: Dry fasting needs fat
sections.body:
A dry fast (no food or water) makes the body "drink" from its own fat, so Kruse says it only works if there is fat to draw on: not below about 20% body fat in strong sun (elsewhere about BMI 24). His "coherent" dry fast is done barefoot and grounded in morning sun, ideally with cold, which, he says, draws membrane layers closer so electrons pass more cleanly, and is broken with saturated fat. An indoor fast under LEDs and wireless backfires: no clean metabolic water can be made, and extra fat or ketones only speed the damage.

When the fat that holds the body's light signal is missing, he adds, leptin, the fat hormone he treats as the brain's report on stored energy, falls toward zero and the brain reads endless starvation.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: The linked protocols: run mainly on saturated fat such as ghee, coconut oil, lard and clarified butter (see “Saturated fat as main fuel”); dry fast only with enough body fat, grounded in morning sun, ideally with cold, broken with saturated fat, and never indoors (see “Coherent dry fast”). After drug-driven fat loss he gives morning sun in a clean field away from wireless, deuterium-depleted water at 90–105 ppm with frequent cold immersion, unshielded early infrared and UV-A, timed (2S)-hesperidin, and the oral baking-soda "bicarb hack". For a very low fat store he uses the same base with gentle 80–85 °F water dips instead of deep cold, plus liquid ionic magnesium and trace copper-histidine timed with morning sun.

articles.title: Field direction, local geology and what global maps miss
articles.summary: Kruse says cells respond to the direction of the local magnetic field and how fast it is changing, not its average strength, and that global field models and ground readings smooth those local changes away.
keyPoints: Kruse says cells respond to which way the local magnetic field points and how fast it changes, not its average strength.
In his model a strong horizontal field steadies the cell's spin filter, while a field tipping toward vertical undermines it.
He argues global field models and ground readings smooth away the local jerks and drift that mitochondria actually register.
He says local rock can hold or scramble the surface field, so places must be judged lot by lot.
He tells people to check satellite data for their own area and, where the field is poor, use a magnetic sleep pad.

sections.body: Kruse argues that what your cells respond to is not how strong Earth's magnetic field is where you live, but which way it points and how quickly that direction is changing. Official maps average those local shifts away, so in his model a place can look normal on paper while its field is tilting in ways that undermine mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of every cell.

sections.heading: Direction matters more than strength
sections.body:
At any spot the field has a horizontal part that runs parallel to the ground (he writes it "Bh") and a vertical part that dives into it ("Bz"). In Kruse's model the horizontal part works like a shock absorber for the cell's "spin filter": his name for the way one-handed (chiral) proteins let through only electrons spinning in one direction, an effect physicists call CISS. When a local field tips toward vertical, he says, that filter fails even if total strength is unchanged, and a vertical-dominated zone has only a "razor-thin" margin when the compass direction shifts.

Declination, the angle between compass north and true north, is in his view a measure of mismatch. The body runs on two references at once: true north, fixed by the planet's spin, keeps time for body clocks and the rotation of body fluids, while magnetic north lines up electron spins. He calls the spinning planet the "stator," after the fixed part of an electric motor, and treats declination as the "error rate" between it and the wandering dynamo inside. As the gap widens, the two gears stop meshing, and the body's internal whirlpools lose their timing, so heavy hydrogen is no longer cleared.

He applies this to real places. Citing the World Magnetic Model (the official field map used for navigation) and ESA's Swarm satellites, he says the US East Coast is losing its horizontal component quickly. The geometry he prefers is the one found nearer the magnetic equator: flat field lines, a strong total field and a compass that points close to true north.

The horizontal part also explains, for Kruse, why the Southern Hemisphere has always been the harder half: field lines gather toward the north and spread apart over the south, and southern lands stayed livable only where a strong horizontal component acted as a "magnetic dam," as across Australia, a component he says is now collapsing.

sections.heading: Speed of change
sections.body:
Kruse puts even more weight on how fast the field changes. Geophysicists call the speeding-up of that change "secular acceleration," and sudden lurches "geomagnetic jerks." In the past, he argues, shifts were slow enough for each generation's body clock to recalibrate; today's pace is new. A chart showing a steady 50,000 nT (nanotesla, the unit of field strength) over a decade can therefore hide a jerk that tilts a horizontal field toward vertical within a year. A fixed offset between compass and true north may be survivable, he says; erratic wandering is the warning sign, because it means the outer core itself is unstable.

Behind this sits a rule he repeats often: almost every natural magnetic field lasts only as long as a conducting fluid keeps moving. Where the molten iron beneath a region slows, the field above it decays, and the surface feels it as drift and jerks.

sections.heading: What global models miss
sections.body:
The standard models, the World Magnetic Model and the IGRF, are smooth mathematical averages built for navigation, and Kruse says they deliberately iron out regional accelerations. Mitochondria, in his view, register the local ripple as it happens, so the models produce a "linearization mirage" of stability. He sees the real driver as the "non-dipole" field: patches at the surface of Earth's core with reversed polarity, which he says are deep and long-lived (citing de Oliveira, 2024) and speed up local decay. Declination stays useful as a shortcut; he calls it a "geographic multiplier" rather than the root cause.

Timing makes this worse. The World Magnetic Model is refreshed only every five years, while non-dipole features such as the South Atlantic Anomaly move and pulse faster, so jerks like those of 2025–2026 appear only after the models are corrected. Ground readings have their own blind spot: local iron deposits, basalt and wireless fields form what he calls a "magnetic fog" over the core's signal. Only satellites above the crust, such as Swarm, can tell a global trend from local interference. Even they record strength rather than the field's twist and coherence, which he likens to measuring a tornado with a thermometer.

sections.heading: The brain senses direction
sections.body:
For proof that people register field direction, Kruse cites the 2019 Caltech study by Joseph Kirschvink and Connie Wang: alpha brain waves dropped by about 25% when the direction of an Earth-strength field was rotated, with its strength unchanged. He takes this to mean that the thalamus, the brain's relay center, works as a magnetic sensor.

Heavy hydrogen, he argues, dulls that sense further. Citing an *eLife* paper, he says a radical pair (two molecules sharing linked unpaired electrons, the basis of many proposed biological compasses) grows less sensitive to weak fields as "hyperfine" interactions with nearby nuclei multiply. Deuterium's nucleus adds exactly that noise, so in his model it blinds the sensor, his "hyperfine noise trap."

sections.heading: The rock under your feet
sections.body:
Local geology, Kruse says, modifies all of this. Volcanic or iron-rich rock carries magnetism frozen in when it formed and can hold a flat "micro-field" at the surface even while the regional field tilts; he names El Salvador's volcanic front and the iron-rich bedrock of New York's Adirondacks. Natural currents in the crust also travel along faults, and saltwater-soaked limestone can carry electrical noise for miles. For these reasons he judges places lot by lot rather than from a national map.

He sums this up as the "local stator" rule: global averages can no longer be trusted anywhere, and the rock underfoot decides. Because cooling lava records the field of its day, old rock can work against the present field. On Hawaii's Kīlauea, he says, compasses spin or point south because older basalt below set during the reversed field before the last pole swap, about 780,000 years ago, and overpowers today's weaker field. He likens such patchworks, in Hawaii and New Zealand's North Island, to standing on a reversed battery: the mineral fuel is there but the ignition is noisy. He prefers thick crust of consistent normal polarity near zero declination, noting that Central America was laid down about 80 million years ago.

In practice, he tells people to look beneath the smoothed maps: compare Swarm data and secular-acceleration charts for their own zip code over time, and move to stable ground if the area shows a jerk or turns toward vertical. Where the local field is poor, the linked magnetic sleep pad protocol uses a static magnet pad at night as a personal stand-in, though he warns that a strong vertical field at night and a very different field by day can confuse the brain's sense of direction.

articles.title: Grounding, and why the ground matters
articles.summary: Kruse says barefoot contact with conductive earth feeds the body electrons that keep oxygen in its safe state and drain the day's built-up charge, but how much it helps depends on the ground, your posture and the local magnetic field.
keyPoints: Kruse says barefoot contact with conductive earth feeds the body electrons that keep oxygen in its stable state and drain built-up charge.
In his model grounding fixes only the electric half of the problem; a weak or shifting magnetic field still needs addressing.
He says the ground matters: salt-soaked limestone near infrastructure carries stray current, while dense basalt insulates against it.
He prefers feet and hands on wet sand, surf, dewy grass or basalt at dawn, with as much skin as possible in open air.

sections.body: Grounding, or "earthing," means skin-to-earth contact: bare feet on soil, sand or rock, or in the sea. Kruse argues it gives mitochondria a steady electrical reference that indoor life removes, and that this matters more as Earth's magnetic field weakens. In his model, though, grounding is only as good as the ground you stand on, and it cannot replace a good magnetic field.

sections.heading: What grounding does
sections.body:
Kruse describes the planet as a battery: the churning iron core (the geodynamo) keeps a large reservoir of free electrons at the surface, and the body is conductive enough to draw on it. Those electrons, he says, keep oxygen in its "triplet" state, its normal and stable spin arrangement, instead of letting it flip into reactive "singlet" oxygen. He adds that grounding restores Zeeman splitting (the way a magnetic field separates electron energy levels) in heme, the iron-containing core of blood and respiratory proteins, which he calls the body's magnetic antenna.

The result, in his account, is a steady electrical baseline for the inner mitochondrial membrane, the surface where energy is made, that bypasses swings in the local field. That is why he treats grounding as a stabilizer where the field is declining or shifting, and why he says sleeping grounded lets the body's night-time repair circuit run.

He borrows a picture from boatbuilding. Boat owners bond their hulls to ground so that stray currents cannot eat the metal away by galvanic corrosion (metal slowly dissolving when an unwanted current runs through it), and he sees grounding a person as the same protection. Through the day, he says, wireless fields and blue light leave the body holding excess positive charge and heat-like disorder; contact with the earth dumps that load into the soil, which he treats as the heat sink for the night's repair work.

He lists what follows. Earth electrons cancel the positive charge that builds up when cells switch into their defensive shutdown mode. Red blood cells regain the surface charge that makes them repel one another, their zeta potential, so the blood runs thinner. Cortisol settles back into its 24-hour rhythm, and mitochondria work better, clearing the way for the bicarbonate flush that carries deuterium out.

He links this to Robert Becker's "current of injury," the small natural current that steers tissue repair, and to a surgeon's chance finding that a weak current can reshape cartilage. The Hunza, he says, get such currents free from their mountains' steady natural field and the sun, which keeps their collagen and elastin supple. He pictures the grounded body as a pyramid, the brain at its apex catching light and the feet as its base on the earth; cut off the ground and, in his phrase, you become a "Maillard oven," slowly browning from inside the way food browns when cooked.

He extends the antenna idea to hair and skin, which he describes as a liquid-crystal "phased-array radar" tuned to the planet's field. Drawing on a clairvoyant's account of needle-thin blue rays (about 435–465 nm) standing at right angles from each hair even when the hair lies flat, he calls these rays a "topological surface state" and the lead wires for Becker's current. Deuterium, he says, "neutralizes" hair and thickens the skin until it carries this information poorly. Acupuncture, in his reading, works by inserting a better antenna: the metal needle acts as a "lightning rod" that re-pins the protons in local tissue water and bypasses the deuterium-frosted skin. He calls shaving a man's beard "magnetic castration," because it removes the anchor for those rays and, in his account, leaves the vagal exhaust unable to set his field right.

sections.heading: Only half the solution
sections.body: Grounding fixes only half the problem, Kruse argues. Melatonin, which cells make at night as an antioxidant shield, needs both electric and magnetic containment. Grounding restores the electric side, but magnetic disorder from a weak field or wireless devices is harder to block. So in a magnetic "dead zone," or where declination changes steeply, standing on grass is not enough on its own.

sections.heading: Not all ground is equal
sections.body: The type of ground matters. Kruse's concern here is not Wi-Fi, which water absorbs quickly, but low-frequency electrical noise such as power-grid leakage and stray currents. Limestone riddled with water channels and soaked with saltwater (karst) conducts that hum sideways for miles, so grounding on it near resorts or heavy infrastructure is, he says, like grounding to a live wire. Dense cities are worse still: in New York underground utilities create jump conduction into sidewalks and manholes, so bare feet on city metal mimics a weakened dynamo — he points people to bedrock parks instead. Quiet rural karst is less of a problem, but he still rates Florida and Mexico's Yucatán as poor places to ground during the decline. Dense basalt, by contrast, insulates against that sideways noise and connects you to the steady local charge of the rock.

sections.heading: Posture at dawn
sections.body:
How you ground matters too. At the beach he prefers only the feet and ankles in wet sand or shallow surf, with as much skin as possible in open air. Water absorbs the near-infrared light of sunrise and, he says, acts like a shield, so neck-deep immersion blocks the dawn signal the skin is trying to catch. Salty water at the shoreline, as on El Salvador's Costa del Sol, links you to the earth's steady current while bare skin charges the melanin antenna, which he says helps move heavy isotopes out through the feet.

His fullest version he calls "mammalian sphinxing": facing east at sunrise on all fours, so that hands as well as feet, with their sweat glands, touch the earth. The extra electrons, he says, let the body capture more of the dawn light, provided its water is in the structured state he scores at about 160 on the dielectric scale (a measure of how well water stores charge) rather than the 78 of ordinary water; sunlight itself pushes that number up. In his account this lowers the body's need to pull electrons from food and quiets mTOR, the cell's main growth signal, at no cost.

Even occasional contact counts in his model. People who sometimes ground or catch morning sun fare differently from those who never do, which he calls the "Earth–Sun circuit breaker": the earth supplies electrons that restore the charge of blood-vessel linings, while sunrise infrared frees cytochrome c oxidase, the mitochondrial enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen. He says people with stiff, weak collagen typically get too little of both.

In practice, the barefoot grounding protocol asks for 20–60 minutes a day barefoot in surf, wet sand or dewy grass or on basalt, ideally at dawn, with basalt or wet volcanic black sand preferred. Avoid salt-soaked limestone near resorts or big power lines, check a spot with a meter if stray current worries you, never join dissimilar metals in a grounding connection, and use a low-resistance indoor grounding system as the fallback.

articles.title: Volcanic ground, basalt and passive anchors
articles.summary: Kruse says magnetic volcanic rock locks in a flat local field and holds water and clouds in place, so grounding on basalt beats any device, and passive stone or copper anchors beat powered ones.
keyPoints: Kruse says basalt's frozen magnetite holds a flat, stable local field at ground level even as the planet's field weakens or tilts.
In his model, grounding barefoot on volcanic rock charges the body's melanin antenna and helps it shed deuterium, beating any powered device.
He calls El Salvador a "geological ark" because of its low latitude, east–west volcanic chain and distance from the South Atlantic Anomaly.
He reads megaliths and pyramids as ancient attempts to copy a volcano's steadying effect on the field and on water.
Where volcanic ground isn't available, he prefers passive basalt, copper rings and copper–rare-earth jewelry to stimulators that push current into tissue.

sections.body: "Volcano Rx" is Kruse's name for living on, and grounding barefoot on, magnetic volcanic rock. In his model basalt holds a stable, flat magnetic field at the surface even when the planet's field weakens or tilts overhead, which makes volcanic regions refuges during the current decline. He ranks this above any device and offers passive stone and copper tools for people who cannot yet live there.

sections.heading: How basalt holds a flat field
sections.body:
Kruse starts from the rock itself. Lava from the mantle is rich in iron, and as it cools below about 550 °C, its Curie temperature (the point below which a mineral can hold magnetism), tiny crystals of magnetite line up like compass needles with the field of that moment and keep that direction permanently. Most volcanic rock is basalt, so large volcanoes and lava tubes create strong local magnetic anomalies. Drawing on Yannick van Doorne's work, he adds that basalt's iron and magnesium make it paramagnetic, so it gathers and concentrates field lines, though only through its tie to the regional field: basalt sand spread through a house with no such connection, he says, "makes zero sense."

Where the regional field is tipping toward vertical, this frozen magnetism bends the lines flat into a horizontal micro-field at ground level, a "lithospheric straightener." Grounding barefoot on basalt then supplies, in his account, a dense stream of earth-current electrons that charge the mitochondrial membrane, help ATP synthase (the rotary enzyme that makes the cell's energy currency) repel deuterium, or heavy hydrogen, and support melanin. He calls the rock a "second battery" for the body's melanin antenna and calls PEMF (pulsed electromagnetic field) devices the "loser option."

Not every volcanic place works. Hawaii's rock, he argues, froze during the reversed field before the Brunhes–Matuyama pole swap about 780,000 years ago, so it can cancel today's field instead of adding to it; El Salvador's younger rock carries no memory of that flip. Active volcanoes pin best, because every magnetic field needs moving charge, and his own homes sit over water-filled lava tubes he likens to a dynamo. Even a good volcano helps only if it is free of heavy wireless exposure.

sections.heading: Cloud caps and black sand
sections.body:
Kruse reads the sky over a volcano as a gauge. Water molecules, being tiny magnets, are drawn into the field the rock gathers around the cone. A cloud that sits on the summit for long stretches, like those over Ometepe or El Salvador's volcanoes, is in his words water "pinned to the stator," shielding the people below from cosmic rays. He says the Maya chose sites near volcanoes and cenotes (natural sinkhole wells) where clouds linger, because that water is lighter in deuterium.

The coast adds a second battery. El Salvador's black-sand beaches are grains of magnetite and ilmenite that keep the field strength of the eruptions that made them, and salty waves washing over them induce a small field of their own. In his view the shoreline is a high-flux zone that resists the South Atlantic Anomaly. He rates the volcano above the beach in the dry season and expects the beach to pull ahead in the wet season, when lightning strikes the lava tubes.

sections.heading: Why El Salvador
sections.body:
Kruse calls El Salvador a "geological ark." It lies near the magnetic equator, where the field already runs flat; its fault zone and volcanic chain run east to west, matching those flat lines; and slowly cooled magma bodies deep below act as a hidden anchor. He adds that it has sat near an agonic line (zero declination) for about 11,500 years. Within the Central American Volcanic Arc, El Salvador packs in more volcanoes per square kilometer than its neighbors, and the arc stays clear of the South Atlantic Anomaly.

He also points to heat from below. Young lava and hot-water vents create local highs and lows in the field that, he says, filter out noise and steady the local signal. Groundwater in volcanic regions, he argues, is low in deuterium because the churning magma works for the planet the way the choroid plexus, the tissue that makes the brain's fluid, works for the body; he drills his own wells into this water. Even earthquakes help in his account, acting as a "mechanical dither" that clears background noise so the body's clock genes can pick up Earth's rhythm.

sections.heading: Ancient builders
sections.body:
Kruse believes earlier cultures understood this. He reads the perforated magnetite blocks at the Olmec site of San Lorenzo as a deliberate grid to restore a stable reference field when the dynamo sagged. Megaliths and dolmens of basalt and quartz-rich stone were, in his view, "paramagnetic sponges" that concentrated a weakening field inside the chamber.

Pyramids, in his reading, were "reverse volcanoes." The Maya, he says, began in volcanic El Salvador and, as they moved north away from the volcanoes, built stepped forms (he cites ~70° faces) to copy their effect. Built over cenotes and aquifers, and finished with limestone stucco that he says carried rare-earth dust from asteroid-scarred ground, such structures in his model spun deuterium out of the water table, leaving lighter water for drinking and crops when paired with copper. At Tikal he says they purified pool water with rare-earth minerals and zeolite, and that assays later found cyanobacteria, deuterium and mercury there. At Chichén Itzá's ball court he reads rare-earth–loaded plaster as a magnetic–acoustic chamber, the effect he copies with volcanic rock at his clinic. When the Yucatán anomaly and rain-only cenote hydrology outran those fixes, cities such as Copán, Tikal and Chichén Itzá were abandoned; living Maya later pinned again on El Salvador's young basalt around Cuscatlán.

sections.heading: Passive anchors: stone, copper and rare earth
sections.body:
On his own buildings he uses laja, a rare-earth–rich volcanic stone from Guatemala and El Salvador, for magnetic-acoustic and magnetic-electric effects like Mayan ball-court plaster. For people not yet on volcanic ground, he prefers passive tools to powered stimulators that push "harsh, non-native" current into tissue. While grounded, rest a smooth basalt stone or volcanic clay behind the ear or on the temple, which he calls a "zero-frequency amplifier," or keep a paramagnetic stone in the pillow. Copper enters in two lineages he now teaches together: Georges Lakhovsky's open rings (ends unjoined) as a Schumann / vagal antenna, and Slim Spurling's closed copper coils, which he links to post-Carrington vineyard hacks that kept oxygen triplet and water light around living tissue. For travel and other ungrounded hours he adds jewelry that mixes copper with a rare-earth such as neodymium — elements he says hold a static magnetic field even when ambient flux is thin — so body electrons stay polarized toward triplet oxygen. The neck remains his preferred target, his "vagal vortex."

In practice, the barefoot grounding protocol says to ground on basalt or wet volcanic black sand. The El Salvador guide lists his preferred spots near active volcanoes such as Ilopango and says to test any lot with mosquitoes and candles before buying. The basalt-and-copper-ring protocol covers the stone, open or closed copper, rare-earth travel jewelry and pillow options, which he frames as a bridge while you fix your location. His Volcano Protocol copies a volcano's answer at body scale, pairing life in a pinned, low-latitude place and sunrise grounding on volcanic ground with steps to shake deuterium from the spine and build up carbon dioxide.

articles.title: Choosing a place to live
articles.summary: Kruse calls location the final arbiter of mitochondrial health and gives three field numbers, a gravity-and-light case for the tropics, a way to read the declination map, geology to avoid and on-the-ground tests for choosing it.
keyPoints: Kruse says where you live decides how hard your mitochondria must work, and no diet or supplement can outrun land with a failing field.
He looks for high field intensity, flat inclination and near-zero declination, ideally where an agonic line meets volcanic ground under strong sun.
In his model the tropics win because weaker gravity, steady strong light and a flat field all lower the cost of shedding deuterium.
He rules out stressed fault zones, the South Atlantic Anomaly and wireless-heavy "smart" homes, and tests a lot with mosquitoes and candles.

sections.body: For Kruse, where you live finally decides how well your mitochondria can run: no supplement, diet or exercise plan can outrun land that has lost its magnetic footing. He gives three numbers to look up, a way to read the declination map and tests for a specific lot, and he says your location sets how hard you must work every day to stay well.

sections.heading: The three numbers
sections.body:
His checklist uses the World Magnetic Model, the official field map. Total intensity, the field's strength in nanotesla (nT), should be as high as possible: above about 45,000 nT, ideally up to 60,000. Inclination, the angle at which field lines dip into the ground, should be 0–45°; flat lines, he says, anchor the body's internal axes, while lines plunging steeply toward the poles destabilize them. Declination, the angle between compass north and true north, should be close to 0°. A line of zero declination is called an agonic line, and on it there is no twist between the planet's spin axis and its field. He also says to avoid the South Atlantic Anomaly, a huge weak patch that, he says, now reaches the Caribbean.

The best places, in his model, are where an agonic line crosses a volcanic chain at a latitude with strong sun: his "fountain of youth coordinate." He prefers young volcanoes that still hold a strong horizontal field along the Pacific Rim — Bali through Central America toward Panama — and treats South America's rim as blocked while the South Atlantic Anomaly dominates it. That corridor cannot absorb mass migration. Agonic lines move about 55 km a year with the poles, so a good 2026 spot may fail in 2027; tens of yards off the zero line can add about 1% declination — his Marcus "car crash." He warns against chasing an agonic line alone (his "Mayan trap"): marry field to sun.

sections.heading: Why the tropics: gravity, light and noise
sections.body:
Kruse adds a reason for the tropics that has nothing to do with the field: gravity. Because the planet spins, it bulges at the equator, so gravity there pulls slightly more weakly than near the poles. Deuterium weighs twice as much as ordinary hydrogen, and he argues that pushing it out of cells and body fluids costs more energy the harder gravity pulls.

He frames this with Maxwell's demon, the imaginary gatekeeper from physics that sorts fast molecules from slow ones. Sorting is never free: Landauer's principle holds that handling information always gives off some heat. In his model each cell is a demon sorting heavy hydrogen from light, and the equatorial bulge is the planet's own, larger demon that lowers the price.

Above roughly 35° latitude, he says, people are squeezed from two sides. Ultraviolet light and the short-wave infrared he prizes are weak or missing for much of the year just where gravity is strongest, so cells must move heavy hydrogen "uphill" with little light to power them. Wireless fields add a third load: in the demon picture they are pure noise the cell must sort, at a heat cost. Weak gravity, steady strong light and a flat field together are why, for him, the tropics always come out ahead.

Altitude counts against a place as well. Cosmic rays, and the tritium they make, increase with height, so within the good zone he favors living nearer sea level. Only some maternal lineages, in his view, cope with high mountain life.

sections.heading: Reading the maps
sections.body:
In his reading of the declination map, green (the agonic line) is best — the zero-degree path that, in his model, lines up cristae and inner-mitochondrial junctions for optimal energy. Red (east) is mixed and bold dark blue (strong west) is very bad. Where the lines bunch, the field can change over tens of miles and warp membranes as you move; that alone is a reason to leave. He treats ESA Swarm / World Magnetic Model maps as a picture of that geometry and compares the same date across years.

The standard UV index, he says, is useless for this, because it ignores declination and the local deuterium load. Sydney and Perth can share a UV reading, yet in his view Sydney, under steadier field conditions, works like a "quantum processor," while Perth, on the approach of the South Atlantic Anomaly, is a "Maillard oven" that browns tissue. Deserts give strong light but a weak magnetic background, and dry sand gives no ground, so he advises against raising children there.

sections.heading: Faults and plate boundaries
sections.body: The geology beneath a region can rule it out. Kruse singles out the New Madrid Seismic Zone between Memphis and St. Louis, which sits on a failed rift over hot, wet, weak mantle. Unlike the frozen magnetism of old lava, he calls it an active "induction zone": under crustal stress, he says, the fault gives off broad-band electromagnetic signals, so the local field turns spiky and the body's repair window unreliable. Watching the zone affect people during 18 months in nearby Cape Girardeau confirmed his earlier move out of middle Tennessee. He is similarly wary of the Azores, where three plates meet.

sections.heading: Testing a lot
sections.body: Before buying land, Kruse reads what lives there. Mosquitoes active by day as well as night, a 24-hour beeswax candle that burns out early and a faltering local water cycle all warn of a weak spot; he used mosquitoes and candles to choose his own property. A "smart" house full of wireless devices, he says, cancels even a good location.

sections.heading: Where he says no, and where he says yes
sections.body: He still rules out California's "double deficit" of high declination and weak steady UV-B — Malibu around −13° — and treats deserts as magnetically poor even under strong UV. From 2024–2026 he ranks the West Coast better than the East because the Pacific thermohaline still runs while the Atlantic (AMOC) and Southern Ocean have stalled; Florida's lost oranges since about 2012 mark the same signal. Texas stays weak. Iceland is not a relocation answer. His longer no-list includes Colorado, Hawaii, Minnesota, Canada, the UK, Germany, Mexico's Yucatán and Australia; South America is most dangerous as the anomaly grows. In the US only the Pacific Northwest is really pinned (a growing offshore lava dome). Pacific Rim spots like Bali, even the Aleutians, can beat Miami. His own choice remains El Salvador's volcanic coast over Yucatán cenotes, avoiding crowded wireless beaches like El Zonte.

sections.heading: After the move
sections.body:
Before a permanent move he often recommends a two-to-three-month stay in a candidate place, so the body can answer whether a city such as New York, Chicago or Miami is still livable. After moving, he warns people can feel worse first. Borrowing Becker's "adaptive healing," he says tissue has to rebuild for the new environment, as modern current through 1920s wiring can burn a house down. Northern lineages should adapt to tropical sun gradually.

In practice, the relocation checklist gathers his criteria: the three World Magnetic Model numbers, avoiding the South Atlantic Anomaly, reading declination and Swarm maps, steering clear of stressed faults such as New Madrid, grounding on basalt or wet black sand, testing lots with mosquitoes, candles and the water cycle, a trial stay of months when possible, no smart house, and ground-floor living. The El Salvador guide adds his local notes: buy an empty lot and build, favor areas near active volcanoes, and use the Costa del Sol beach for sunrise grounding.

articles.title: Electroculture: growing food in a weakening field
articles.summary: Kruse says a weakening magnetic field and deuterium-heavy water are cutting crop yields, and that electroculture, basalt and low-deuterium water can keep food growing where the field still holds, while melanized fungi keep the rain coming.
keyPoints: Kruse says a weakening field and deuterium-heavy soil water slow photosynthesis, and that lighter water raises crop yield by about 40%.
In his model, buried magnetic antennas and basalt create soil currents and gradients that push deuterium aside, echoing Steiner and Schauberger.
He reads magnetic C4 crops giving way to C3 crops, and an eastward-moving 100th meridian, as signs of the field's decline.
He sees melanized fungi seeding rain as nature's backup, and says electroculture only pays where the field still holds.

sections.body: Kruse argues that plants suffer the same physics he describes in human mitochondria. As Earth's field weakens, soil water carries more deuterium (heavy hydrogen), photosynthesis slows and harvests shrink. He says lowering the deuterium in a plant's water raises yield by about 40%, and that raising it costs about the same. Electroculture, the practice of using buried wires, magnets, antennas and stone to shape the electrical and magnetic environment of soil, is in his view a practical, decentralized way to keep food growing through the decline.

sections.heading: Deuterium and the harvest
sections.body:
Deuterium in a plant's water, Kruse says, causes the same "kinetic isotope drag" it causes in people: enzymes slow, proteins and their water shells stiffen, protons tunnel less easily and the chloroplasts (the plant's light-harvesting compartments) lose efficiency. Lighter water reverses this. The plant makes metabolic water faster, its water holds charge better, it takes up nutrients more readily and it photosynthesizes more efficiently, which he gives as the basis of his 40% figure.

He expects photosynthesis itself to come under attack. Over the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA), the large weak patch in Earth's field, more particle radiation gets through, loading air and water with heavier hydrogen and raising reactive oxygen in chloroplasts. A weak field also disturbs the plant's own magnetic sensors, the cryptochromes, and the iron–sulfur proteins of its electron chain. Plants, in his account, pay the same entropy price that mammals pay.

sections.heading: How electroculture works in his model
sections.body:
He points to Yannick Van Doorne's magnetic antenna: a galvanized steel wire laid north–south 20–30 cm underground and connected to a beeswax-coated magnet with its north pole facing geographic north. Van Doorne reports yield gains of 30% or more in the first year, building over three to five years. Kruse's explanation is that such antennas set up tiny vortices, telluric currents (natural ground currents) and magnetic gradients in the soil water that push the heavier deuterium aside, a plant version of the burst of deuterium-depleted metabolic water that ketones give a person.

He traces the roots to Rudolf Steiner's biodynamic farming and Viktor Schauberger's work on vortexing water and avoiding steel tools that disturb its structure. Neither used the word deuterium, he says, but both were chasing the same coherent, low-deuterium water. He adds that placing basalt, or minerals such as jade, in particular geometries raises the dielectric constant (charge-holding capacity) of water in soil or in the body. Steiner knew it, he says, and growers will have to relearn it to feed people in a magnetic decline. The pyramids of the ancient world, built over aquifers and cenotes, are in his reading the monumental version: devices that concentrated the field into the water table to yield lighter water for crops.

sections.heading: Plants as field sensors
sections.body:
Kruse treats plants as living sensors of what he calls the "Universal Stator," his term for the field that organizes living systems. Building on a member's note that the ash of C4 plants is far more magnetic than that of C3 plants, he says C4 species such as maize, sorghum and tropical grasses carry two to four times more iron oxide and raise the soil's magnetic susceptibility (how strongly it responds to a magnet) by 30–40% after burning. He calls them "magnetic athletes," built for a strong dynamo. C3 crops such as wheat and rice are the plant kingdom's "safe mode," and their dominance on the Great Plains is, to him, the signal of the field's "Siberian Jerk" and the SAA's spread, compounded by the oxygen-poor, isotopically heavy water of a failing Atlantic overturning current (AMOC). Glyphosate, he says, chelates (binds and strips) the soil's magnetic iron; it keeps the crops alive but leaves them high in deuterium and low in what he calls magnetic torque.

He reads the map the same way. John Wesley Powell marked the 100th meridian as the line between the humid East and the arid West, a warning Kruse dates to 1860, a year after the Carrington Event. Powell took the line as fixed; Kruse says it is tied to the dynamo and is now moving east; he notes that tornado alley has shifted from Tulsa toward Nashville and that in 2025, for the first time, most confirmed US tornadoes struck east of the Mississippi. The Ogallala aquifer running dry forces surface water that evaporation has made heavy; Texas's Edwards Aquifer and springs such as Barton Springs, he says, face the same emptying and deuterated rain; the Mississippi valley's water is more deuterium-heavy than ever, so the food it grows will be too — the same deuteration he blames for Florida's lost orange industry.

sections.heading: Fungi as the backup rainmakers
sections.body:
When the field fails, Kruse says, the biosphere reroutes through older, radiation-hardened life. He cites a new Science Advances paper, summarized in Anton Petrov's April 24, 2026 video and backed by work in PNAS, reporting that Mortierellaceae fungi release soluble ice-nucleating proteins into the soil. The fungi acquired the gene for these proteins from bacteria (a relative of the bacterial InaZ gene) by horizontal gene transfer. The proteins form complexes of more than 100 units, drift into the air and seed ice, and so rain, at warmer temperatures than volcanic mineral dust, and could one day replace silver iodide in cloud seeding.

His addition is the "missing layer": melanin-armored fungi survived the weak-field intervals of the Neoproterozoic, about a billion years ago, and keep the water cycle running when the dynamo falters. Fungi weather basalt aggressively, so he expects basalt soils and melanized fungi to become nature's geoengineering stack in a decline, with measurably more soil fungi inside the anomaly. Mammals, by contrast, have no such backup and pay what he calls a "POMC/SCN time-over-energy tax."

sections.heading: Where it works
sections.body: Electroculture is not a fix everywhere. Asked whether biodynamic vortexed preparations, spiral horns or field-broadcasting "towers of power" could help farms, Kruse says they become superfluous where the field has already gone; the wise watch what happens to living things in the ground and adjust. He sends growers to basalt-rich regions with magnetic promise such as El Salvador, where he says C4-type life still thrives without chemical help, and no longer treats high-latitude basalt such as Iceland as a place to relocate. He says two growers he lectured, Billy and Logan, tested his claims in the US, one of them in North Carolina, in what he calls "magnetic excursion land," found them borne out, and now plan to bring their methods to El Salvador, his "ARK," which he predicts will become North America's new Midwest.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Kruse's “Eat food from your own zip code” approach applies here: eat food grown where the field and water are good, and avoid crops from weak-field zones. He says he would not eat from the Canadian prairie or the US breadbasket now and that North Americans should be eating from the Pacific. For growers in a still-good field, he points to electroculture antennas, basalt in the soil, low-deuterium water and vortexed water, with setups mapped against SAA contours and basalt soils. Where the field has already failed, he says the better move is to relocate rather than spend on vortex preparations and towers. The same deuterium-depletion tools he uses for people, ketones from fat and deuterium-depleted water, are in his view the human side of the same fix.

articles.title: Haplogroup and the "magnetic zipcode"
articles.summary: Kruse says your maternal mitochondrial lineage sets the gearing of your energy engine and so decides which local field and sun suit you, that a mismatch speeds aging, and that as the field grows turbulent, location matters more than lineage.
keyPoints: Kruse says your maternal haplogroup is the blueprint of your energy engine and your local field, your "magnetic zipcode," is the dial.
In his model each lineage set ATP synthase's gearing for the light and field where it settled, so a mismatch makes the engine misfire.
He ranks lineages by how they tolerate a weakening field, and says the mismatch can run both ways, from too little sun to too much.
As the field turns turbulent, he argues, where you live now matters more than your lineage.
Northern lineages moving to the tropics should build a "solar callus" gradually, never pushing sun exposure to redness.

sections.body:
A haplogroup is a maternal lineage traced through mitochondrial DNA, which passes from mother to child. Kruse calls it the blueprint and your "magnetic zipcode," the field where you live, the dial. When the two don't match, he argues, aging speeds up, so the same place can suit one person and harm another.

He frames it as a chain: the haplogroup is the blueprint, Marcus theory (the physics of how fast electrons jump between molecules) is the law, the magnetic zipcode is the dial, and energy failure is what follows a mismatch. Lineages arose, he says, as answers to past changes in Earth's field. As people left Africa for colder climates, the M and N lineages picked up changes that let some of the mitochondria's energy leak away as heat instead of being stored, a trait called "uncoupling" that helps in the cold.

He builds on Doug Wallace's map of how mitochondrial lineages spread across the globe, reading each one as an electrical adaptation to the field and sunlight of the place it settled. He calls this impedance matching, the engineer's term for tuning a circuit to its power source so little energy is lost. Moving a lineage built for strong light and field into a weak-field, wireless-heavy setting, in his view, makes its engine misfire.

sections.heading: Isotopic gearboxes
sections.body:
Kruse calls lineages "isotopic gearboxes." Each one, in his model, set the gear ratio of ATP synthase, the cell's rotary energy motor, to suit local conditions. Tropical L lineages run it flat out, at a speed he puts at 9,000 RPM, which needs strong light and free-flowing, light water; northern lineages such as H and J are deliberately "leaky," dropping to about 6,000 RPM and turning the difference into heat.

In his recovery road map he sorts lineages into three kinds of engine. Equatorial and African L lineages are high-voltage engines that need the most UV and infrared, and they falter in the north's artificial-light "electronic winter." H, J, U and T are "internal heaters," built to uncouple and make their own light; they need cold exposure to set that off, or, he says, deuterium settles in the fourth ventricle. Indigenous American and East Asian lineages (A, B, C and D) are high-pressure "centrifuges" suited to the Ring of Fire, needing volcanic ground and a strong field to keep the brain's fluid vortex turning.

sections.heading: Different tolerances
sections.body:
Kruse ranks lineages by how they cope as the field weakens. African L lineages, especially L1, evolved near the equator, where the field is flat and naturally weak, so in his model they function with little magnetic help. Declination is a separate matter: for an L lineage, he says, even 2–4° of offset between compass and true north can stall the engine.

The European H lineage, his own, is "leaky": when magnetic pinning slips it can drop its voltage and shed the surplus as heat, which he says clears deuterium and resets the cell. East and Southeast Asian D5b1 and F lineages are the most vulnerable. They stayed where strong sun and the dense magnetic pinning of the Pacific "Ring of Fire" volcanoes were constant, so they have neither L1's low-field tolerance nor H's heat release. Mismatch runs both ways. Move an L-lineage person to Canada, with its high declination and weak UV, and the fast engine stalls. Northern lineages placed under strong UV or heavy radiation, such as the anomaly's fringe in Australia or Brazil, overheat instead into what he calls a "singlet flashover" and age faster; for this reason he warned one H-lineage member not to move to Hawaii. As the field shifts, he adds, places that once supported a full-speed engine now support only the slower one.

For D5b1 and F in a weak field he says cold therapy backfires. They should avoid deep cold (water around 55–65 °F) until they are magnetically pinned, first maximizing morning UV and infrared light, grounding fully and shielding strictly from wireless fields.

sections.heading: When the field turns, place beats lineage
sections.body: Under a stable field, Kruse says, matching your lineage to your latitude was enough. With the north pole racing toward Siberia and the anomaly deepening, the planet's magnetic rhythm now wobbles like a slipping timing belt, and Wallace's map now tells him less about where to live than about who will falter first — the environments those lineages evolved in are no longer the planet underfoot. The more turbulent the field becomes, the less a lineage protects you and the more of your environment you must get right, so in most cases, in his view, where you live now matters more than your haplogroup.

sections.heading: Running the numbers
sections.body:
Kruse turns this into a personal sum with three inputs: latitude and altitude (how much sun you get and how close you sit to the radiation belts), local field strength and haplogroup. Below roughly 30,000 nT, as under the South Atlantic Anomaly, he says cells need a longer quiet spell to complete repair. If a place demands about seven seconds of that quiet time and your body can hold only three, you must cut your deuterium load, and he says to redo the sum every month. A strong field alone is not enough if the sun is too weak for most of the year to keep melanin production running.

He has grown wary of commercial DNA-testing companies and offers a functional test in their place. If your body "switches on" under the strong ultraviolet found between about 20°N and 20°S, and its systems run freely when you ground on volcanic soil, you have found what he calls your "Home Frequency."

sections.heading: Northern bodies and the field
sections.body: Kruse says northern peoples shed skin melanin, the pigment he treats as a spin filter, and leaned on strong polar field lines instead. He calls this "Zeeman outsourcing," after the Zeeman effect by which a magnetic field splits electron energy levels. A strong polar field plus cold, he argues, let them grow larger, using the body as a bigger solar panel. Paler irises, in his view, let more weak northern light reach the brain's master clock.

sections.heading: Moving to the tropics
sections.body:
A northern lineage moving into strong tropical sun must, in his view, adapt gradually. A sudden plunge into equatorial UV can overwhelm a leaky H mitochondrion, while stepping through the day's light and grounding on basalt or wet black sand builds a "solar callus," skin and tissue adapted to strong sun, without changing DNA. Redness, he says, means you pushed too far. That adaptation runs through MITF, the pigment cells' control switch, and takes days to months; a lineage itself changes only over many generations.

In practice, the four-phase sun day protocol lays out that schedule: sunrise red and infrared light with feet on basalt or wet black sand, mid-morning UV-A, a few minutes of midday UV-B that grows slowly as you tan, and late-day sun, never to the point of redness. The relocation checklist reminds you that your maternal haplogroup sets how much declination you can tolerate and that latitude, field strength and lineage have to be weighed together.

articles.title: The South Atlantic Anomaly, muons and failing regions
articles.summary: Kruse says Earth's weakening field, worst under the expanding South Atlantic Anomaly and across the Southern Hemisphere, lets in particles that load the body with deuterium and tritium, and names the regions he sees failing.
keyPoints: Kruse says Earth's magnetic shields are failing together, and the damage is worst under the growing South Atlantic Anomaly.
In his model the thinner shield lets in muons that cancel membrane charge and let deuterium settle in nerves and the brain's fluid.
He says a weak field also raises deuterium and tritium in rain, air and food, so he avoids food grown under the anomaly.
He no longer considers the Southern Hemisphere habitable long term and names US regions he calls "cooked."
He says to track your own zip code's field data and move before official charts catch up.

sections.body: Kruse argues that Earth's magnetic shield is weakening and that the damage is worst under the South Atlantic Anomaly, a huge and growing patch where the field is weakest. In his model the thinner shield lets in particles that load bodies, water and food with heavy hydrogen, and he names the regions he expects to fail first.

sections.heading: Failing shields
sections.body:
Kruse says three "cosmic shields" are failing together: a filter of interstellar hydrogen around the solar system, the heliosphere (the Sun's protective bubble) and the geodynamo (the field made by Earth's core). He puts the loss so far at about 10% of field strength since about 2012 — a sprint he equates with roughly 320 million years of Cambrian-scale change packed into about fourteen years — falling roughly 5% a decade from a decline he dates to 1859, when the magnetic pole began moving fast. Another 10–30% drop would, he says, be an evolutionary bottleneck, and his main worry is a 30–50% loss within 50 years.

Comparing a 2005 survey map with the 2025 World Magnetic Model, he notes the north magnetic pole heading for Siberia and the anomaly still deepening. The pole has also crossed the prime meridian, a first in recorded history, and he says that shift alters declination everywhere, moving the "carrier wave" the body's water uses to orient itself so the fourth ventricle's spinning flow struggles to stay in step with the planet.

The body is meant to cope with some of this radiation. In his model melanin converts incoming radiation into a steady direct current cells can use. When blue light has detuned that pigment and the body's water has stiffened to its ordinary state, the same radiation instead becomes a mutagen, something that damages DNA, which he places at the root of the body's breakdown.

sections.heading: The anomaly
sections.body:
The South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) is where the shield is thinnest, below about 22,000 nT against the 45,000 nT or more he looks for. Citing ESA's Swarm satellites, he says it has split into two lobes: the main low drifting west over South America, deepest near Paraguay and southern Brazil, and a second stretching toward southwest Africa. He says it now covers all of Argentina, and its northern edge reaches the Lesser Antilles, which is why he treats the Caribbean as off-limits. Under it, he says, the radiation belts reach down to about 200 km, so residents live in low-orbit conditions without knowing it: "astronauts walking on Earth."

He explains its location by heat flow: the South American landmass and the Andes, he argues, insulate the core beneath them so the dynamo stalls there, leaving the Western Hemisphere over a "stalled stator."

sections.heading: Muons and deuterium
sections.body:
His key study is a paper by Augusto and colleagues. Under the anomaly the "cutoff rigidity," the minimum energy a cosmic particle needs to get through the field, collapses, and muons (heavy cousins of electrons made when cosmic rays strike the air) rise up to tenfold at ground level. Muons pass through walls and tissue, and in his model act as positive "dopants" that cancel the negative charge of cell membranes and knock light hydrogen out of its channels, so deuterium (heavy hydrogen) builds up in the basal ganglia, heart and liver.

He describes a healthy field as a "janitor" that sweeps deuterium to the outer edge of the body's whirlpools, such as blood flow and spinal fluid, where it can be cleared. Under the anomaly the janitor is "on strike": deuterium settles in nerves and in the brain's fluid spaces, and the body's water slides from its structured state (160 on his scale) toward ordinary water (78).

The lower belts also, he says, change how moisture is ionized in the air, raising deuterium in rain and so in grass and groundwater. A weaker field also lets the solar wind energize hydrogen ions high in the atmosphere until they escape into space; the lighter hydrogen goes first, so the water left behind grows steadily richer in deuterium, a "heavy water trap." The Atlantic's great overturning current (AMOC) runs straight through the anomaly, which he calls a "ground fault" that makes it harder for the current to sink near the poles; a stagnant ocean means stagnant air and deuterium-heavy rain.

sections.heading: Tritium
sections.body:
Cosmic neutrons striking nitrogen make tritium, the radioactive form of hydrogen, which rains onto South American farms and rivers. As the shields thin, he says, people breathe in more heavy hydrogen just as their means of clearing it is failing; he calls this "isotopic back-pressure" and says wear that once took 70 years to show now appears in people in their thirties. If deuterium is grit in the engine, tritium in his phrase is radioactive shrapnel. The body builds it into DNA as if it were ordinary hydrogen; when it decays into helium, which cannot bond, the chemical link snaps from the inside.

For this reason he avoids food from the SAA, and he says seeds germinate poorly in its weak field. Heavier water slows the enzymes of photosynthesis, he says, while extra cosmic radiation damages chloroplasts. The deep sea, whose "fossilized" light water has been cut off from the surface for centuries, he sees as a cleaner food web.

sections.heading: The Southern Hemisphere
sections.body: Kruse treats the whole Southern Hemisphere as exposed. Field lines gather toward the north, his "input," and spread out over the south, the "exhaust," so as the main field weakens the anomaly behaves like a low-pressure hole drawing deuterium and tritium down from the upper atmosphere, which he calls "isotopic insufflation." With the radiation belts lower there since 1859, he says, the southern food chain has been loading with deuterium for about 150 years. He no longer considers anywhere in the Southern Hemisphere habitable for the long term, and he says the north magnetic pole's rush toward Siberia, his "Siberian jerk," adds strain to the southern weak spot like one side of a tug-of-war.

sections.heading: Who fails first
sections.body:
Zip codes near the expanding anomaly, Kruse predicts, will be the first to run out of energy, with lives shortening where magnetic flux is weakest. By late 2026 he treats the US East Coast as already under the anomaly's reach — up toward Hudson Bay — while ranking the West Coast relatively better than the East for 2024–2026 because the Pacific thermohaline still runs; California still carries a "double deficit" of high declination and weak steady UV-B, and Texas stays weak. Florida, he says, was "swallowed" in about 14 years. He names the Pacific Northwest as the only US option that is really pinned. The fittest, he says, feel it first: high-demand athletes, whose engines run closest to the limit, are the canaries.
