In practice, the “Track your local field” protocol says to watch declination drift, secular-acceleration ("jerk") charts and Swarm data for your own zip code, comparing the same date across years, along with unusual blocked weather and your own heart-rate variability. If your area shows a jerk or turns toward a vertical field, move before official charts catch up. He also keeps a watch-list for a bigger shift: field loss reaching 30–50% of the Laschamp collapse, sudden changes in the SAA and faster pole drift.

articles.title: Solar storms, the Schumann signal and the "thalamic GPS"
articles.summary: Kruse says the thalamus works as a position sensor locked to Earth's field and resonance, which solar storms and high declination knock out of alignment, and that each storm is a stress test the body's water passes or fails, with effects on sleep, mood, hearing and even earthquakes.
keyPoints: Kruse says the thalamus works as a "thalamic GPS" that locks onto Earth's field and the 7.83 Hz Schumann resonance.
In his model a solar storm jams that signal, thickens spinal fluid and makes the cell's rotary motor lose its magnetic lock.
He treats each storm as a stress test: a body low in deuterium rides the wave, while a deuterium-loaded one cannot absorb the jolt.
High local declination, he says, does the same thing slowly by denying the thalamus a stable reference.
On storm days he says to ground for longer than usual and expect a rough night or two.

sections.body: Kruse argues that the brain keeps track of where the body is by locking onto Earth's magnetic field and its natural electromagnetic rhythm. Solar storms, and more slowly a skewed local field, knock that internal position sense out of alignment, which in his model explains storm headaches, drained energy on storm days and the unease some people feel in open spaces.

sections.heading: The Sun and the thalamic GPS
sections.body: Kruse treats the Sun as one node on a galactic electrical circuit, with its 11-year cycle an induced response. In the body the receiver is the thalamus, the brain's relay center. He calls it a "thalamic GPS," a three-axis position panel whose axes he places along the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull, the vagus nerve and the heart. It locks onto the Schumann resonance, the 7.83 Hz electromagnetic hum of the space between the ground and the upper atmosphere — the cavity tone made when solar wind and lightning drive the ionosphere — and onto the horizontal and vertical parts of the field. He adds that the thalamus itself emits near that same 7.83 Hz, so every living thing, in his telling, is tuned to Earth's guitar-body rhythm; cut the lock and man-made fields find an open cockpit. The brain's alpha rhythm, around 10 Hz, acts in his model like a strobe that keeps cell membranes aligned.

sections.heading: What a storm does
sections.body:
A solar flare or coronal mass ejection (CME, a burst of charged solar material) compresses the magnetosphere, the field's protective bubble, and drives an induced surge through the ground. Kruse says this jams the Schumann signal and uncouples the thalamic GPS, disturbing alpha waves. Cerebrospinal fluid, in his account, loses its charge, thickens and drains poorly, so pressure inside the skull rises; hence storm headaches. He tells members that a bad night can come from a CME rather than from what they ate.

He describes the cell's side of this as a motor slipping. Earth's field is the outer "stator" and ATP synthase, the cell's rotary motor, is the inner rotor; a storm makes the stator turbulent and the rotor loses its magnetic lock. He gauges storms by the K-index, a 0–9 scale of how disturbed the field is: from about 5 upward, he says, the field that normally guides charged particles in the spinal fluid turns chaotic, the fluid's smooth whirl breaks into turbulence and heavy water settles back into the brain's fluid spaces. Storm currents also run through the body's own circuits, not just power lines, pushing against the motor's rotation, which in his account is the drained feeling and "cognitive haze" people report on storm days.

Storms change the light as well. The upper atmosphere sinks during a storm, he says, shifting the mix of ultraviolet that reaches the ground and scattering the photons the skin's pigment system depends on, an effect he calls "atmospheric tanning."

Melatonin takes a hit too. About 95% of it, he says, is made inside mitochondria, and he cites a paper showing levels fall 15–33 hours after a geomagnetic spike, which he calls an "isotopic hangover." Mood shifts with it, he adds, pointing to Robert Becker's 1960s work and Soviet research gathered under the heading of heliogeophysics, both of which tracked human behavior against storms.

The ground answers as well. He calls earthquakes detectors of magnetic anomalies, and cites 2025–2026 statistical studies finding that quakes worldwide rise about 27–28 days after major geomagnetic storms; the storm's currents in the ground, he says, seep into fragile faults and warm them.

He adds that the field also shifts over each ordinary day. Sunlight charges the upper atmosphere, whose currents nudge the ground field by roughly 10–100 nT; after sunset those currents fade and the field settles to a quieter night baseline. As an extreme storm he cites the 1859 Carrington Event, when auroras reached the Caribbean, and ties it to the collapse of European vineyards in the years that followed. He also suspects that storm permanently shifted the background Schumann hum, and that once alternating-current power added its own noise in the early 1900s, the heart's internal positioning lost its lock. Yet he does not see a big storm as purely bad: the Sun, as the parent oscillator, may in his view send a Carrington-scale ejection that works like a defibrillator, jolting the wobbling core back into steady flow.

sections.heading: Storms as stress tests
sections.body: Kruse treats each storm as a test of the body's water. A body low in heavy water, with well-structured water, "rides the wave"; one loaded with deuterium cannot absorb the jolt. In his account a storm induces an electric field in the ground, blood thickened by deuterium cannot soak up the voltage spike, and the shifting field throws off the nervous system that steadies the heart. People, in his view, now struggle with the Sun's periodic "defibrillation" because they carry too much deuterium to tolerate it. Shaking ground may help: one reason he chose El Salvador over Mexico, he says, is that its constant seismic activity may leave residents more resilient to storms.

sections.heading: Slow uncoupling from the local field
sections.body: High declination, Kruse says, does the same thing slowly. A field twisted relative to true north, or changing quickly, keeps the thalamus from locking a stable reference. That lowers tone in the right vagus nerve and makes mitochondria leak DNA, which the immune system treats as an alarm. He pictures the thalamus as "overclocked," hunting for its lost position signal, much as it does for astronauts in the magnetic vacuum of space and for many people on the ground under wireless fields and the field's decline.

sections.heading: Open spaces as a navigation load
sections.body:
Kruse reads the unease some people feel in wide open spaces as this navigation system running short of capacity. The brain's grid cells and place cells, which map position, rely in his model on structured water held in order by the field. In ungrounded, sleep-short people living under blue light, that water slides toward ordinary bulk water and its capacity roughly halves, so position signals blur, which he calls "spatial aliasing." Open spaces carry more information than the weakened channel can handle. The answer, he argues, lies in restoring that medium.

In practice, the space-weather days protocol says to ground for longer than your usual 20–60 minutes during solar or geomagnetic storms and to expect possible storm headaches and a rough night or two; he also treats auroras seen over your own home as a sign the field beneath is poor and a reason to move. The brain, eye and ear protocol gives his steps for rebuilding the position sense: remove wireless fields, ground daily, get morning solar infrared, lower deuterium and live where the magnetic field is strong.

articles.title: The planet's story: excursions, the magnetic forge and volcanic CO₂
articles.summary: Kruse reads Earth's field history — excursions, ozone, oxygen, oceans, volcanoes and the creatures that survived past collapses — as the large-scale version of the physics that runs the cell.
keyPoints: Kruse reads Earth's magnetic history as cell physics at planetary scale: a steady field allowed complex life, a faltering one culled it.
In his model reversals cause extinctions by stripping ozone, while shorter excursions such as Laschamp select survivors and reshaped modern humans.
He says today's weakening is a "magnetic forge," a planetary re-tuning not caused by humans, about 9% of the way to a Laschamp-scale collapse.
He ties ocean currents, Arctic warming and volcanic CO₂ to the dynamo, and welcomes more CO₂ as a shield during field loss.

sections.body: Kruse reads Earth's magnetic history as the large-scale version of the physics he sees inside cells. In his model, periods when the field steadied allowed complex life, periods when it faltered reshaped or culled it, and the weakening under way now is another such turning point: a planetary re-tuning rather than an extinction.

sections.heading: Excursions and reversals
sections.body: A reversal is a full swap of the magnetic poles; it takes thousands of years and then holds for 100,000 years or more. An excursion is an aborted reversal: the field weakens and wanders for a few centuries up to about 2,000 years, then recovers, as in the Laschamp excursion about 41,000 years ago. Fast-settling lake and deep-sea sediments record hundreds of them, along with spikes in beryllium-10 and carbon-14 that mark extra cosmic rays. Reversals, in his view, cause extinctions because ozone is stripped for thousands of years; excursions select survivors. The field has collapsed about 500 times with only five mass extinctions, he says, but he believes several human civilizations were lost to such events. He reads the Permian "Great Dying," which killed about 96% of life, as a magnetic event in which heavy isotopes piled up while the field faltered. As the field weakened, he says, oxygen sank back toward levels of a far older Earth, and he notes researchers' finding that the steadiness of the link between field and oxygen tracks the five great extinctions. In his account the Siberian Traps, the vast lava floods of that time, knocked the dynamo out of step with surface chemistry. The survivors were "hard" life that could keep its internal spin order with its own melanin and DHA, an "internal sun." Animals shrank afterward (the Lilliput effect): a smaller body, he says, lets a smaller internal vortex keep its charge.

sections.heading: A steady field made complex life
sections.body:
Kruse argues that complex life arrived only once Earth's dynamo steadied. During the "Boring Billion," the long, quiet middle of Earth's history, a weak and unstable field let the solar wind strip ozone, leaving the surface scorched by UV. In the Ediacaran period just before the Cambrian the field was, he says, 10–30 times weaker than today, hydrogen bled into space, water grew heavier and life stayed simple.

The Cambrian explosion began in his account when the inner core hardened, the field stabilized and oxygen locked into its stable triplet state, letting one-handed molecules such as collagen and melanin act as spin filters. He cites a 2025 *Science Advances* study linking atmospheric oxygen to the strength of Earth's field over 540 million years, with joint peaks between 330 and 220 million years ago, the window in which he says the mammalian blueprint was built. Oxygen, he stresses, did not drive that leap alone — the magnetic dynamo did; without polarized spins there is no coherent light and no complex life beyond archaea and bacteria. Under a later excursion, he says eukaryotes "travel back in time" toward simpler forms, with the circadian system as an electrical-resistance circuit protecting helical DNA while the field swings.

sections.heading: Who survives a stall
sections.body: The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs is, for Kruse, a different kind of event: the field and oxygen stayed strong, so life bounced back. He expects no such rebound from a core-level stall. Asked who would make it through one, he names neither birds nor most mammals: a bird's heart, beating 600–1,000 times a minute, would in his view stall in flight with just 1% more deuterium. His survivors are older designs: crocodilians, with a heart valve they can work like an "isotopic valve" and months of fasting on tail fat; sharks, whose electrosensing organs he says couple them to the core; tardigrades; microbes at deep-sea vents; and deep-sea squid and octopus. If birds disappear, he says, the food web has become an "isotopic dead zone."

sections.heading: Laschamp and modern humans
sections.body:
At Laschamp, Kruse says, the field fell below 5% of normal and auroras reached the equator. He links the event to the "chromosome 2 fuse," the spot where two ancestral ape chromosomes fused in humans, which sits beside genes for melanin and metabolism; in his model it tripped and reset human metabolism. Neanderthals, he says, "short-circuited" rather than lost a war, while modern humans emerged with a larger melanin shield and a burst of cognition and cave art.

Modern humans won, in his telling, partly by shrinking. Neanderthals carried about 125 g more brain, which in a weakening field became dead weight, while a smaller brain with relatively larger fluid-filled ventricles spins its spinal fluid faster and clears deuterium better. He says human brains are shrinking again today for the same reason. Large animals fared worse: they need strong "magnetic buoyancy" to push blood against gravity, he says, which is how he explains the loss of North America's megafauna.

sections.heading: The magnetic forge today
sections.body:
Kruse frames current changes as planetary rebalancing, not something humans caused. Earth, he says, is leaving a sunlight-dominated era for a "magnetic forge" like Laschamp's. He puts the present at about 9% of a Laschamp-scale collapse; at 30–50% he expects Earth's core and outer shell to decouple, his "Tau" stage. By his stochastic estimate, a roughly 10% field decline multiplies biologic stress about two-and-a-half-fold — reason enough, in his view, for the scale of modern mismatch. He cites satellite work showing that molten iron under the equatorial Pacific switched from westward to eastward flow in 2010 and has weakened since about 2020.

He also sees the planet keeping a sleep–wake cycle, as Robert Becker found the body's direct current does: today's racing pole is a night-to-day flip he dates to 1859, felt by deuterium-heavy people as a kind of jet lag.

sections.heading: Oceans, weather and volcanoes
sections.body:
Moving, salty ocean currents such as the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) make their own magnetic fields and, in his model, stall when the dynamo weakens — the planet's "vagal exhaust." He reads Arctic warming about four times faster than the rest of the world as a "magnetic Arctic flashover" as the north pole races toward Siberia, and calls "climate change" a software name for that hardware failure.

Warming seas release iodine that destroys ozone; volcanoes answer with CO₂ that locks iodine back as bicarbonate. He welcomes more CO₂ during an excursion and reads recent greening as a living shield against field loss. In practice he treats this history as a reason to act: anchor to a stable field, protect internal water, build melanin with sunlight and escape blue-lit indoor life. He rejects "balance" during an excursion, and puts location ahead of every other choice.

articles.title: nnEMF: wireless, wiring and the "hyper-local excursion"
articles.summary: Kruse says man-made electromagnetic fields jam cell signalling, scramble electron spins, push heavy-hydrogen fuel into the cell and act like a local magnetic excursion, with low-frequency AC fields the first thing to check and children the most exposed.
keyPoints: Kruse says man-made fields create a "hyper-local magnetic excursion," doing around a person what the weakening planetary field does globally.
In his model they scramble the electron spins that set the timing of oxygen radicals, draining mitochondrial voltage and NAD⁺.
He names low-frequency AC magnetic fields from wiring and appliances as the first thing to check, ahead of wireless.
He says pulsed RF can open the blood–brain barrier and that wireless signals jam cell signalling and can fake a "phantom tan."
Children take the hardest hit until myelin finishes around age 25; keep devices off the head and measure before mitigating.

sections.body: nnEMF is Kruse's term for "non-native" electromagnetic fields: the man-made fields from wireless devices, wiring and electronics that did not exist in nature. He argues they do locally what the weakening planetary field does globally, stripping cells of the steady magnetic reference they need, scrambling electron spins and draining cell voltage. Low-frequency fields from household wiring and appliances, he says, are the first thing to check.

sections.heading: The same problem as the planet
sections.body:
In Kruse's model Earth's field supplies a constant, gentle "torque" that keeps electron spins aligned inside mitochondria. Wi-Fi, smart meters and Bluetooth, he says, swamp it and create a "hyper-local magnetic excursion" around the person. Cytochrome c oxidase, the enzyme that hands electrons to oxygen, loses its alignment, oxygen flips into its reactive singlet form, and the cell behaves as if starved of oxygen even when oxygen is present, a state called pseudohypoxia. Planetary decline and nnEMF, he says, "cause the same problem," though he now ranks a roughly 10% planetary field drop as far larger than focal wireless — nnEMF is still additive, and phones hurt most near packed west-declination or anomaly lines — which is why copper–rare-earth jewelry on a plane is, for him, mandatory even if jump conduction is a worry. A cell already carrying faulty mitochondrial DNA or a heavy deuterium load is primed for this, so a router or smart meter can tip it over.

He roots this in spin chemistry. Superoxide, a common oxygen radical, forms in radical pairs whose electron spins rock between two states, and Earth's field normally sets the timing of that rocking, which lets cells use these radicals as signals. Radio-frequency fields, he says, jam the hyperfine coupling that keeps the timing, leave pairs stuck in the wrong state and let the radicals slip past the cell's own clean-up enzymes and give off disordered light. He adds that natural and artificial fields alike act through the metal centers of enzymes, whose electron energy levels are split by the protein atoms around them.

sections.heading: Low-frequency AC fields first
sections.body:
His first suspect is AC (alternating current) magnetic fields under 100 kHz from power lines, appliances and indoor wiring. He says they knock spin-aligned electrons out of step and drain the charge on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The resulting singlet oxygen damages the iron–sulfur clusters of Complex I, the first step of the energy chain, so NAD⁺ falls; that is the molecule that repair enzymes, sirtuins and the body clock run on. He also cites Liboff and Blackman's work on ion cyclotron resonance: a 60 Hz field layered on Earth's steady field can match the natural frequency of calcium ions and drive calcium out of place, pushing magnesium down.

He sets the grid against the body's own wiring. The vagus nerve, he says, runs coherent rhythms tuned to the Schumann resonance, while 60 Hz is a "heavy" frequency that distorts the shape of the inner mitochondrial membrane and lets deuterium in. A computer chip, he adds, moves charge but ignores electron spin, so it wastes energy as heat; melanin's spin-sorted current, by contrast, carries information with little heat.

Fields also change what the cell burns. Citing a 2011 study by Nora Volkow finding that a phone held to the head raises glucose use in the nearby brain, Kruse argues that such fields break up the thin water shells around proteins and the body responds by flooding the blood with glucose, which he regards as deuterium-heavy fuel. At Complex I, deuterium then takes ordinary hydrogen's place and, he says, slows electron tunneling six- to tenfold.

sections.heading: Wireless and the cell's own signals
sections.body:
5G and other wireless signals, Kruse argues, jam the terahertz signals that neighboring cells use to coordinate (ephaptic coupling, meaning communication through fields rather than synapses) and collapse the structured water around membranes. He rejects the idea that non-ionizing radiation is harmless because it cannot break atoms apart, likening it to calling a black mamba safe because it can't throw a punch. He points to a Rockefeller University patent by Jeffrey Friedman and Sarah Stanley on using radio waves to switch heat-sensitive channels in cells, as proof that fields reach the leptin pathway that governs appetite and metabolism.

Wireless signals can also, in his view, fake a sunny day. Responding to a member's paper showing that RF fields activate p53, the cell's repair guardian, he argues that cells mistake RF jitter in their water for UV damage and start making melanin through POMC, the hormone precursor sunlight normally switches on. Because the signal is incoherent, the new pigment never forms a stable lattice and is broken straight back down into dopamine; he calls it a "phantom tan" and sees in it the physics of phone compulsion: phone, repair alarm, pigment, dopamine high, crash, and back to the phone.

Children, he says, take the hardest hit. Their thinner skulls let RF reach deeper, and myelin — the fatty insulation that speeds nerve signals — is not finished until about age 25, so an immature myelin and melanin shield leaves the developing brain more open to pulsed fields. Their plentiful neural stem cells, which RF can slow, are still building the circuits that calm the brain's alarm center.

sections.heading: Barriers, pulsed fields and the head
sections.body:
Kruse leans on Allan Frey's work that electromagnetic radiation, especially pulsed microwaves and RF, can open the blood–brain barrier. Once that shield leaks, he says, high-atomic-mass material that does not belong in the brain can enter and ruin the fidelity of the thalamus's Schumann-tuned antenna — the same 7.83 Hz lock he calls the body's GPS. Disconnect people from that natural signal, in his account, and man-made fields have an easier path to scramble sense and timing. The cochlea's melanin sheet and the endolymphatic sac, which also lack a blood–brain barrier, are another doorway: pulsed energy there uncouples the head's antenna and loads the dense petrous bone with deuterium.

Phones and wireless earbuds sit on that doorway. They disturb the nerves that drive saliva in narrow bony canals and cancel sound therapy by adding the very fields it aims to undo. Wearables act from the inside, in his view: a tracking ring worn at night gives off enough radio energy to cut melanin production.

In practice, the nnEMF reduction protocol says to look first for AC magnetic fields and artificial blue light; not to sleep or live near smart meters, routers, 5G arrays or wind turbines; to keep phones and earbuds off the head and neck and devices off the lap; to skip wireless rings and other wearables; to avoid phones in the car, distrust airplane mode and skip smart houses; and to measure before mitigating, ideally with a credentialed assessor, because cheap fixes do little. He suggests judging a shielded home partly by digestion: its occupants should settle into a smooth, well-formed Bristol type 4 stool. The “Low-EMF, daylit work space” protocol moves wiring, power supplies and appliances away from where you sit and favors daylight and incandescent bulbs, and the air-tube headphones protocol replaces Bluetooth with wired air-tube headphones or a speaker.

articles.title: Astronauts on Earth: indoor, high-rise and airborne life
articles.summary: Kruse says people living indoors, high above the ground, sealed in steel or in frequent flight are cut off from sun and field like astronauts, children most of all.
keyPoints: Kruse says people who live indoors, high up or in frequent flight are cut off from sun, ground and Earth's field much as astronauts are.
In his model, gravity, magnetism and grounding are separate needs, and none can stand in for another.
He says living form and beauty concentrate where the magnetic field is strong, not where potions and gyms are sold.
He says high floors and plane cabins leave the body shedding electrons and its water losing structure.
He frames jet lag as a short magnetic excursion and says to fly less, skip food aloft, drink carbonated water and wear static magnetic jewelry.

sections.body: Kruse argues that people who live indoors, high above the ground or in frequent flight are cut off from the sun and Earth's field much as astronauts are. He calls them "astronauts on Earth" and sees much modern ill health as spaceflight sickness without the rocket, with children the most exposed. Beauty and dense life, in his reading, track the same map: the Amazon holds forms the Sahara never does, so magnetism, not cream or gym culture, is what sculpts living form.

sections.heading: The indoor Faraday cage
sections.body:
A Faraday cage is an enclosure that blocks electromagnetic fields. Kruse describes buildings as one, cutting people off from sunlight, the planet's field and the ground. Add LED lighting and wireless fields on a planet whose dynamo is weakening, and indoor life, in his model, recreates conditions in orbit.

He points to space research: NASA findings and a 2026 *Nature Communications* study showing that microgravity silences mitochondrial genes and stalls electron flow even though food, water and air stay the same. He takes this as proof that the physical environment drives the change. Astronauts and cosmonauts, he stresses, eat carefully measured, high-quality rations, yet within days the sensory system frays and within about two weeks they can lose roughly a fifth of their muscle: the magnetic and electric fields and solar plasma around them have changed, mitochondria enter Marcus inversion, cardiolipin is damaged and cell water falls from his structured "160" toward ordinary "78." Gravity, magnetism and grounding are, for him, separate needs that cannot substitute for one another. Children kept indoors under blue light and off the ground, he says, have no field to guide their electron spins while they develop.

Without gravity, he argues, the body loses the steady pull that spins heavy water down and out of the brain's fluid spaces. He reads the swollen optic nerves and flattened eyeballs NASA reports in astronauts as heavy water pooling once that pull stops. A speech lapse reported in astronaut Michael Fincke aboard the space station is, to him, the brain's language region flooding with unspun, deuterium-heavy spinal fluid, and proof that gravity and magnetism run human physiology.

Daily modern life, in his view, is a rehearsal for Mars — "astronauts on Earth" whose zip code, not their plate, has already put Complexes I–III under magnetic interference. Sitting still is "microgravity" for lymph flow, while wireless fields and blue light stand in for cosmic radiation.

sections.heading: Pressure as the broom
sections.body:
Pressure is his answer to lost gravity. "If oxygen is the fuel, pressure is the broom," he says. Outside pressure squeezes deuterium out of the water shells around proteins the way you wring a sponge. He links this to Henry's law (the more pressure on a liquid, the more gas it holds) and says it recreates the centrifuge that gravity normally supplies. He goes so far as to suggest everyone may need to learn to dive.

He separates pressure from oxygen, though. Forcing pure oxygen into a body already stuck in fermentation and bathed in wireless fields, he warns, does damage rather than repair. Future habitats, in his view, will need "chiral chambers," spin-shielded pods that control light, water pressure and cold together.

Submariners, sealed in steel for months, are his other test case. He says they lose the Schumann signal, the planet's background electromagnetic rhythm, and ties that loss to the skin and mood problems common among them. They also show gut and breathing trouble from rebreathed COâ‚‚, and tooth trouble that older data linked to deuterium entering the teeth.

sections.heading: High-rise living
sections.body: High floors add what he calls a voltage trap. The atmosphere carries a vertical electric field of about 100â€“150 volts per meter, so a person on the 24th floor sits thousands of volts away from ground potential. In his account, that person acts like an antenna shedding electrons. He says electron-microscope images from an Australian high-rise dweller resembled those of astronauts. His answer is to live and sleep on the ground or first floor.

sections.heading: Flying
sections.body:
Flying, Kruse says, takes you off the ground and closer to the Van Allen radiation belts, causing "magnetic shear" and raising cell-free mitochondrial DNA, the fragments released from stressed cells. He now frames jet lag itself as a short magnetic excursion: leave the tectonic plate, ride nearer a weakened dynamo, and tritium and deuterium load the body the way they do astronauts — an electron-spin and isotope-fractionation problem first, not a food or clock problem. Frequent ungrounded travel loads the body's water with deuterium and thickens blood. That moves the body toward "lattice lock," his term for tissue stiffened by deuterium-heavy water.

Planes and mountains, he says, raise the risk of muscle loss, and circumpolar plus long east–west flights over the Atlantic and the South Atlantic Anomaly are the hardest on the nerves and spine. At cruising altitude inside a metal cabin the field's steadying effect drops, which is why he says never to eat on a plane and to drink carbonated water instead as a short magnetic-flux offset.

In the cabin, he adds, extra wireless exposure and no ground push the body's water from its structured state (about 160 on his scale) toward ordinary water (78) or lower. In his model this weakens immune proteins and makes barriers such as the blood–brain barrier leakier, so someone already run down by where they live has little margin left when they board.

sections.heading: What he says to do
sections.body:
The “Live outdoors, not as an "astronaut on Earth"” protocol moves as much of life outdoors as possible. It gives children unfiltered morning UV-A and infrared on eyes and skin, bare feet on the earth and a home without Wi-Fi or artificial night light. Where possible he adds regular time under water pressure, such as diving or swimming in natural water.

The ground-floor living protocol says to live no higher than the first floor. If you cannot move yet, he suggests his "High-Altitude Counter-Faraday Shield," conductive mesh around the bed wired to deep ground rods, or copper vortex devices such as Slim Spurling coils and Lakhovsky rings with grounded carbon mats.

The flying protocol cuts unneeded flights — especially circumpolar ones — skips food in the air, drinks carbonated water, and treats copper–rare-earth or other static magnetic jewelry as mandatory once you leave the ground. Some muscle loss after flights or time at altitude is expected.

articles.title: Magnets, pads and powered devices
articles.summary: Kruse's view of static magnetic pads and stimulation devices: sometimes useful stand-ins for a lost field when set up correctly, but always behind location, sun and grounding.
keyPoints: Kruse says a static magnetic sleep pad can stand in for a weakening planetary field, but always ranks behind location, sunlight and grounding.
He recommends sleeping on it all night at about 10â€“20 gauss, north pole toward the body, a grounding sheet on top and Wi-Fi off.
In his model the wrong pole, a random orientation or too strong a field over-clamps tissue; copper–rare-earth jewelry is mainly for flights and other ungrounded hours.
He cites a study where a weak static field raised mitochondrial respiration only within a narrow dose window.
Powered devices such as TMS and PEMF rank lower still; he says relocating or grounding on basalt comes first.

sections.body: Kruse sees artificial magnetic fields as a two-edged tool. A static magnetic sleep pad can stand in for a weakening planetary field, but the wrong magnet, pole or strength can "over-clamp" tissue, and every device ranks behind location, sunlight and grounding.

sections.heading: Sleep pads
sections.body:
As the geodynamo weakens, Kruse says, an outside static field can serve as a personal micro-shield. After ice baths, he ranks a static magnetic sleep pad (he names Magnetico, about 20 gauss, rare-earth ceramics) as the next everyday hack — all night, not short bursts — alongside pure DHA and raw morning UV-A. Red-light panels and grounding sheets help a little but, like the pad, cannot replace a good zip code. Children stuck in a poor magnetic place, he says, need one. A cheaper option is a coil of heavy-gauge copper pipe under the pillow: by Lenz's law, incoming wireless fields induce small opposing currents in the copper. In El Salvador he calls a pad pointless for anyone who spends time outdoors, because the volcanic ground does the job.

Night is when a pad earns its place, in his account. Sleep is when the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-clearing flow, flushes its fluid spaces, and in a weak, noisy field he says there is too little "torque" to move heavy hydrogen out. A steady, one-direction field of about 10â€“20 gauss keeps the spinal-fluid vortex turning through the night and drowns out the alternating-current "static" from Wi-Fi in what Robert Becker described as the body's direct-current nerve network; with that noise gone, he says, p53, the cell's repair guardian, can finally spot the deuterium-heavy methyl tags (CDâ‚ƒ) on DNA that need fixing. The field also helps hold structured water in place after dark, when without sun its dielectric value drifts back toward the 78 of ordinary water. Lineage matters here too: for an equatorial L lineage living in the north, the pad supplies missing field strength, while for northern lineages it adds torque to their heat-making.

Setup decides whether it helps. He says to face the pad's north (negative) pole toward the body, lay a grounding sheet over it so electrons and field arrive together, and switch off Wi-Fi and keep devices away, which he calls critical: using a pad in a room full of live wireless is, in his image, like gathering iron filings with a magnet while someone keeps jolting the table. In a bad environment a pad can even backfire and let deuterium collect in tissue, and he tells heavy tech users to skip it.

Where the field is collapsing outright, he sees little point either. In the Southern Hemisphere he calls a pad, like other such devices, superfluous: the better choice there is not to "jump into the jet engine while it's running," while in the Northern Hemisphere a pad makes more sense. He adds that he never set out to promote pads; members learned in consults that he used one and spread the word.

He flags one risk. A strong vertical field from a pad at night, followed by a steeply tilted and noisy field by day, can in his model give the thalamus (the brain's position sensor) a mismatched reference, especially without strong tropical sun to steady it.

sections.heading: Poles and jewelry
sections.body: Magnet makers, Kruse says, ignore polarity. The north pole in his model calms and organizes electron spins, while the south pole speeds activity and can tip oxygen into its reactive singlet form. A randomly oriented magnetic necklace creates a shifting field every time you move, rattling the tissues around the carotid arteries, and heavy static bracelets over-clamp; in one member's candle test, a bracelet slowed the burn and left unburnt wax. He allows magnetic jewelry only on flights, and an open 12-inch copper ring is his safer passive loop. He dismisses "Biomagnetic Pair" magnet therapy as charlatanism.

sections.heading: Dose has a window
sections.body:
Kruse cites a 2025 study by Beutner and colleagues in which isolated rat-heart mitochondria exposed to a static field far weaker than a fridge magnet raised their respiration by about 40% while producing fewer free radicals, but only within a narrow range; stronger fields lost the effect. He reads this as the radical pair mechanism, the spin chemistry by which a weak field tips the outcome of electron reactions.

A magnet also needs the sun's help. Without daylight raising the body's water toward its structured state of 160, he says, even a strong magnet has little "grip" on it, and a user who feels no lift from the pad is, in his reading, carrying a heavy deuterium load.

sections.heading: Powered devices rank lower
sections.body:
For other devices his rule is location first. Relocate before trying transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), and ground on basalt rather than buying a PEMF (pulsed electromagnetic field) device, which he calls the "loser option." In declining areas a gentle TENS unit, a small skin-electrode nerve stimulator, may be wiser than a magnetic pad. External counterpulsation (EECP), which uses leg cuffs to send pressure waves through the blood vessels, recharges vessel walls in his view, but the gain lasts only with sun and grounding. Electrolysis, he adds, can restore color to grey hair by re-pinning the follicle's local field with a burst of current.

In practice, the magnetic sleep pad protocol says to sleep on the pad all night at 10â€“20 gauss, toward the top of that range, with the north pole toward the body, a grounding sheet on top and Wi-Fi off; choose a north-seeking pad during the decline along with DHA and morning UV-A, give one to children living in poor magnetic zip codes, and use a heavy-gauge copper pipe coil as a cheap alternative. Skip the pad in El Salvador if you get outside, and if you live in the Southern Hemisphere put relocation ahead of any device. If you try a cheaper pad, measure the field it gives off and how you respond. Avoid heavy static-magnet jewelry, and keep magnetic necklaces for flights.

articles.title: Reading the field at home and in the body
articles.summary: Kruse's do-it-yourself readouts of a place's magnetic quality and the body's state: beeswax candles, mosquitoes, clouds, auroras, animals, tans, blood smears, teeth, lab markers, clinic tests, heart-rate variability and a personal scorecard.
keyPoints: Kruse treats human health as the most sensitive magnetometer, and gives members simple ways to read a place's field before official data catch up.
His best-known place test is a rated beeswax candle: burning fast means a weak field or heavy wireless load, slow and clean means a strong one.
He reads mosquitoes, auroras, volcano cloud caps and animal behavior as signs of whether a place's field is holding or failing.
In the body he reads routine labs, blood smears, teeth, bone and pupils as physics readouts of charge, water and deuterium.
His running gauge of progress is heart-rate variability in deep sleep, alongside a personal scorecard.

sections.body: Kruse treats human health as the most sensitive magnetometer there is: fertility and death rates tracked by zip code, he says, show field change before official data do. Because those data are smoothed and slow, he gives members simple ways to read a place and their own body.

sections.heading: Reading a place
sections.body:
His best-known proxy is a rated beeswax candle burned where you live. On schedule means normal. Faster, such as a 24-hour candle gone in 18, means field decline or a heavy wireless load. Slower and clean means a strong local field, while slower with leftover wax means an artificial "over-clamp," as when a member set a candle on a magnetic bracelet. He reads the flame as a check of the local dielectric constant — the same charge-holding property he tracks in cell water — because that dielectric shapes the ionosphere's water content above you and how readily energy moves between ground, ocean and air. He uses only beeswax, which he describes as deuterium-depleted and made of one-handed molecules, because paraffin is heavy in deuterium and spoils the reading. He also reads the World Magnetic Model declination map the same way: green agonic for aligned cristae, packed blue or red lines for local interference that mirrors the warped junctions in mitochondrial images.

Auroras are a reading in themselves. Seeing them overhead means, to Kruse, that the field beneath you is poor and that it is time to move. The aurora that reached Puerto Rico, at 18Â°N, in May 2024 is his warning to everyone living along the Atlantic from Greenland to the Caribbean.

On land he pairs candles with mosquitoes: insects active by day as well as night mark a weak spot, a method he calls "magnetic dowsing" and used to buy property in El Salvador. Insects work as sensors, he explains, because their chitin shells are piezoelectric, turning pressure and fields into tiny currents. Mosquitoes spreading into Iceland show him that the magnetic barrier that kept them out has given way. In a humid region the sky offers another clue: a volcano that has lost its cloud cap signals a local "magnetic stall," a cone no longer able to hold its water.

Animals tell the same story. In his account, traditional trackers read land by behavior: herds splintering into small erratic groups, dull dry coats even near water, and grazing shifted to pre-dawn and dusk. His shortlist of signs that a place is failing is aurorae, unwell people and dying animals, especially birds, bees and fish. He watches reports from his Gulf of Mexico shrimp supplier and names godwits, Arctic terns and albatrosses as bird canaries.

Instruments have limits. Even a high-grade ground magnetometer, he says, cannot see what he is tracking, which has to be measured from above by the Swarm satellites. He expects diamond-based quantum magnetometers could one day map crustal "oases" where the local field still holds strong.

sections.heading: Reading the body
sections.body:
In the blood, a rapidly shifting potassium level means, to Kruse, that the nearest agonic line (where compass north and true north agree) is moving away or that the person is spoiling their own magnetic tracking. High ferritin, the iron-storage marker, reflects a weak local field and poor choices around light and grounding. His four everyday proxies are morning blood sugar (his "magnetic dawning phenomenon"), LDL, vitamin B12 and new pigment changes.

Other routine labs he reads as physics. A blood urea-to-creatinine ratio near 10 shows, to him, well-hydrated cell water easing proton flow, while one above 20 shows structured water collapsing. A strong cortisol rise after waking alongside high HRV means the morning reset has locked in. Vitamin D of 40â€“60 ng/mL with low blood calcium signals a motor spinning well, whereas a reading above 100 with high calcium he calls a "crime scene" of lost charge.

A tan shows only the outside, though it can still test official numbers: his clients in Calgary all report they cannot hold a tan, which makes him doubt the field strength quoted for the area. For what he calls the "interior tan," the state of melanin and water deep inside, he looks at homocysteine and TMAO, which he treats as "silt" markers of poor deuterium clearance, and at slow flow on thermal imaging, which he calls the ideal fast test because it reflects how thick the blood is. He predicts that a zip-code map of homocysteine would overlay the declination map, peaking in weak-field zones.

sections.heading: Blood, teeth and bone
sections.body:
A blood smear is another window. Red cells that turn spiky, called burr cells, have in his reading lost their membrane charge as deuterium stiffens the membrane, and cells stacked like coins (rouleaux) signal magnetic collapse. Healthy cells carry enough surface charge to push one another apart and float freely, and as charge returns, he says, the cells separate again.

He watches the hard tissues too. Under a UV-A/UV-B flashlight, teeth that look dull and yellowish-grey turn a translucent, bluish white as deuterium clears, and bone in the jaw and shin should feel springy rather than heavy and brittle when pressed.

sections.heading: Clinic and home checks
sections.body:
At his clinic he uses what he calls a "Quantum Biometric Dashboard." Pupils that constrict sluggishly under blue light but respond faster to red point to a deuterium-clogged brainstem. Gas discharge imaging of hair and nails gauges how readily the body gives off electrons. A cool core with warm skin shows the body's cooling working, and stool richer in deuterium than the blood shows heavy hydrogen leaving.

For parents he offers home checks: a lag between hearing an instruction and acting on it, pupils that stay wide or sluggish in sunlight, frequent static shocks, frizzy hair or dry, ashy skin that calm when the child goes barefoot, and poor balance or car sickness that vanishes in a bath or pool, which he reads as deuterium load.

sections.heading: His problem-solving method
sections.body:
Kruse adapts George PÃ³lya's *How to Solve It*, as his neurosurgery mentors taught it, into four steps. First, define the problem as a local voltage drop and check for AC magnetic fields and blue light. Second, work back from oxygen in its stable triplet state, restoring the field with grounding, sun and natural resonators such as basalt. Third, act with targeted cold, breathing and light, patiently. Fourth, look back and check the result by another route.

He judges progress on a personal scorecard: salivary D/H (the ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen in saliva) below 130 ppm, the body's ultra-weak light turning quiet and coherent, and nerve voltage back near âˆ’90 mV. Heart-rate variability (HRV, the beat-to-beat variation in heart timing) in deep sleep is the running gauge, though he cautions it cannot warn of a sudden local loss of field.

In practice, the beeswax candle test protocol uses a rated pure-beeswax candle and reads it alongside day-versus-night mosquito activity. The HRV tracking protocol makes deep-sleep HRV the main progress gauge, adds the markers, smear, tooth and bone checks and scorecard above, and treats high ferritin and fast-shifting potassium as warnings. The “Track your local field” protocol adds watching your zip code's Swarm data, auroras, local animals, insects and fisheries, and the cloud caps on nearby volcanoes.

articles.title: Sleep sanctuary
articles.summary: Kruse calls poor sleep a light-and-magnetic hardware failure, so the bedroom must be dark, cold, grounded, wireless-free and aligned with the field.
keyPoints: Kruse treats poor sleep as a hardware problem of light and magnetism in the bedroom, not a chemical shortage.
In his model the melatonin that matters is made inside cells by mitochondria overnight, and light after dark switches it off.
He says melatonin needs both electric and magnetic containment, so grounding alone is not enough while Wi-Fi and wiring run.
A cold room, he argues, speeds the brain's fluid vortex that flushes deuterium out during deep sleep.
His bedroom is dark, cold, grounded, wireless-free and on a north–south line with the head to the north.

sections.body:
Kruse treats poor sleep as a hardware problem, not a chemical shortage: in his model the body cannot sleep well when the bedroom's light and magnetic environment is wrong. That is why he says sleeping pills and melatonin supplements make things worse, and why he puts the room itself at the center of sleep repair.

His reasoning starts with melatonin. The melatonin that matters most to him is not the small amount the pineal gland releases into the blood, but the much larger amount mitochondria (the cell's energy-producing units) make inside cells overnight. Drawing on Russel Reiter's work, he sees this nightly melatonin as a repair signal: while you sleep, it calms stressed cells and nudges them back toward normal behavior.

Light after dark switches that repair off. Kruse points to the white LED, built by coating a blue LED with a yellow phosphor to save energy. Its strong blue peak fires the eye's daytime sensors (light-sensitive retinal cells that tell the brain clock it is day), so a screen or LED bulb at night tells the clock it is noon, and cells skip their overnight melatonin.

Darkness alone is not enough, he argues. Making melatonin needs two kinds of "containment" around the mitochondrial membrane, one electric and one magnetic. Grounding (skin contact with the earth, or a grounded sheet) restores only the electric part. The magnetic part depends on the field around the bed, which is why Wi-Fi, wiring and electric beds can ruin sleep even in a pitch-black room. He is blunt that an electric bed is a mistake.

Cold matters for a separate reason. In deep sleep the spaces between brain cells widen and spinal fluid moves through the brain in a spiral he calls a vortex. In his model a cold room contracts brain tissue slightly, which narrows the vortex and makes it spin faster. That flings deuterium (heavy hydrogen, which he says jams the mitochondrial motor) out of the brain toward the lymphatic drains in the neck.

The last piece is direction. Kruse wants the bed on a north–south line with the head to the north, so the brain's magnetic iron crystals and the iron-containing proteins in mitochondria lie parallel to Earth's field lines all night. Because the magnetic pole is now moving quickly, he says this alignment should be checked against today's field rather than set once and forgotten.

sections.heading: What he says to do
sections.body:
He calls the result a "magnetic sanctuary." His “Sleep sanctuary” protocol asks for Wi-Fi, routers and other wireless devices switched off before sleep, and total darkness, with red incandescent light or full red blockers after sunset instead of LEDs. It also means no electric bed and no Bluetooth sleep trackers. Rings and wearables, he adds, cannot measure what he thinks matters most: how scrambled indoor life has left the brainstem.

The room should have a grounded sheet and be cold, ideally on the ground floor rather than high in a building. His north–south bed protocol adds the head-north alignment, rechecked as the pole moves. Where the local field is weak he suggests sleeping all night on a static magnetic pad, or, if that is unaffordable, putting a coil of heavy copper pipe under the pillow. Sleeping pills and melatonin pills stay on his avoid list.

articles.title: Sleep in his model: adenosine, myelin and the nightly flip
articles.summary: Kruse explains sleep as the nightly recharge of an electrical grid: adenosine signals the membrane is tiring, myelin recharges as a proton battery, the brain flips polarity to purge deuterium and write memory into water, and how you wake (or wake at 2 a.m.) shows whether it worked.
keyPoints: Kruse explains sleep as the nightly recharge of the body's electrical grid, not simple rest.
In his model adenosine is a smoke alarm that the membrane voltage is sagging, and it triggers sleep.
He says myelin works as a proton battery recharged overnight, so sleep need scales inversely with white-matter volume.
At night the brain should flip electrical polarity to purge deuterium and write memory into brain water.
He reads how you wake, and whether you wake at 2 a.m., as a readout of whether the night's work got done.

sections.body: Kruse explains sleep as the nightly recharge of the body's electrical grid rather than simple rest. In his model three things happen in sequence: a chemical alarm signals that the grid is tiring, the brain's white matter recharges like a battery, and the brain reverses its electrical polarity to clear deuterium (heavy hydrogen). When any step fails, he says, sleep breaks down.

sections.heading: The adenosine alarm
sections.body:
During the day, mitochondria hold a very strong electric field across their inner membrane (he gives 30 million volts per metre). In his view this field is what lets the membrane let in ordinary hydrogen and keep heavy hydrogen out. Hours of waking work create friction that slows electrons, so the voltage sags and the water inside cells drifts from its structured, charge-holding state toward ordinary "bulk" water.

To avoid a blowout, which he calls Marcus inversion (electron flow stalling once it is pushed past its best rate), the cell strips phosphate groups off its ATP fuel. The adenosine left over is his "smoke alarm": it tells the brainstem's arousal network that the grid is tiring and taking on deuterium, and that triggers sleep. He adds that an ungrounded day also builds up oleamide, a fatty signal that eventually shuts the connections between brain cells and stalls the thalamus, the brain's relay and pacing center. It is cleared overnight. For this reason he places sleep in the state of brain water and the heat of the spinal fluid, not in microtubules.

sections.heading: Myelin as a proton battery
sections.body:
Kruse hails a 2026 hypothesis by Felix Scholkmann and colleagues as support for his model. Myelin, the fatty wrapping around nerve fibers, is not passive insulation but a proton battery charged during sleep. Myelin basic protein, packed with positively charged amino acids, is the "anode" that grips protons. Proteolipid protein, which spans the membrane, is the "wire" that carries them to ATP synthase, the motor that makes ATP.

Because myelin has few mitochondria of its own, he says mitochondria ship working ATP synthase to it overnight in small membrane packages. At the same time melatonin cools the brain by 1–2 °C, which tightens the relevant enzymes so deuterium is filtered out as the battery refills.

Several conclusions follow in his model. Sleep need scales inversely with white-matter volume: bats sleep about 20 hours, humans about 8, elephants about 3.5. Sleep loss and marathons drain the battery, and an indoor, blue-lit life lets myelin water collapse in a way no sleeping pill can fix. He also says there is no genetic night owl. A habitual night owl, to him, is an ungrounded person whose cellular battery is so low the master clock cannot find its starting line, and environment, not clock genes, resets it.

sections.heading: The nightly polarity flip
sections.body:
By day, Kruse says, electrons moving across Earth's field lines create a "biological Hall voltage." At sunset, melanin in the skin and brain, with the hippocampus acting as a switchboard, should reverse polarity. Following Robert O. Becker's direct-current research, he describes current then flowing outward from the body's core to its edges. This "nocturnal Hall current inversion" is his main deuterium purge engine, and in dream sleep the brainstem paralyzes the body while it runs.

The flip also has a memory job in his model. He holds that long-term memory lives less in the strength of connections between nerve cells than in brain water itself, stored in how that water bends light and in the spin states of its atoms. Reversing polarity at night is what lets these "magnetic bits" be written so they last without a constant power supply.

He reads the firm, settled feeling of deep sleep as the brain's structure being rebuilt. The fluid chambers widen, the tiny beating hairs (cilia) that line them re-form what he calls a "magnetic mold," and tanycytes, the gatekeeper cells lining the floor of the third ventricle, regain control over what reaches the hypothalamus.

Night is also when the system is most exposed. Once the sun is down, the near-infrared and UV-A light that kept cell water thin all day are gone, so the water stiffens back toward the state he scores as 78 and the spin of fluid in the fourth ventricle slows. Deuterium that the daytime spin held in suspension can then settle on the breathing centers of the lower brainstem, and in his model the brain stops prompting deep breaths.

Screens, Wi-Fi, jet lag, a poor local field and too little near-infrared light all stop the flip and leave the spinal fluid loaded with deuterium; grounded sleep lets melanin make the switch. He reads night-time gasps and leg jerks as emergency jolts the body uses to restart a stalled circuit. The flip also depends on a melanin-based brainstem-to-gut nerve circuit, and when that is clogged with lipofuscin (his "rusted melanin," degraded pigment debris), it cannot start.

sections.heading: Reading the morning after
sections.body:
Kruse treats the way you wake as a readout of whether the night's work got done. After restorative sleep, in his model, cell water has climbed back from 78 toward the structured state he scores as 160. Meanwhile the vagus nerve's overnight bicarbonate flush and the pumping of the abdomen have moved stagnant fluid out of the tissues toward the bladder. A good night therefore leaves you feeling dry and lean. Puffy eyes or stiff fingers mean the fluid stalled and deuterium stayed put.

Waking in the small hours is a different signal. Around 2 a.m., he says, the brain attempts its main deuterium flush. If the exhaust route is blocked, pressure builds, the vagal centers on the floor of the fourth ventricle sound the alarm, and the adrenal glands release a burst of cortisol to force a restart. The sleeper ends up wide awake yet worn out, which he calls a "glymphatic backlog."

Vision is his second gauge. Waking to sharp, high-contrast sight means the light-handling circuits came through the night clear. Fog or a heavy head means the base of the brain did not flush its deuterium during dream sleep, so the brain starts the day short of stable oxygen.

A flat, sluggish day is the daytime face of the same failure. Tanycytes and the hypothalamus, he says, sense deuterium in the spinal fluid and turn down hypocretin, the brain's wakefulness signal, leaving a person in what he describes as a "zombie" state.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: He points to his “Sleep sanctuary” protocol (a dark, cold, grounded, wireless-free bedroom with the bed north–south) so the battery and the flip can work. He pairs it with daytime sun that includes near-infrared, and morning sun and grounding to reset a night owl. His binaural sleep audio, a theta-to-delta tone glide while falling asleep, is meant to sync the brain's nightly fluid pulsing. He judges the result by how dry, clear-eyed and clear-headed you wake, and reads 2 a.m. waking or a sluggish day as a sign the drain needs work. For sleep or white-matter problems he recommends changing the environment, including relocating, rather than taking pills.

articles.title: Cold thermogenesis and the brain's fluid vortex
articles.summary: Kruse calls cold a "quantum vice" that compresses tissue to keep deuterium out and the discharge that follows sun's charge — an override for poor sun or field, with lineage and timing caveats.
keyPoints: Kruse calls cold a "quantum vice" that tightens tissue so deuterium cannot get in, the main override when sun or field is poor.
In his model sun charges the body's battery and cold discharges it, so cold builds on sunlight rather than replacing it.
He cites a study where cold water raised dopamine about 250% for hours without a crash, and draws a daily dose of 60–180 seconds.
Targeted cold on the palate, chin, neck, teeth or belly, he says, speeds the fluid vortex that flings deuterium out.
He warns that some East Asian lineages in a weak field should hold off on deep cold until well grounded and sunlit.

sections.body: Kruse calls cold thermogenesis (deliberate cold exposure) a "quantum vice": a squeeze that tightens tissue so deuterium (heavy hydrogen) cannot get in. It matters in his model because cold is the main override when sunlight or the local magnetic field is poor, as in winter, at high latitude or in a bad location.

sections.heading: How the vice works
sections.body:
When nerve tissue is chilled it contracts, and cells must reorganize their fats to keep their membranes from freezing stiff. In white matter, Kruse says, this squeeze narrows the spacing in myelin's proteins so they clamp onto protons, and narrows the entry channels so the deuteron (deuterium's nucleus, about twice the mass of ordinary hydrogen) no longer fits. The result in his model is cell water restored to its structured, charge-holding state, which he scores as "160" against 78 for ordinary water, even when your location is poor.

He adds a point about phase change. Heavy water freezes at 3.8 °C rather than 0 °C and changes state differently from ordinary water, so a sharp cold shock at the skin surface changes local water conditions in a way he says helps shake deuterium loose.

Slowing down is part of the benefit. He points to NASA research on synthetic torpor, a hibernation-like state planned for deep-space crews, in which cooling can lower metabolic rate by as much as three-quarters. In his reading, cellular motors that turn more slowly make fewer errors and give heavy water less chance to do damage, so cold works as a shield as well as a squeeze.

sections.heading: Cold and dopamine
sections.body: Kruse leans on Pavel Šrámek's study from Charles University in Prague, in which ten young men sat neck-deep for an hour in water at 32, 20 and 14 °C. At 14 °C, norepinephrine rose about 530% and dopamine about 250%. He stresses that the dopamine stayed raised for two to three hours and drifted back without dipping below baseline, so there is no crash or tolerance. In his model, cold clears deuterium loading in the brain's hypothalamic and limbic regions. The daily dose he draws from this is short: 60–180 seconds on bare skin, cold enough to make you want out, ideally in the morning.

sections.heading: Sun loads, cold discharges
sections.body:
Kruse pairs cold with sunlight rather than treating one as a stand-in for the other. Sun, in his model, charges the battery: it thins cell water toward the 160 state and loosens the heavy water held in it. Cold is the discharge. It sets off a burst of ultra-weak photon emission (the faint light living cells give off) that flips the polarity of the body's direct-current system, the one Robert Becker described. Grounding, he says, magnifies both steps.

Timing follows from that pairing. He wants the evening meal finished about two hours before sunset, while the sun's infrared is still available, so the stomach can reach its peak acidity and the alkaline response that follows can run. Cold taken too close to a meal, he warns, risks "freezing" the food mid-digestion. Cold after sunset, once the day's sun has already thinned the water, boosts the overnight flush: the photon burst helps clear deuterium from the fourth ventricle, the fluid chamber at the base of the brain, during sleep. Humans are, in his phrase, "costly in time, not energy," so when you use cold matters as much as how much.

sections.heading: Where cold fits, and its limits
sections.body:
In his hierarchy, cold — especially an ice bath — is the ultimate override for winter and poor locations and should come before any diet change; he ties the gain to Curie physics (colder matter holds magnetism better). Used alone in a place like California he calls it unsustainable, and heavy cold superfluous once someone is already pinned under good sun. He pairs it with Buteyko under-breathing when he wants both deuterium fractionation from cold and the magnetic-flux lift from retained CO₂.

He sets limits. For East and Southeast Asian maternal lineages (haplogroups D5b1 and F) in a weak field, water at 55–65 °F can "freeze" the energy engine, because the short-lived electron pairs the cell relies on need a strong field. Those people should first maximize morning UV and infrared light, ground fully and shield from wireless fields. At dawn, neck-deep water absorbs the infrared part of sunlight, scrambles the light's angle and acts like a Faraday cage, so he prefers feet in the surf with the rest of the bare body in the air. In the tropics, natural water is always cooler than the body, so ordinary swimming counts as cold therapy.

sections.heading: Targeted cold and the head's fluid vortex
sections.body:
Kruse also uses cold on specific spots. Ice on the roof of the mouth, under the chin or on the back of the neck contracts tissue and blood vessels and narrows what he calls the cranial "vortex chamber," so spinal fluid spins at a sharper angle and faster. Deuterium, being heavier, cannot hold the tight orbit and is thrown out to the salivary and lymphatic drains. Strong cold also, he says, widens the band of structured water lining the fourth ventricle, giving the fluid a nearly frictionless track toward the vagus nerve's drain. Sleeping in a cold room does the same overnight. He adds that cold packs the inner mitochondrial membrane more tightly, so its first energy-extracting complex strips electrons from food faster.

The teeth are another target. Kruse says chewing ice cleared the fluoride marks from his own enamel. The temperature gap made the fluoride-laden enamel brittle, and ice cracking against tooth gave a strong piezoelectric discharge (current produced by mechanical stress) that, in his account, drove out fluoride and deuterium. The jolt through the trigeminal nerve, the main nerve of the face, also restarted his gut's bicarbonate flush. Cold teeth, he adds, favor the ferrous form of iron, which handles oxygen well and supports melanin. He traces the idea to cold-water free diving he did about 20 years ago.

The belly is the last target. When the gut has stalled, he leans on cold, light and ground together. Local cold on the abdomen, in his model, locks the local field in place, raises the oxygen available to tissue and spins deuterium out. Violet (380 nm) and red (670 nm) light on the skin restores the direct current that runs through collagen. Grounding steadies the signal so healthy mitochondria can restart the gut's muscular wave.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His “Cold thermogenesis” protocol is a daily 60–180 seconds of cold on bare skin, ideally in the morning, leaning on cold more heavily in winter or a poor location and always building on sunlight rather than replacing it. At sunrise he wants feet in the surf rather than full immersion, and in the tropics he counts natural-water swimming. He adds targeted ice on the palate, under the chin or on the back of the neck, chewing ice for the teeth, cold on the abdomen with skin light and grounding for a sluggish gut, and a cold bedroom. A cold session after sunset is an option, kept well away from an evening meal eaten about two hours before sunset. People from D5b1 or F lineages living in a weak field should hold off on deep cold until they are well grounded and sunlit.

articles.title: Movement, and when exercise becomes a toxin
articles.summary: Kruse supports daily outdoor movement but says exercise turns harmful when the body is deuterium-loaded or unpinned, when muscle is built under artificial light at the brain's expense, or when it happens in sealed, high-CO₂ gyms, so environment comes before fitness.
keyPoints: Kruse supports daily movement but says exercise only helps a body whose environment is already right: environment first, fitness second.
In his model movement matters electrically, because bone and collagen make current when loaded and abdominal contractions pump the brain's fluid.
He says exercise becomes a toxin in a deuterium-loaded or unpinned body, and that muscle built under LEDs steals power from the brain.
He warns that sealed, crowded gyms carry high carbon dioxide that acidifies spinal fluid during hard breathing.
His protocol is moderate daily movement outdoors, grounded and in sunlight, added only after leaving wireless fields and getting morning sun.

sections.body: Kruse supports daily movement, but argues that exercise only helps a body whose environment is already right. In a body loaded with deuterium (heavy hydrogen) or "unpinned" (not anchored by a stable magnetic field, grounding and sunlight), he says exercise becomes a toxin. His rule is environment first, fitness second.

sections.heading: Why movement matters
sections.body:
In Kruse's model the real purpose of exercise is electrical. Bone and collagen are piezoelectric (they make a small current when squeezed or bent), so movement releases current that supports the spiral flow and charge of the blood. That keeps deuterium circulating and away from the mitochondria, and moving joints spin deuterium out of themselves. Mechanical and gravitational loading, together with a stable local field and grounding, also keep the elastin in artery walls healthy.

He adds a pump. Citing a 2026 Nature Neuroscience mouse study by Greenawalt, Drew and colleagues, he says abdominal muscle contractions physically move the brain and drive the fluid flow that cleans it during waking hours. Astronauts lose this pump as their core weakens in microgravity. He thinks the researchers stopped short: in his model the motion does more than wash the brain, it sorts its water, spinning heavy water away from light. He calls this "centrifugal fractionation."

He also reads one study's gene data as showing that single workouts produce only weak, messy changes, while weeks of steady training produce an ordered shift. Long-running pulsed electric current in sea squirts produced the same shift, which in his model shows that sustained current, not effort itself, rebuilds the cell.

Working muscle makes deuterium as well as using it, in his view. He points out that Olympic athletes and racehorse trainers load up on bicarbonate before events, and argues the real reason is not lactate but heavy hydrogen: rapid ATP turnover builds deuterium in the muscle, and fatigue sets in when the pancreas cannot clear it fast enough. He describes muscle as partly a water reservoir the body uses to keep its electrical resistance low.

sections.heading: When exercise turns harmful
sections.body:
Kruse cites a Nature Aging study that defines muscle aging as an energy crisis in which the key energy-making enzymes decline. He agrees that structured training beats counting steps. But in his view exercise is a toxin when cell water is deuterium-loaded or when oxygen has flipped into its reactive "singlet" state instead of its stable "triplet" state — spinning ATP against water thickened like maple syrup. Where someone is already on a good agonic line under proper sun, he rates extra gym work near zero benefit. Deuterium-loaded people, he says, lose lifespan when they train, most visibly astronauts.

He lists specific traps. Compression-and-cooling machines such as Vasper, he says, cause bursts of reperfusion damage in energy-poor muscle. Building muscle in old age is one of the costliest things a cell can do and steals energy from DNA repair, immunity and overnight brain clearance, leaving "a big frame on a bankrupt core." Watching television and then working out undoes the benefit, because screen light loads the cell with deuterium and disrupts its clock, and years of running ungrounded in rubber-soled shoes wear out joints. Flights and altitude raise the risk of muscle loss.

sections.heading: The price of bulk
sections.body:
Kruse calls extra muscle "biological inflation." Muscle, in his account, diverts the body's light-derived energy away from the brain and heart into an expensive periphery. He adds a physics image: more mass raises the body's moment of inertia, and if angular momentum is conserved the rate of spin has to drop, slowing what he calls the body's "speed of truth." Humans, in his story, gave up the brute strength of earlier hominins in exchange for a bigger brain.

He backs this with Kleiber's law, the rule that metabolic rate rises with body mass to the three-quarter power, and with the idea of a lifetime budget of roughly 1.5 to 2 billion heartbeats. Metabolically demanding muscle spends that budget faster. A gorilla carries about four times our muscle and a third of our brain and is worn out by its late thirties.

Light sets how steep the price is. Building muscle under gym LEDs, without sunlight's near-infrared and 380 nm violet, is what he calls "rhino-ification." The body cannot keep its cell water charged, so new muscle steals power from the brain. Fascia (the connective sheets wrapping the muscles) stiffens and loses its ability to carry light and charge, and the stress signal GDF-15 climbs. He says the brain pays most where melanin is thinnest, as after menopause, unless the skin is used as a solar panel to make up the shortfall.

sections.heading: The air inside gyms
sections.body:
Gym air is a separate trap. Outdoor air holds about 415 parts per million (ppm) of carbon dioxide, while sealed, crowded gyms often reach 1,200 to more than 2,000. He says sleep and focus slip above roughly 800 ppm, and cites the 2012 Lawrence Berkeley Lab study in which decision-making fell on six of nine scales at 1,000–1,500 ppm. Hard breathing pulls that air, along with solvent fumes and fine particles, deep into the lungs.

In his model, excess carbon dioxide taken in during exertion acidifies the spinal fluid, collapses structured water and lets deuterium lock the tissue's water in place. Years of indoor team training, he says, take that toll on the brain, and in a declining magnetic field even light indoor sessions carry risk.

sections.heading: Overtraining and the brain
sections.body:
Overtraining harms the brain too. Kruse presents a Cell Metabolism study (Huang and colleagues) in which excess lactate in strained muscle makes it release mitochondrial "pretenders": vesicles that cross into the hippocampus, block the delivery of healthy mitochondria and occupy their docking sites at synapses. In the study's data, he notes, moderate exercise was protective for the ageing brain while vigorous exercise beyond a threshold reversed that.

He compresses the chain into a single line. Overtraining raises GDF-15, which switches off AMPA receptors (the fast-signaling receptors at nerve connections) in the melanin-linked tissue of the nervous system, and the body slides into the cell danger response, its defensive shutdown mode.

To him, a fit person who collapses in competition had spinal fluid already locked with deuterium that needed clearing ("de-fragging") before any training. He says marathon running wrecks the heart's own spiral flow, and that it is now survival of the wisest, not the fittest.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His exercise protocol is daily movement outdoors, grounded and in sunlight, at moderate rather than extreme intensity. Order matters to him. First leave the wireless "soup," ground and sleep in a low-EMF bedroom, then get morning sun with its infrared, and only then add training. He would not start an unwell, unpinned person on Zone 2 or interval training, and wants a deuterium-loaded person cleared before training at all. He also warns against going straight from a screen to a workout, running ungrounded in rubber soles, training in sealed or blue-lit gyms, using compression machines while deuterium-loaded, chasing marathons, and making muscle-building a goal in old age. Where strength work is done, he wants it done with skin in the sun rather than under LEDs.

articles.title: The vagus nerve: deuterium drain and its stimulation
articles.summary: Kruse calls the vagus nerve the body's main deuterium drain and a sensor of the deuterium load, and tunes it with voice, chewing, sound and gentle stimulation, with firm guardrails on devices.
keyPoints: Kruse calls the vagus nerve the body's main exhaust pipe for deuterium and a sensor that reads the deuterium load in spinal fluid.
In his model it drives the pancreas's daily bicarbonate flush, which binds deuterium and sweeps it out of the body.
He says the voice evolved as a deuterium exhaust, so humming, chanting, singing and chewing are ways to tone the nerve.
Slow belly breathing with long exhales is his top everyday vagal stimulus, with sunlight and grounding giving the nerve its torque.
Electrical stimulation, he says, must be gentle and on the left side only, never on the neck or right side.

sections.body: In Kruse's model the vagus nerve, the long nerve running from the brainstem to the heart, lungs and gut, is the body's main exhaust pipe for deuterium (heavy hydrogen). Together with lymph and spinal-fluid flow, it carries disorder out of the system. He calls it the body's "renormalization operator," and when its tone fails he says heavy hydrogen backs up into the brain. His advice aims at keeping this drain open.

sections.heading: The body's exhaust pipe
sections.body:
Kruse says the vagus supplies a steady rhythmic signal that keeps the barrier cells of the gut, lungs and blood vessels electrically charged. That charge keeps potassium in place and the water around those cells structured, which he says physically screens out deuterium. When vagal tone fades from wireless exposure, artificial blue light and lack of grounding, heavy hydrogen leaks in. It then backs up through the gut's nerve network into the brain past the fourth ventricle, the fluid chamber at the base of the brain.

The traffic runs both ways. Spots on the ventricle floor, chief among them the area postrema, are circumventricular organs: places where the blood–brain barrier is naturally missing, so they can taste the deuterium load in blood and freshly made spinal fluid. Deuterium makes that fluid denser and less able to hold charge, and when the sensors read the drop, vagal tone is turned down and the heart's rhythm loses its steadiness. When the load is heavy, the vagus's motor center signals the gut and lungs, and neuropod cells (sensor cells in the gut lining wired to the vagus) release serotonin to start the muscular "stirring" that moves contents toward the pancreas's bicarbonate exhaust. In this picture the vagus is a sense organ for deuterium, not just a calming nerve.

The nerve leaves the skull through the jugular foramen, an opening it shares with the jugular vein, so he reads a squeezed jugular vein at the top of the neck as a nerve being strangled. Through heart rate variability (HRV, the beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm) it keeps the heart locked to the solar day. HRV is therefore his dashboard gauge of vagal tone, and a sudden halving means the nerve has lost its grip on the heart.

He ties the vagus to digestion through what he calls the bicarbonate "tailpipe." In a strong field, the vagus drives the pancreas and duodenum to release about two liters of bicarbonate a day, and this negatively charged carrier binds deuterium and sweeps it out of the body. Sugar under blue light, or a disturbed field, "welds the tailpipe shut."

sections.heading: The eye as a vagal switch
sections.body: Kruse links the eye to the vagus through the ciliary ganglion, a small nerve relay behind the eye. Full-spectrum light on the iris and focusing muscles, he says, sets the idle speed of the gut's bicarbonate flush, while glasses and contact lenses send a false "dark" signal that slows the drain.
