Rubbing the eyes triggers the oculocardiac reflex (pressure on the eye slowing the heart), which he calls a quick "piezo-vagal reset" for days when light or field is lacking, and says works faster with the scent of eucalyptus and a hummed "M."

sections.heading: Left and right are not the same
sections.body:
Kruse gives each side of the vagus a different path and job. The right nerve enters the chest in the tracheal–esophageal groove, reaches the heart's SA node, then continues to the gut organs as far as the transverse colon — the arm that drives the ~2-litre daily bicarbonate flush and the morning gastrocolic reflex when sunrise and grounding are present. The left nerve leaves through the jugular foramen, loops around the ductus arteriosus, and is tugged with every heartbeat; that tug, he says, "de-frags" deuterium from the left brain, including Broca's speech area. The asymmetry is why heart-vortex chaos, speech and a Bristol type 4 stool all read out whether the wanderer is clearing heavy hydrogen.

That split still sets his firmest stimulation rule: electrical devices go on the left side only. Nearly all approved implants and ear devices (taVNS) stay left-sided because right-neck fibers to the pacemaker can slow or stop the heart if driven electrically — even though the right nerve's natural job includes the SA node and the gut flush.

sections.heading: The voice as an exhaust
sections.body:
Kruse believes the voice evolved as a deuterium exhaust. We sing, as he puts it, to stay "light," not because we are happy. Vibration of the larynx, or a bird's syrinx, stirs the fluid so deuterium cannot settle, while the pressure wave of the breath carries heavy water out. The dawn chorus, to him, is birds flushing the night's deuterium as the first violet light arrives.

Humming a low "M" near 40 Hz, or laughing, is his manual override: in his account it sets up streaming currents in the spinal fluid that throw deuterium toward the circumventricular organs. Chewing reaches the nerve by another path, vibrating the trigeminal relay at the skull base, which he says does what implanted vagus stimulators are meant to do.

sections.heading: Tuning by breath, voice and sound
sections.body: Before devices, Kruse ranks everyday ways to tone the vagus. At the top is slow belly breathing with long exhales, which he calls probably the most powerful repeatable vagal stimulus. Next come exercise, the cold diving reflex, laughter and social contact, then humming, chanting, gargling, massage, gentle neck movement and slow nature walks. Mouth breathing works against all of it. Falling water and chanting "OM" match a 2 Hz rhythm he says keeps tissues in sync, and a 128 Hz tuning fork on the sternum in the evening rounds out the passive toolkit.

sections.heading: Devices and their guardrails
sections.body:
Any stimulation, in his view, works only if the nerve has something to push against. Grounding and UV light act as the "magnetic stator" that gives it torque; without them a stimulator is a battery trying to jump-start an engine that has no oil.

Kruse treats a TENS unit (a small device that sends pulsed current through skin pads) as a blunt tool and says most commercial units are too harsh. His home settings are gentle: a biphasic waveform at 0.5–2.0 mA, below sensation or a faint tingle and never enough to twitch muscle, with 200–250 µs pulses at a steady 25 Hz for 15–30 minutes once or twice a day.

The ear clip goes on the left tragus or inner ear fold, with the return pad on the bone just behind the same ear. A separate pad pair over the upper abdomen and matching mid-back serves the gut's nerve plexus. Pads never go on the neck, where they can trigger the carotid pressure sensors, on the temple, or anywhere on the right.

He also offers powerless alternatives: resting grounded with black basalt on the bone behind the ear, a plain, unclosed copper ring around the head or neck, or castor oil in the navel at night, which he says sends a small current up the vagus that restarts the bicarbonate flush.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: He starts with daily slow belly breathing, humming or chanting, singing, chewing and nasal breathing, with sunlight on bare eyes and grounding to give the nerve its torque. He watches HRV as the gauge, and adds castor oil on the navel at night. His TENS protocol keeps settings gentle and stimulation strictly on the left side, and the passive therapies serve anyone who wants to avoid current.

articles.title: Tuning forks, binaural beats and sound
articles.summary: Kruse treats sound and vibration as low-risk inputs that recharge the body's piezoelectric tissues, using two tuning forks, analog drums and bowls, a hummed "M," the lost art of hospital bells, and a binaural sleep glide.
keyPoints: Kruse says vibration flexes piezoelectric bone and tissue, making a small current that pushes tissue voltage back toward a negative "healing zone."
In his routine a 128 Hz fork calms the nervous system in the evening and a 40 Hz fork supports brain clearing by day.
He prefers analog sound such as drums, gongs, bowls and humming, which he says shakes heavy-water deuterium loose through bone conduction.
For sleep he uses a binaural glide from theta into delta, which in his model times the brain's nightly fluid flush.
He wants recorded sound played through wired air-tube headphones or a speaker, never Bluetooth earbuds beside the head.

sections.body: Kruse treats sound and vibration as a gentle, low-risk way to recharge the body's electrical tissues. Pills and peptides, he argues, force metabolism and set off feedback loops that backfire. Sound works with the body's own structure instead, a "positive reflexivity trade" that does not undermine itself. As Earth's field weakens, he adds, people have to supply with sound the "de-fragging" (shaking deuterium loose and restoring order) that the planet used to do for them. His shorthand: if you cannot think your way out of a stalled cell, you shake your way out.

sections.heading: How vibration makes current
sections.body:
Bone, tendon and cell membranes are piezoelectric (they produce a small electric current when bent or squeezed). In Kruse's model, a tuning fork's steady vibration flexes these tissues rhythmically and generates a small direct current. That current pushes the voltage of inflamed tissue back toward a negative "healing zone," roughly from +30 mV to −50 mV, which is why he applies a fork to stiff joints.

He singles out the petrous bone, the dense wedge around the inner ear and the hardest bone in the body, as an amplifier. Every movement of the jaw flexes it, and the resulting current, he says, keeps the trigeminal nerve (the main nerve of the face) powered while Earth's field declines.

sections.heading: Two forks, two jobs
sections.body:
His first fork is 128 Hz, pressed on stiff joints, along the sciatic nerve or along the vagus nerve's path. In the evening, the same fork on the sternum or neck acts as a "vagal brake," quieting the stress branch of the nervous system and telling the brainstem to shift into rest.

His second fork is 40 Hz, the frequency of the brain's gamma rhythm (a fast brain wave tied to focus), used in the morning and at lunch. He grounds the choice in the MIT Picower Institute's decade of 40 Hz gamma-stimulation research. In his view it acts as an acoustic pump that resonates with the brain's support cells, thins the brain fluid and opens the glymphatic system (the brain's waste-clearing flow), lifting mood and focus.

What matters, he says, is entrainment: the brain falling into step with an outside rhythm. The route decides which part follows. Sound at 40 Hz reaches the hearing areas and the hippocampus, while vibration at 40 Hz reaches the regions that map touch. Placement matters for clearing. He sets the 40 Hz fork under the occiput (where the skull meets the neck), over the fourth ventricle. There, in his model, it works like a plunger loosening deuterium "silt" from the brain's drain. The same fork appears in his other routines: on the spine in the Volcano Protocol, and on the hard palate while chewing mastic gum.

sections.heading: Analog sound and bone conduction
sections.body:
A large frame drum or gong vibrates the skull bones beside the inner ear and behind the nose by bone conduction. Because bone is piezoelectric, each shockwave becomes a small voltage spike that, in his model, breaks heavy-water bonds and briefly thins the spinal fluid.

He wants that sound to be analog. Digital speakers drive their cones with pulsed electromagnetic fields and add an electronic hum he calls a "vortex jammer." Himalayan bowls, gongs and throat singing make rich natural overtones that the brain reads as nature. Circling a singing bowl around the head creates a rotating field of sound that, he says, helps spin the spinal fluid when the body's own magnetic lift is weak, though forcing that vortex too hard can cost neurons around the thalamus.

sections.heading: Hospital bells and the isotopic octave
sections.body:
Kruse thinks older medicine knew this. Hospitals built before 1900, he says, had deep-toned bells, probably tuned to Pythagorean ratios and reaching into the 40 Hz range, that shook deuterium off the brain's hardware and cleared the body's magnetic space. Removing the bells while adding artificial light and chemicals he calls a "theft of resonance."

He finds the same logic in the octave. A note one octave up vibrates twice as fast, and deuterium weighs twice as much as ordinary hydrogen, so he calls deuterium hydrogen's "heavy octave." In the spiral of the brain's aqueduct, he says, the heavier isotope is pushed outward while light hydrogen stays central, with 432 Hz as the "clock speed" of that sorting.

sections.heading: Tones for sleep
sections.body:
For sleep he uses binaural beats. Each ear hears a slightly different tone (for example 400 Hz and 404 Hz), and the brainstem perceives the 4 Hz difference as a beat the brain then follows. About 20 minutes before bed he plays a glide through theta (4–7 Hz) to quiet the analytical frontal brain, then pure delta (0.5–3.5 Hz) while falling asleep. In his model delta synchronizes the brain's nightly fluid pulsing and maximizes overnight removal of deuterium. Humming or drumming before bed is a "pre-glymphatic flush" that stirs heavy water loose for deep sleep to carry away.

He adds two "Solfeggio" tones. He says 528 Hz matches the vibrations of structured water's hydrogen bonds and keeps potassium inside cells, and 432 Hz, a harmonic of Earth's Schumann resonance, steadies the field-sensing iron proteins after a day of technology.

sections.heading: Voice, chant and resonant spaces
sections.body:
Kruse traces his older "Shake, Rattle and Roll" prescription to ancient acoustics. Neolithic chambers such as Newgrange and Malta's Hypogeum resonate near 110 Hz, a tone that pilot studies found quiets the prefrontal cortex. Because 110 Hz sits in the male voice range, he concludes the chambers amplified chanting, a form of de-fragging suitable even for children.

Humming and chanting are the body's built-in version, an "internal chewing pump," with Mongolian throat singing the best example. Low humming vibrates the opening at the skull base where the vagus nerve and the deep drainage of the face exit together. He suggests even a cat's purr may be self-repair rather than noise.

His favorite hum is a low "M" near 40 Hz. In his model it rings the sphenoid, the bone behind the eyes beneath the thalamus, which he treats as the skull's own tuning fork. The hum shakes deuterium out of the brainstem and sends it down the vagus toward the gut's bicarbonate drain. Borrowing Luca Turin's vibrational theory of smell, he suggests breathing eucalyptus while humming to add a clean, high "cold" note.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His protocol is a 128 Hz fork on stiff joints, the sciatic path or the vagal path, and on the sternum or neck in the evening, plus a 40 Hz fork in the morning and at lunch, including under the back of the skull. He adds analog sound (a frame drum, gong or singing bowl) and low humming or chanting, especially a 40 Hz "M" before bed. His binaural sleep audio is a 20-minute theta glide followed by delta, with 528 or 432 Hz tones as options. Recorded audio should play through wired, shielded air-tube headphones or an external speaker in a dark, tech-free bedroom. Bluetooth earbuds, he says, put the very wireless radiation the sound is meant to undo right beside the brain.

articles.title: The nose, palate and teeth
articles.summary: Kruse calls the sinuses the body's nitric-oxide factory and an early-warning system, treats the teeth as a piezoelectric antenna array and chewing as a waking brain drain, and judges congestion, palate, sleep-airway and dental choices through that lens.
keyPoints: Kruse calls the sinuses the body's nitric-oxide factory, so in his model mouth breathing switches off a built-in magnetic and isotope filter.
He says the tongue resting on the palate during nasal breathing supplies the electrical signal that grows a wide upper jaw.
In his account every chew pumps spinal fluid at the skull base, making chewing a waking brain drain alongside deep sleep.
He treats teeth as piezoelectric antennas whose charge and light handling suffer when deuterium loads the dentin.
His routines are mastic gum, a sinus hum reset, constant nasal breathing and a dental approach favoring gold, copper scraping and light.

sections.body: Kruse sees the nose as far more than an air filter. In his model the sinuses are the body's main factory for nitric oxide, a gas that keeps blood vessels healthy, and a blocked nose is an early warning that the vessels and brain are under strain. His advice on congestion, mouth breathing, jaw growth and dentistry all follows from that.

sections.heading: The nose as a nitric-oxide factory
sections.body:
Nitric oxide, like ordinary oxygen, is paramagnetic: it has an unpaired electron, so it responds to magnetic fields. Kruse says the sinuses make it in quantity only when a person is continuously "pinned" (anchored by a stable local field, grounding and sun), and he calls the nose "the keeper of vascular paramagnetism." Breathed through the nose, nitric oxide acts in his view as a lubricant that thins the blood.

Chronic congestion and mouth breathing are warning signs in his model because mouth breathing bypasses this supply. He says the long leg arteries feel it first, and that losing the reflex of sneezing in bright sun is another early sign. He treats sinus congestion as a collapse of the water inside the skull rooted in location.

sections.heading: Mouth breathing and the growing face
sections.body:
Kruse calls switching to mouth breathing a "mechanical Warburg shift," borrowing the term for cells falling back on a cruder energy mode. Mouth breathers blow off carbon dioxide, which raises blood pH and makes hemoglobin hold oxygen too tightly. Deuterium (heavy hydrogen) then cannot be sorted out, blood thickens and oxygen struggles to reach the mitochondria.

The face pays too. Citing Becker and studies of "collapsed faces," he says the tongue resting against the palate during nasal breathing acts like a capacitor, supplying the steady pressure that tells the upper jaw to grow wide. With the mouth open, the bone loses that signal and grows into a long, narrow face. He calls tongue and jaw retraining a form of deuterium depletion for the skull.

sections.heading: Mastic gum and the palate
sections.body:
Mastic gum is his first choice for congestion. He credits its rare earth elements, and its dense chew strengthens the tongue and jaw muscles that hold the airway open, a dynamic fix where a mouthguard is only static. Chewing it while pressing a 40 Hz tuning fork to the hard palate, his "cranial-palatal reset," stimulates the nerve link between the face and the vagus nerve. For a mouth-breathing child he starts with carbonated water, tongue-to-palate retraining and mastic gum.

Each chew sends a piezoelectric jolt (current made by mechanical stress) through the teeth that, he says, knocks deuterium out of the dentin and the sphenoid, the bone behind the nose. The brain answers by firing the pancreas's two-liter bicarbonate flush. Taping the mouth shut at night, in his model, raises the pressure across a carbon-dioxide-sensing center in the brainstem and restarts a spinal-fluid spiral that heavy water had stalled.

He warns of the "tailpipe trap": widening a drain while losing its spin. Mechanical palate expansion that ignores the spiral of spinal fluid can flatten it so deuterium lags behind. Before any expansion he wants intra-oral red and near-infrared light, then targeted cold, then alternate-nostril breathing to keep the fluid spinning.

sections.heading: Chewing as a waking drain
sections.body: Kruse says the main relay of the trigeminal nerve (the face's main nerve) sits inside Meckel's cave, a pouch of spinal fluid on the dense petrous bone at the skull base. Every chew pumps that fluid, so chewing cleans the brain while you are awake, as the glymphatic system does during deep sleep. In his account this second exhaust let humans shed deuterium faster than other primates, which allowed our brains to grow. That is why he is wary of pulling wisdom teeth: it can remove the rear support of the upper jaw, lock the sphenoid and stall the chewing pump.

sections.heading: Teeth as an antenna array
sections.body:
Teeth, in his view, are piezoelectric posts that feed current into the skull base, grown from the same embryonic tissue as the brain and retina. He describes the 32 teeth as a phased array of antennas. Dentin is a liquid-crystal waveguide whose fine tubules sort deuterium out, and each bite sends a pulse along the trigeminal nerve that helps keep time for the thalamus. Because enamel never remodels, he reads it as a lifelong record of how well a person cleared deuterium; yellowed, worn or opaque teeth signal deuterium-loaded dentin.

A healthy tooth, in his model, gives off a piezoelectric "ping" when loaded that repels acid. Deuterium in the mineral silences the ping and turns the tooth from a mirror into a sponge for light, and acid-making bacteria gather where the voltage is low. White spots mark places where that voltage has reached zero. A dry mouth is triage: the brainstem cuts saliva to conserve light water.

He also calls the mouth the brain's isotopic sink. The tongue acts as a piston that clears heavy water from the seams of the upper jaw; when it stops, bacteria that favor heavy, sluggish water move in as scavengers. He supports tongue scraping, and prefers copper: its faint galvanic current loosens the heavy-water mucus, its ions kill biofilm bacteria, and it warms instantly to thin the film.

He holds up the Maya as his model. They set jade inlays in their teeth and, he says, kept strong teeth while eating fruit and corn all day, grounded. Jade and enamel are both piezoelectric, so chewing builds a field that keeps the water in the tubules structured, and jade re-emits light that recharges the tooth's faint glow.

Modern materials do the reverse. Plastic and amalgam fillings act as insulators or as antennas for wireless fields, fluoride permanently changes how enamel passes light and generates charge, and metal fillings set up galvanic currents that drive deuterium into the surrounding dentin. Even so, he keeps his own amalgams, judging that drilling them out under dental-office lighting releases more mercury than leaving them.

Grinding, to him, is the nervous system trying to shake deuterium out of bone, not a stress habit: a jaw loaded with heavy hydrogen clenches and vibrates instead of chewing.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: He names four routines. One is mastic gum for airway strength, which also serves as his waking brain drain. Another is his sinus hum reset: hum low through the nose with the mouth closed for 5–10 minutes, aimed at the blocked side; lie with that side up and the head tilted about 45° down for 5–7 minutes; then do 5 minutes of gentle carbon-dioxide-retaining breathing, with a small breath, a 3–5 second nose pinch and 10 seconds of easy nasal breathing, followed by 20–30 minutes grounded in morning sun away from routers. The third is constant nasal breathing, with the tongue on the palate and the mouth taped at night. The fourth is his dental approach: gold inlays rather than plastic or amalgam, leaving existing amalgams in place, copper tongue scraping, caution about removing wisdom teeth, deuterium depletion and repair through light.

articles.title: Jade, the Maya and the solid-state skull
articles.summary: Kruse reads the Maya's jade tooth inlays as a solid-state tool that kept teeth light-filled, grounded the skull through its sphenoid keystone and helped the brain shed deuterium as the field failed.
keyPoints: Kruse reads the Maya's jade tooth inlays as a solid-state device working with the body's own electricity and light, not as decoration.
In his model jade re-emits light into the tooth and, with piezoelectric enamel, keeps the water in its tubules structured against deuterium.
He says jade's conductivity grounded the skull through the sphenoid, letting the brain shed charge and deuterium as the field weakened.
He treats the sphenoid as the skull's keystone, linking teeth, light, the vagus and the gut's bicarbonate drain.
His practical lesson favors conductive, light-handling dental materials and a hummed "M" to ring the sphenoid and teeth.

sections.body: Kruse believes the Maya understood something modern dentistry has lost. They set jade into their teeth, and in his reading this was not decoration but a solid-state device, a piece of crystal that works with the body's own electricity and light. It protected the teeth, grounded the skull and, he argues, helped the Maya stay clear-headed when the magnetic field over their land collapsed. He sees in it lessons for living through the present decline.

sections.heading: Builders for a weakening field
sections.body: Kruse says the Maya began among El Salvador's volcanoes and, as they moved north away from them, built pyramids to mimic volcanic flux, with observatories alongside that suggest they linked a magnetic field in the sky to their volcanoes and pyramids. He reads the pyramids as passive magnetic transducers that "pinned" proton spin as the planet's dipole weakened, "magnetic lighthouses" that held off a collapse into what he calls atavism (a slide back to older, simpler biology), and the Great Pyramid as a planetary deuterium filter rather than a tomb. He ties this to a physics finding of a universal magnetic field threading space, imaged by the LOFAR radio telescope, which he says fits his "Universal Stator" idea. The Maya, he adds, also found ways to bring that protection to individuals, and jade is his main example.

sections.heading: Jade in the teeth
sections.body:
Enamel and dentin, in his account, are biological semiconductors that manage the body's light. Teeth give off ultra-weak photon emission (UPE), the faint light living tissue releases, as a by-product of the living pulp. Translucent jade (nephrite or jadeite) acts as a crystal "dopant," an added material that changes how a semiconductor behaves: it captures ambient light and re-emits it, which he says recharges the tooth's light field and keeps the fluid in its fine tubules holding charge, so the tooth does not stagnate.

Jade and enamel are both piezoelectric, producing a charge when squeezed. Chewing therefore builds an electric field where jade, the Maya cement and enamel meet. That field, he says, keeps the water in the dentinal tubules structured (his "EZ" water), which blocks deuterium in saliva from reaching the blood through the tooth's pulp.

He thinks the antibiotic effect of the Maya cement was partly photodynamic, driven by light, not just chemical. By steadying the tooth's faint emission, jade turned the tooth into a "UV lighthouse" that kills microbes, keeps the pulp cells from switching to fermentation (the Warburg shift) and resists plaque biofilms, which he calls primitive atavistic colonies. Tribal Maya in El Salvador, he says, still keep the practice.

sections.heading: Grounding the skull
sections.body:
Because jade conducts better than damaged enamel, Kruse says it improves the skull's grounding and lets the brain dump excess charge and deuterium. In places where the field is declining, he suggests, this may help keep the spinal fluid's vortices turning, and even de-frag the fluid's structure through the sphenoid bone at the skull base without a cochlear or Neuralink-type implant. By contrast he sees plastic and mercury-amalgam fillings as insulators or antennas for wireless fields that dim the tooth's light.

He goes further for the incisor inlays. Jade there, he says, was an ancient form of TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) that let the Maya stay conscious when the South Atlantic Anomaly reached them after their Classic period, and it was critical for clearing the drag of deuterium's kinetic isotope effect, the slowing of reactions by heavier atoms. He calls jade the first auricular vagus nerve stimulator (VNS) and, in a Patreon post (CPC #87), the Maya's original "Neuralink" against the last magnetic excursion.

sections.heading: The sphenoid keystone
sections.body:
The bone at the center of all this is the sphenoid, the bat-shaped bone behind the eyes that Kruse calls the skull's keystone. It cradles the pituitary gland in a saddle-shaped hollow, forms the canal that carries the optic nerve and its dawn light signal, and passes the trigeminal nerve (the face's main nerve). Through the linked trigeminal and vagal circuits, he says, the way the teeth erupt and meet gives the brain a pressure map that primes the gut's emptying reflex and its bicarbonate drain, and the chewing muscles anchored to the sphenoid stir the fluids of the head. A sphenoid out of alignment kinks these nerves and leaves the vagus blind to the deuterium load.

He maps the arteries around the bone as antennas. The middle meningeal arteries near the temple act as high-frequency receivers, the internal carotids lying in a groove of the sphenoid couple it directly to the blood, and the basilar artery behind the clivus (the sloping bone at the skull base) carries direct current from the brain's melanin and water. Together, in his model, they lock the brain to the sun's short-wave infrared reset at 1878 nm.

A rhinoceros, he says, needs none of this. It is a simple, always-grounded, small-brained animal whose melanin-rich horn works as a passive, high-gain antenna. Humans have no horn, so we must set the sphenoid and the row of teeth ringing ourselves, with a hummed "M," to reach the same clarity. Jade in the teeth was, in this light, a way to make that dental array conduct and glow better.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His dental approach favors gold inlays over plastic composites and amalgam, deuterium depletion and light-driven repair; jade is his model for what a filling should do. Humming a low "M" is his everyday way to ring the sphenoid and teeth. Behind both sits his larger point: in a magnetic decline, conductive, light-handling natural materials in and around the skull help the brain keep shedding deuterium.

articles.title: Releasing lattice lock: Volcano Protocol, hypnosis and shoreline air
articles.summary: Kruse's routines for releasing lattice lock: a body-scale copy of the planet's volcanic response, a water-and-salt flush, hypnosis working from the top down, sunrise sea spray, water pressure, and daily upkeep.
keyPoints: Kruse calls stiff, deuterium-loaded body water "lattice lock" and offers routines to release it, mainly along the spine.
His Volcano Protocol pairs carbonated and deuterium-depleted water and sauna with a water jet and 40 Hz fork on the back, then sunrise grounding.
In his model hypnosis works top-down, sending a calming direct-current shift down the spinal cord before the fork and jet.
He says negative ions in breaking-wave spray at sunrise travel from the smell nerves to the gut and loosen the lock.
He frames release as daily upkeep, because a high deuterium load and weak field let the water stiffen again.

sections.body: "Lattice lock" is Kruse's name for body water that has turned stiff and deuterium-loaded (heavy hydrogen), jamming the cell's energy motor and leaving tissue rigid. He offers three routines to release it: the Volcano Protocol, hypnosis and sunrise shoreline air, backed by a water-and-salt flush. His main target is the spine, but he applies them to stiff, locked tissue wherever it appears.

sections.heading: What is being released
sections.body: In his model the lock builds when screens, Wi-Fi, jet lag and a poor local field stop the brain's nightly polarity flip and leave the spinal fluid deuterated. Proteins then fall out of solution as sticky webs, and the body binds nerve roots to the spinal sheath. He reads this as containment, not malfunction; nature, he says, does not make mistakes. Some people inherit a share of the load from their parents' deuterium-loaded germline, while others acquire it. Anesthesia, wireless exposure and chronic mouth breathing, he adds, speed the stiffening.

sections.heading: The Volcano Protocol
sections.body:
When Earth's field declines, he says, volcanoes release carbon dioxide that shields brains, and the Volcano Protocol copies that response at body scale. Because the planet no longer supplies a steady background signal, he argues, the body now needs active magnetic measures such as grounding on strongly magnetic ground, especially for people on the Pacific Rim. The protocol has three parts.

First, carbonated water paired with deuterium-depleted water, plus traditional sauna valued for the carbon dioxide it builds rather than its heat, creates a carbon dioxide–bicarbonate loop in the spinal fluid that works against deuterium.

Second, a high-power water jet on the mid and lower back (vertebrae T5–T12) with a 40 Hz tuning fork on the spine shears the coiled collagen of the spinal sheath. That produces a piezoelectric current (electricity made by mechanical stress) that, in his model, shakes deuterium loose from clumped nerve roots: a spinal "de-frag," his word for clearing deuterium and restoring order. A cranial version adds mastic gum and the fork on the hard palate.

Third, sunrise grounding in a magnetically pinned, low-latitude place supplies 380 nm violet light (read by neuropsin, a UV-A sensor in the eye and skin) and solar near-infrared. In his model this rebuilds the mitochondrial membrane's charge, keeps oxygen in its stable form and halts the binding process. The payoff he describes is freer spinal-fluid flow and a flexible heart rate variability (HRV, the beat-to-beat variation he uses as his gauge). He says anyone promising a timeline is lying.

sections.heading: Clearing the motor and flushing the pipes
sections.body:
Kruse pairs deuterium-depleted water (DDW) with hypertonic saline (salt water stronger than blood, 3% in his use) and UV light. He calls DDW clearing at the ATP motor itself: it keeps new deuterium out and removes the heavy-hydrogen "bridges" that let charge leak across the inner membrane. The saline is plumbing on the large scale. The salt surge, he says, pulls deuterated fluid out of the brain's chambers and pushes it down through the base of the brain into the spinal "exhaust."

He gives each part a role. Saline is the burst that clears the nerve-root sleeves and the venous spaces behind the eyes. DDW is the maintenance that stops deuterium returning, and cold is the final gear. Combined with UV light he calls it "tanning the interior": thinning the inner fluid until light signals reach the pineal and pituitary glands again. Lighter spinal fluid, he adds, is less dense, so it spins faster through the brain's channels and gains more lift.

sections.heading: Hypnosis
sections.body:
Kruse treats hypnosis not as relaxation but as a top-down amplifier. Trance shifts the cortex from fast rhythms into slower alpha and theta waves, mimicking the start of the nightly polarity flip; he cites Becker's 1961 work and Bukalo's study of nerves firing in reverse. In his model it sends a direct-current shift down the spinal cord that lowers resistance around the nerves and clears "electronic dams" holding the lowest nerve roots.

Slow belly breathing during trance raises carbon dioxide into bicarbonate, which thins the spinal fluid, and calm suppresses cortisol surges. That is why he wants the fork and water jet applied straight afterward, while the person is still deeply relaxed.

sections.heading: Shoreline air
sections.body: Breaking waves electrify their spray, a process called the Lenard effect. Heavier droplets keep a positive charge and fall back, while the finest spray carries a negative charge, so the shore is blanketed in negative ions. Breathed at sunrise, he says, these ions stimulate the thinly insulated smell nerves, and the charge travels down a brainstem-to-gut nerve tract to the gut's nerve centers. There it neutralizes "rusted melanin" (degraded pigment debris), restores structured water and turns a rigid HRV flexible. Any net negative-ion exposure counts, including falling water; ion-poor indoor air is the reverse.

sections.heading: Pressure and the quantum nudge
sections.body:
Water pressure is another lever. The hydrostatic squeeze of diving, he says, presses heavy water out of the narrow spaces between tissues, a process he calls "mechanical fractionation."

He also borrows the Woodward effect from propulsion physics, the proposal that an object whose internal energy changes while it is shaken picks up a net push without fuel, and says the body's fluid vortices do the same. The burst of faint light that cold or sunlight releases makes deuterium "silt" briefly lose its grip, a "quantum nudge" that lets the vagus nerve and the stomach's pumping flush it away. Late-morning UV-A, around 11 a.m., is his finishing polish, shaking loose the last deuterium from the melanin traps of the skin and gut.

sections.heading: Why relief doesn't last
sections.body:
Kruse explains why massage or vibration relief often fades within about two days. Pressure supplies the energy to break heavy-hydrogen bonds and briefly loosen the tissue, but while the deuterium load stays high and the field stays weak, the water stiffens back to its locked state. The same rule covers a successful de-frag: return to a bad environment and the lock comes back.

So he frames this as ongoing upkeep, the way a mechanic services a car. His daily "fractionation" maintenance is sunrise light, bare feet on magnetic volcanic soil or sand, low-deuterium water as a flush, and stronger magnetic measures when the lock is advanced.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His Volcano Protocol and spinal lattice lock protocols combine carbonated and deuterium-depleted water, sauna, the water jet with the 40 Hz fork on T5–T12, and sunrise grounding on pinned volcanic ground, while avoiding flights across time zones. Progress is tracked by HRV in deep sleep. His hypnosis de-frag starts with learning hypnosis or self-hypnosis; fifteen minutes before a session he drinks a glass of deuterium-depleted or carbonated water, does the session grounded in a pinned place, and applies the fork and jet right afterward. His shoreline wave breathing means breathing breaking-wave spray every morning with the sunrise. He adds regular diving pressure and late-morning UV-A where possible, ranks peptides as temporary, and pairs 3% saline with deuterium-depleted water and UV as a gentler osmotic reset. Morning infrared light, grounding and a good location are what he calls the lasting fix.

articles.title: Time, mind and consciousness
articles.summary: Kruse ties the felt speed of time, memory, wisdom, belief and consciousness to light, water and oxygen's spin in the brain, and casts consciousness as a brief delay the neocortex builds into incoming light.
keyPoints: Kruse says time feels compressed when the thalamus's mitochondria stall, so inner processing lags behind the outside world.
In his model consciousness is a few-millisecond delay the neocortex builds into incoming light, letting a mammal choose its response.
He says consciousness needs structured cell water, 380 nm violet light and carbon dioxide working together, with water as the gate.
He treats beliefs, habits and mood as imprints of the field and the environment, which the mind cannot simply override.
His time-expansion routine pairs novelty and questioning with fixing light, water, magnetism and the company you keep.

sections.body: Kruse treats the mind as a physical readout of light, water and magnetism. In his model, how fast time seems to pass, how well we remember, what we believe and even whether we are conscious all depend on the electrical state of brain cells. Fixing that state, not willpower or drugs, is how he says to change the mind.

sections.heading: Why time seems to speed up
sections.body:
When days blur together and life seems to rush past, Kruse calls it "time compression." In his model the mitochondria of the thalamus (the brain's relay and pacing center) are stalled in Marcus inversion, a state where electron flow jams because it is being pushed too hard. Inner processing then lags behind the outside world, and the body's clocks run fast even though wall-clock time has not changed. This, he says, is how people "lose time" as Earth's field weakens.

Memory depends on contrast. A vivid memory, he says, needs a sharp burst of reactive oxygen and a flash of light inside the cell to switch on the genes for BDNF (a growth factor that builds connections between nerve cells). Monotony flattens that signal and memories smear together.

He also says biological time is manufactured. Light itself experiences no time; time appears when matter slows light down and when magnetic and electrical resistance at Complexes I–III steps excited electrons into the body. That proximal signal, in his account, reaches the PER2 clock network in the retina before it is rewritten as a biomechanical and then electrical message for the brain's master clock. Oxygen's spin sets the direction: reactive "singlet" oxygen subtracts biological time and stable "triplet" oxygen adds it.

He locates a later delay in the neocortex, its six-layered outer sheet. Its layers, in his model, act as a delay line that holds incoming light signals for a few milliseconds, so the animal perceives time rather than mere brightness. That short buffer is what he calls consciousness: the step from a reptile simply driven by light to a mammal that can choose its response.

He gives it an origin story. When the sky cleared after the impact that ended the dinosaurs, small night-active mammals were hit by a surge of solar energy, and the survivors routed the excess into a larger neocortex. Intelligence, in his telling, is a by-product of a brain built to slow time and protect DNA, a "temporal damper." Long childhoods are calibration time, in which the eye and the brain's master clock learn to match internal light signals against the sun.

sections.heading: Time as schedule
sections.body: Kruse borrows two Greek words for time. Chronos is ticking clock time; Kairos is the right moment. DNA, in his picture, is the Chronos side, an inert parts list, while the body clock is the Kairos side, deciding when each gene runs. Without that timing he calls DNA a "seized library." He frames each day as an entry in a ledger. A day lived in step with light and dark adds a coherent "block" to health's chain, while leaning on tech substitutes for sun and dark splits the chain. Lost time is inflation charged against your lifespan.

sections.heading: What consciousness needs
sections.body:
In Kruse's model consciousness needs three coupled inputs: cell water in its structured, charge-holding state; 380 nm violet light reaching neuropsin (a UV-A sensor in the eye and skin); and carbon dioxide as a buffer. Because water, not microtubules, gates the process, he reads recent work on a 71-terahertz water vibration as undercutting Hameroff and Penrose's Orch-OR theory, and calls microtubule theories that leave out the water "dry biophysics." Deuterium in that water, he says, adds mass that anchors the tubule's proteins so they cannot vibrate fast enough to hold memory.

Anesthesia shows the same rule. He credits Robert Becker with first linking physics to consciousness, citing his finding that the body's direct-current polarity reverses under anesthesia. Anesthetic gases, in Kruse's account, disorder the water around proteins and scramble electron spin in melanin and the final enzyme of the energy chain. Without spin-sorted electrons the brain's forward arrow of time falls apart, and conscious processing dissolves while automatic processes carry on. Sunlight is his counter: UV-A and red and near-infrared light supply ordered light that realigns spins and restarts the eye's clock.

He reads Nikola Tesla's remark that his brain was only a receiver literally: the brain picks up thought rather than generating it. A 2026 preprint on weak, patterned stimulation convinces him the brain responds to pattern, not power, which in his model is why wireless signals and evening blue light harm thinking.

sections.heading: Wisdom needs quiet
sections.body:
Kruse ties wisdom to timing inside the cell. He says the brain needs about 7.2 seconds free of collisions with heavy hydrogen for its electrons to cross into the stable triplet state, and a noisy, deuterium-loaded interior never gets that quiet. Thinking then drops into an older, survival-driven mode, like an operating system downgraded to DOS. He reads today's widespread apathy and brain fog as people who are "cognitively lattice locked." Waking with the answer to yesterday's problem shows the brain reached coherence overnight.

Logic, in his model, runs on linear optical pathways suited to getting from A to B, while imagination runs on nonlinear ones, so questioning yourself and others does more for growth than repeating what you already know.

sections.heading: Belief, mood and the field
sections.body:
Beliefs and habits, to Kruse, are field imprints, recorded the way cooling volcanic basalt locks in Earth's magnetism; he calls habits "magnetic craters." Dread is a readout of cells melting down, and brain fog is the thalamus losing its spin-filtered current. Low mood, in his model, follows a collapse of energy density, so he clears deuterium first and then adds sun and grounding rather than nudging one chemical.

Ignorance, in his "Rhino Creed," tracks dopamine, and the hardest blind spot is the light people are missing, UV and infrared.

He does not think the mind can simply override a bad environment. It can break the rules, but pays in entropy, and bad thinking is meant as feedback. That is why he rejects Joe Dispenza's feel-good approach: first feel what the environment is telling you and move somewhere better, then expect to feel good. In a magnetic decline the six people closest to you matter more, because they can tell when your dopamine is leading you astray. Speech follows the same rules: a grounded, sunlit speaker spin-aligns the oxygen in the airway so words carry, while an ungrounded speaker under fluorescent light produces "empty words."

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His time-expansion protocol pairs novelty with environmental repair. He recommends new routes, hobbies and learning, journaling or mindfulness, asking questions rather than repeating answers, and slow, deep breathing, alongside fixing light, water and magnetism, living each day in step with light and dark, and choosing your closest company with care. For prayer or intention: ground first, cut nearby EMF and avoid fluorescent light. For brain fog he prescribes dawn barefoot on surf, sand or dew, sunrise on bare eyes without glasses or contacts, and routers off at night. After anesthesia he favors recovering in sunlight. Where the place itself is the problem, he puts moving ahead of mindset work.

articles.title: Drugs and supplements as "atomic impurities"
articles.summary: Kruse says foreign compounds add electron traps to the body's semiconductors, that some drugs only seem to work in a deuterium-loaded body, and that pills skip the light-driven steps that make the body's own versions work, leaving "isotopic debt" behind good-looking lab values.
keyPoints: Kruse says foreign compounds act like stray atoms in a chip, trapping electrons in the mitochondrial membrane instead of passing them on.
In his model some drugs only seem to help because the body is already deuterium-loaded, and turn harmful once the water is restored.
He argues pills skip the light-driven steps that make the body's own versions work, so good lab values can hide "isotopic debt."
He says synthetic molecules scatter heavy isotopes and wrong-handed forms where living enzymes would place them carefully.
In place of pills he puts morning sun, grounding, cold, removal of AC fields and a good location.

sections.body: Kruse argues that most drugs and supplements do more harm than good because of what they do to the cell's electrical wiring. In his model the proteins of the mitochondrial membrane behave like semiconductors, passing electrons along a chain. A foreign compound acts like a stray atom in a computer chip: it traps electrons instead of passing them on. He prefers a chip-fab picture to a music metaphor: a semiconductor clean room fails if any wrong atomic mass lands on the board, and the cell's ubiquitination machinery is that clean room's janitor. When Earth's field is slowing metabolism, he says, peptides that ramp transcription floor a seized engine — worst under the South Atlantic Anomaly or in a desert.

sections.heading: Electron traps
sections.body:
Borrowing Ramon Sun's term, he calls such compounds "atomic impurities." His list includes GLP-1 drugs, statins, synthetic peptides, NMN and other NAD⁺ precursors, metformin, rapamycin and Epitalon. Each adds traps to a misaligned network, deepens the blood–brain-barrier leak and speeds energy loss as heat. He labels statins and GLP-1 drugs "magnetic strippers," and says no drug can fix a bad location.

In network terms, each heavy foreign atom raises the barrier between nodes, so an overdriven node still fires but its energy cannot travel on. It turns into heat and leaks out as "alien" ultra-weak light, and the body stops working as a resonant cavity and becomes a "pressure cooker."

NAD⁺, a molecule that shuttles electrons in energy production, is his clearest example. He says the ratio of NAD⁺ to NADH simply reflects the membrane's charge, so it rises without pills when you remove AC fields and add morning sun and cold. Since whole-blood NAD⁺ stays flat with age, he says, NR and NMN push the system rather than repair it.

Injected peptides cause a similar problem in his view. The body cuts its own peptides from a larger precursor on a light-timed schedule set by the brain's master clock. Flooding the blood with synthetic versions reads as a surplus, so the clock shuts down native production and the user ends up dependent on the needle. He calls Melanotan, an injected tanning peptide, a "fake battery": it forces a tan without the voltage or isotope clearance real sun brings.

sections.heading: Drugs that only seem to work
sections.body:
Kruse argues that several popular drugs help only because the body is already deuterium-loaded. Metformin works by slowing Complex I, the first step of the energy chain, which he says makes sense only when the cell's NADH carries heavy hydrogen. Once the cell's water is restored and deuterium is kept out of the chain, metformin becomes a poison. He applies the same logic to statins.

Methylene blue is his "ungrounded quantum bypass." It hands electrons from NADH almost straight to the end of the chain, skipping two steps. In a cell whose water is degraded, or a place where the field is unstable, he says this forces current through a system that cannot contain it. He calls its focus boost a brief rush that clears no deuterium.

Creatine, in his image, is coal shoveled into a steam engine whose pipes are clogged. Fluorinated antidepressants he calls "deuterium bombs," since fluorine is the most electron-hungry element; he says they thicken tissue fluid and lower its ability to hold charge.

sections.heading: Pills that skip the light-driven steps
sections.body:
Kruse says pills skip steps that sunlight is supposed to run in mitochondria. Melatonin and vitamin D pills bypass the light-driven routes that make the body's own versions work. A vitamin D pill comes without the companions that arrive with sunlight, the faint light emissions and the infrared thinning of the blood, so the body cannot put the vitamin to work in its DNA-guarding systems. Blood levels look ideal in a body that is still "welded shut." Magnesium helps at first, but a cell running at low voltage cannot hold onto it, his "missing dopant" problem.

He likens supplements to photoshopping a bank statement: they give a false sense of security while "isotopic debt," the slow build-up of deuterium, keeps growing until the body goes bankrupt.

He goes on through the list. Chronic vitamin C blocks melanin renewal, supplemental copper damages the body's own melanin, and aspirin is a mitochondrial toxin that lowers melanin. He does accept sulforaphane and allicin as short-term aids. Hair dye and bleach make his list too: he treats hair as a waveguide for light, and says dyes suppress the enzyme that makes melanin, "shaving the antenna."

sections.heading: Fever, antioxidants and hospital fluids
sections.body:
For about 25 years Kruse has rejected the antioxidant story. Radicals and oxygen, he says, are fuel for the cell's light-driven engine; the real problem is a weak magnetic field that cannot contain them. Isolated ascorbic acid in a low-oxygen body can turn pro-oxidant and drain glutathione, while whole-food vitamin C comes with flavonoids that let it recycle itself.

Fever, in his model, is a repair program, a "hypothalamic de-frag" that uses infrared heat to speed enzyme repair. Acetaminophen breaks it, because its breakdown product uses up glutathione.

He says MRI and CT contrast agents enter the brain and stay, and calls avoiding gadolinium one of his most important long-term rules, since a contrast scan can pin deuterium back in the brainstem after someone has cleared it. He lists thyroid hormone replacement, hyperbaric oxygen, supplemental oxygen and ozone as risky. By contrast he calls Lactated Ringer's, the IV fluid he used as a surgeon, the hospital's "stealth" deuterium-depleting fluid.

sections.heading: The isotope problem
sections.body:
Isotopes add a second layer. Citing Cameron Borg, Kruse says living enzymes place light hydrogen exactly where electrons and protons must tunnel and park deuterium in harmless spots. Chemical synthesis scatters heavy atoms at random, so even a "deuterium-depleted" pill can put a heavy atom on a working hinge. Whole food eaten in sunlight lets the body filter isotopes smoothly; concentrated pills force it to spend energy ejecting mismatched atoms. Handedness matters the same way: a wrong-handed molecule behaves like deuterium, breaking symmetry and making the brain's 40 Hz clock stutter.

Lithium is his sharpest case, a "subatomic monkey wrench." Natural lithium mixes two isotopes with different nuclear spins, and he says the mixed signal jams the thalamus, which he describes as an FM radio locking the body clock to Earth and Sun.

sections.heading: Reflexivity
sections.body: He frames the whole category with "biological reflexivity," borrowed from George Soros's idea that investors move the markets they bet on. Every drug, and every biomarker a person chases, changes the biology it targets. The supplement trade thrives, in his view, because a shortcut is easier to sell than telling people to leave their indoor, wireless-filled routines for the light.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: His "pills he avoids" list includes oral vitamin D3, chronic vitamin C, NMN, NR and NAD⁺ injections, metformin, rapamycin, statins and aspirin. It also covers GLP-1 drugs, Epitalon and sleep or repair peptides (he names BPC-157, CJC-1295, Ipamorelin and Pinealon), Melanotan, melatonin pills and chronic magnesium pills. Isolated antioxidants, copper supplements, lithium and modafinil round it out, along with methylene blue, creatine, fluorinated antidepressants, acetaminophen for fever, thyroid hormone replacement, gadolinium contrast where it can be avoided, and hyperbaric or supplemental oxygen. He adds hair dye and bleach. In their place he puts the inputs he says the pills imitate: morning sun, grounding, cold, removal of AC fields and a good location.

articles.title: His critique of "centralized medicine"
articles.summary: Kruse argues that modern medicine dropped physics (and even sound) for biochemistry and drugs, recast the sun as a hazard, measures too late to catch light's effects, and urges members to verify for themselves and act on light, field and ground.
keyPoints: Kruse says centralized medicine built itself on biochemistry and drugs, ignoring a deeper layer of light, water, magnetism and membrane voltage.
He traces the split to the 1910 Flexner Report, which in his account tied medical training to a chemistry-set model of the body.
In his view money flows to patentable molecules and diagnostics, while the high-leverage base of light, field, water and rhythm is neglected.
He argues lab values arrive too late, because light reshapes biology millions of times faster than any hormone shift can be measured.
He urges people to verify rather than outsource their thinking, and to act first on location, light and grounding.

sections.body: Kruse uses "centralized medicine" for the mainstream system of drugs, guidelines and institutions, and argues it has built itself on the wrong layer of biology. Beneath biochemistry, in his model, runs a deeper operating system of light, water, magnetism and membrane voltage, and medicine was trained not to look at it. Understanding that history is, for him, the reason to take health into your own hands.

sections.heading: How the split happened
sections.body:
He traces it to the 1910 Flexner Report, funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller foundations. He grants that it improved medical training, but says it tied accreditation to a chemistry-set model of the body. That pushed out biophysics, naturopathy and chiropractic and gave rise to a drug industry that barely existed before. Illness was redefined as a local chemical shortage rather than a failure of field, spin and structure, his "pharma over physics." In his image, molecules are only the letters of biology; the light signal is the sentence and the spin of oxygen and metals is the meaning.

Sound was lost in the same shift. Hospitals built before 1900 had bells, and he says taking them out was an economic decision dressed up as science. In his reading their tones helped the nervous system shed deuterium (heavy hydrogen), and the Flexner era swapped that "acoustic medicine" for a chemical monopoly.

Dropping biophysics, he says, is what made drugs that slow the mitochondrial energy chain look necessary. It also hid the fact that the chain's final enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase, makes deuterium-depleted water so the cell can run on light hydrogen.

In physics language, he says medicine manages only the "kinetic" side of the body, calories and pills, and ignores the "potential" side: the membrane's charge, the state of cell water and the magnetic spin of the ATP motor. When that potential has collapsed from too little red and UV-A light or too much deuterium, more food only feeds a shorted circuit.

sections.heading: Following the money
sections.body:
Money follows the same split. He describes a health pyramid in which investment flows to drugs and diagnostics at the top, while the base with the most leverage gets little: light, magnetism, deuterium, water and daily rhythm. Medicine targets molecules, he says, because only molecules can be patented, and consensus then forms around what can be sold. Consensus is not science in his view; dissenters such as Ignaz Semmelweis get branded cranks, and prizes reward ideas that sell drugs.

The same incentives run through the wellness world. The longevity industry (David Sinclair, Aubrey de Grey and the Valter Longo fasting school) and diet experts (Ben Bikman, Peter Attia, Andrew Huberman) stay trapped in biochemical models and ignore light. Health influencers who sell subscriptions, supplements and drug or peptide regimens are, to him, "time thieves" who build dependency. He also warns that AI chatbots default to consensus and flatter their users.

sections.heading: Blind spots he names
sections.body:
Biochemistry, in his view, assumes Earth's magnetic field never changes, so its textbook diagrams fail once oxygen flips into its reactive state. The same mindset assumes slow, steady change and cannot see magnetic excursions. Doctors themselves, he argues, live in the same indoor, deuterium-loaded state as everyone else, so they cannot perceive the problem and reach for more drugs.

Lab testing is another blind spot. When light reaches the retina, its pigment molecule changes shape in about 200 femtoseconds, which he puts at roughly ten million times faster than a nerve impulse. Light has therefore reshaped your biology long before any hormone or "chemical imbalance" shows up, so a lab value records what he calls a "photonic crime" that is already over. That is why he says hormone panels cannot steer a fix for a light problem.

He sees the same error in wireless safety rules. Heat-based limits, he says, resemble the "ultraviolet catastrophe" of classical physics around 1900, applying smooth reasoning to a system that works in discrete steps: the harm comes through electron spin, not heating. Life divides its activity into day and night, which he calls biology's Planck constant, and an always-on world forces a continuous pattern onto it.

Medicine, in his phrase, sees a clog where there is a stall. His mechanic's analogy is a car with its exhaust welded shut: pressure builds until the head gasket blows, however good the fuel. Wireless exposure and missing UV and infrared, he says, weld shut the vagus nerve's bicarbonate drain, so deuterium backs up into the brain, inner ear and gut. The mindset also builds human guidelines on nocturnal rodents, animals with inverted daily rhythms and different skulls and eyes, his "nocturnal mouse fallacy." Birds, active by day, are to him the better model: like us they use the morning sun to prime the energy motor and melanin to protect their water. Studying human biology in mice, he says, is like repairing a 747 from a submarine manual. Drug trials, in his reading, share one uncontrolled variable: every participant lives indoors under wireless fields and drinks ordinary deuterium-rich water, so any drug that slows mitochondria can look protective.

sections.heading: How the sun became the enemy
sections.body: His longest history concerns sunlight. He traces sun worship to the Sumerians, a legal right to sunlight in Justinian's Roman code, and the 1903 Nobel Prize awarded to Niels Finsen for light therapy. From the 1980s the message flipped: block all UV and take a pill instead of the source. To him it is telling that the sun was recast as a hazard in the same century the supplement was patented, and he reads Hawaii's 2026 ban on six sunscreen chemicals as the first official sign that we have been poisoning our own light antenna.

sections.heading: Cautionary tales
sections.body: His stories share one moral: institutions protect shareholders and products before people. The Radium Girls, dial painters of the 1910s and 1920s, were told radium paint was harmless while executives handled it behind screens, and their lawsuit helped create workplace safety law. Harvey Wiley's "Poison Squad," twelve volunteers fed food preservatives for five years, forced the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act, and with today's constant low-dose additives he says "we are all the twelve men." He traces anti-meat advice to a religious vision rather than a trial, and keeps a timeline of confident advice that aged badly, from industry reassurance about smoking to low-fat guidelines. The lesson he draws is that a doctor's confidence is itself a risk.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Kruse's prescriptions are about mindset rather than a protocol. "Verify, don't outsource your thinking," and start from wherever your own understanding is. Because institutions replaced a moral "should" with a legal "must," and because non-clinicians now dictate what doctors may prescribe, he treats refusing to comply with an ungrounded establishment as an ethical duty. He does leave centralized medicine one role, as an acute toolkit of drugs, fluids and procedures for genuine emergencies, with root-cause work following the physics. And he asks members to accept "Personal Quantum Solvency": food, exercise and drugs cannot fix a changing magnetic environment, so act on location, light and grounding.

articles.title: Hot pepper, eucalyptus, lavender and sweat
articles.summary: Kruse uses chili heat, eucalyptus cold, the scent of lavender and old-fashioned sweating as cheap ways to push deuterium out through the glands, skin and nerves, and adds a caution about needling skin that is already loaded.
keyPoints: Kruse treats chili heat, eucalyptus cold, lavender scent and sweating as cheap levers that push deuterium out through glands, skin and nerves.
In his model capsaicin's burn fires the bicarbonate flush and sweating, while eucalyptus imitates cold shock without an ice bath.
He calls lavender a "software patch" for the thalamus, grounding it in Luca Turin's vibrational theory of smell.
He reads salt lost in sweat as a deliberate isotope purge, trading sodium to tow heavy water out.
He would clear the skin's deuterium load with sun and grounding before relying on acupuncture needles.

sections.body: Kruse treats a few everyday sensations as levers on the body's exhaust system. Chili heat, the cooling bite of eucalyptus, the scent of lavender and a good sweat each, in his model, help push deuterium (heavy hydrogen) out through the glands, the skin and the nerves. None of them needs a prescription.

sections.heading: Heat: capsaicin
sections.body: Capsaicin, the compound that makes chili peppers hot, switches on TRPV1, the heat-and-pain sensor in nerve endings. Kruse points to cultures that eat very hot peppers, in parts of Mexico, Thailand and the Caribbean, and explains the effect in his own terms. The burn sets off a calcium and sodium "voltage spike." It makes the salivary glands and pancreas pour out their secretions, pushing out the roughly two liters of bicarbonate a day that he treats as the gut's isotope exhaust, and it brings on sweating, which in his account dumps deuterium through the skin by way of the cooling system built by the sweat-gland gene EDAR. The heat-shock response it triggers, he says, also switches on MITF, the master switch for making melanin, so pigment gets rebuilt. A very hot dose, in his view, can jolt the brain out of the "cell danger response" (the body's defensive lockdown) and restart a stalled gut through the gastrocolic reflex, the urge to empty the bowel after eating.

sections.heading: Cold: eucalyptus
sections.body:
Eucalyptus works on the opposite sensor. Its main compound, cineole, stimulates TRPM8, the cold receptor. Breathed in, or applied over the path of the vagus nerve, it imitates cold shock and the mammalian dive reflex without an ice bath, and Kruse says it quiets the overactive AMPA-receptor "noise" of a light-starved brain. He credits it with thinning the thick secretions of the glands, clearing the sinuses (and so, in his model, the teeth that act as the skull's antenna), and lowering GDF-15, a stress signal from struggling mitochondria. He ties it to work from the Blau lab on the PGE2 and 15-PGDH signaling loop, which he says eucalyptus helps restart.

Paired with capsaicin, it becomes what he calls a "Quantum Contrast Flush." Alternating hot and cold makes the small vessels clamp and relax in turn, and that pumping, he says, squeezes deuterium-laden fluid out of the fine tubules of the teeth and the ducts that carry bicarbonate.

sections.heading: Scent: lavender
sections.body: Kruse calls lavender, through its compounds linalool and linalyl acetate, a "software patch" for the thalamus. In his account it changes how AMPA receptors switch off, lowers background noise in the brainstem, raises the calmer alpha and theta brain rhythms, thins the water at cell surfaces and helps clear deuterium. He grounds this in Luca Turin's vibrational theory of smell: the nose identifies a molecule by how it vibrates, sensed through electron tunneling, which is why, on that theory, a deuterium-swapped version of the same molecule (deuterated acetophenone, for example) smells different. Kruse says Turin, rather than Richard Axel, deserved the Nobel Prize for explaining smell.

sections.heading: Sweat and salt
sections.body:
Sweating is his oldest example. He says the temazcal, the traditional sweat lodge of Mesoamerica, was how shamanic cultures depleted deuterium, and he accepts sweating in a geothermal sauna for the same reason.

He reads salt loss through sweat the same way. Losing salt, in his model, is an emergency cooling and isotope purge rather than a defect: the body gives up charge, in the form of sodium, to shed mass, in the form of deuterium, using sodium to tow water out osmotically. Humans, he says, are the only primates that separated sweating from panting. Salt-losing traits most likely arose in the deuterium-rich tropics, where water and the sugars of tropical fruit run heavy, because constant sun recharges the body's "battery" and lets it afford the leak. A film of salt on the skin may also act as a conductive shield against electromagnetic interference, protecting the thalamus's 40 Hz clock.

sections.heading: A caution about needles
sections.body: The skin is also where Kruse places a warning about acupuncture. A needle has to pass through the skin to reach the fascia, the connective sheets beneath it. If the dermis is loaded with deuterium, he says, that mass ruins the needle's gain as an antenna and acupuncture can leave a person worse.

sections.heading: In practice
sections.body: Kruse's suggestions are simple: hot peppers with meals, eucalyptus breathed in or applied along the vagus nerve's path (he likes it with a hummed "M"), alternating hot and cold, lavender in the air for a noisy brain, regular sweating in a sauna or sweat lodge, and real salt to replace what sweat removes. He would clear the skin's deuterium load, with sun and grounding, before relying on needles.
